records.title: Building a Digital Media Platform for the European Public Sphere
records.authors: Christoph Neuberger
records.abstract: Introduction The currently dominant digital platforms are associated with many negative effects on democratic societies, such as disinformation, hate speech, and propaganda. In the case of X, the platform has become a personal megaphone for its owner Elon Musk. The “Great Sysop” has gained considerable power over public opinion formation and is promoting “platform illiberalism” (Magalhães et al.). However, Twitter has also added valuable features that have enhanced public communication, particulary in journalism, which is the focus of the present article. Journalists used Twitter for purposes such as live reporting, news aggregation, including citizens as sources, organising debates (Artwick), and fact checking (Coddington et al.). Hermida coined the term “ambient journalism” to describe journalism’s role on Twitter as a novel “awareness system”. In 2014, a newsroom survey in Germany compared the use of different platforms in journalism (Neuberger et al.). Twitter was most often used for brief breaking news and real-time reporting. Editorial staff also utilised Twitter and Facebook relatively often for investigation and monitoring. Twitter was used especially to contact elite sources, such as experts and prominent people, and for monitoring their public appearances. Twitter and Facebook were the preferred platforms for user participation in journalism. Twitter served as a testing ground for new forms of journalism. But this is all history. These achievements have been lost since Elon Musk took over the platform. This raises the questions: how should a common good-oriented platform be designed and governed? What lessons can be learned from the journalistic adaptation of Twitter? I will address these questions by focussing on the transnational European public sphere. European Public Sphere as Goal The philosopher Jürgen Habermas (Für Europa), who passed away in March 2026, continued to advocate for European autonomy, integration, and democratisation, particularly in the context of today's polycrisis. He believed that establishing a common European public sphere by transnationalising the many national public spheres is essential (Habermas, Demokratie 188–91). But the European public sphere still has significant shortcomings (e.g., Brüggemann and Kleinen-von Königslöw; Brüggemann et al.). There is a lack of European media, audiences interested in European issues, and European perspectives in national media. Europeanisation is particularly evident in the vertical dimension (“looking towards Brussels”), but less so in the horizontal dimension. Looking beyond national borders at other national discourses is therefore crucial here. Another weakness is the low citizen participation in the European public sphere. The question of a European public sphere has regained importance in recent years. In light of the current geopolitical situation, the European Union (EU) is striving for greater digital sovereignty. This concept emphasises state authority over the Internet, replacing the earlier concept of “multistakeholderism”, which viewed the Internet as a distinct, decentralised, and transnational space beyond the reach of politics (Pohle and Santianello). The call for digital sovereignty encompasses not only the technical and economic dimension, but also the political and cultural dimension. Digital sovereignty “must not be conflated with isolation or protectionism, in the European context, it can be described as the capacity of being independent while remaining open to collaboration and committed to shared values such as transparency, democracy, and the rule of law” (Bria et al. 10). European values are often cited as the goal of digital sovereignty (e.g., Di Marco et al.; Kagermann and Wilhelm; Roberts et al.), but are not precisely defined. The EU is often criticised for over-regulating platforms and AI, hindering innovation and competitiveness. However, there are serious doubts as to whether this criticism is valid (Bradford, False Choice). Nevertheless, the EU must not only regulate, but also provide better platforms. This requires a change in mindset: regulation only defines the minimum normative requirements that must be met in every case. This negative approach must then be complemented by a positive one that describes how platforms can promote the common good. The EU could offer a more appealing alternative to the libertarian approach of the US and the authoritarian approach of China (Bradford, Digital Empires). Public Sphere and Public Value But how can the common good be defined? In the media sector, it is usually referred to as “public value”. This management concept was introduced by Mark H. Moore in his seminal book Creating Public Value. It was intended as a practical framework for public sector management, offering an alternative to the market-oriented, neo-liberal “new public management” and its premise that the public good is simply the sum of individual consumer interests. In contrast to this market-oriented view, the public value concept focusses on contributions to society’s common good beyond individual self-interest (Alford and Hughes 132; Moore, “Reflections” 366–9). The BBC adopted it in its programmatic statement Building Public Value. In this statement, public value was defined through three “public principles” (universality, fairness and equity, accountability) and five “public purposes” (democratic value, cultural and creative value, educational value, social and community value, global value) (7–8). A recent paper, Creating and Measuring Dynamic Public Value at the BBC, distinguishes between individual value, social value, and industrial value (Mazzucato et al. 23–8). The BBC’s public value test for public broadcasting outlets has been adopted by many EU countries (Collins; Donders). Some scholars have criticised a lack of clarity about what public value means substantially (e.g., Benington 42–6; Collins 175). Others have argued that public value cannot be defined “in some absolute sense” (Alford and Hughes 133) because public value must be, at least partially, open to the outcomes of democratic political processes (Alford and O’Flynn 175–8; Benington 233–4). The concept of hybrid common good offers a solution for these contradictory expectations (Blum; Neuberger, Auftrag). According to this approach, the common good comprises a substantive component consisting of liberal-democratic values to be realised in the value creation process, alongside public discourse as procedural component, in which those values are interpreted and concretised. These values are the “guardrails”, setting the boundaries for possible outcomes of the democratic public discourse, and also the standards for the discourse itself. How can the European values be defined more precisely? One obvious option is to derive them from normative theories of democracy. Several proposals have been made as to how normative theories of democracy can be applied to the public sphere and journalism (e.g., Christians et al. 95–105, 125–7; Ferree et al.; Gerhards; Martinsen; McQuail; Strömbäck). While these typologies differ, the theories agree that the media should at least create a common public sphere and a shared body of knowledge on current topics of public interest. Both are necessary prerequisites for the formation of individual and collective opinion. Valid and shared knowledge requires news production to be based on journalistic standards and to allow freedom of information and equal access to knowledge. However, beyond this, the theories make different demands regarding the process of opinion formation. Deliberative theory sets higher normative expectations for discourse progression than liberal and participatory theory (Martinsen). It demands a rational, respectful, and domination-free discourse in which the persuasiveness of the better argument—in the best case—leads to consensus. In summary, nine values of the public sphere can be derived from theories of democracy, whose normative expectations partially overlap: news and discourse quality, freedom, equality, diversity, power symmetry, criticism and control, security, and integration (Neuberger, Öffentlichkeit). Initiatives to Build a European Media Platform A more democratic digital public sphere cannot be achieved simply by regulating existing platform and AI companies. It is equally important to create media platforms and AI applications that are oriented towards the common good as an alternative to the commercial offerings that currently dominate the market. Although Habermas acknowledged the potential of the digital public sphere to contribute to the emancipation of citizens, he viewed the Internet as an “ambivalent explosive force” (Habermas, New Structural 35). He missed a “substitute for the professional selection and discursive examination of contents based on accepted cognitive standards” (38–39) on these platforms. Since 2017, there has been an ongoing discussion about the idea of a European media platform oriented towards the common good that would fulfil European values, create a European public sphere, and strengthen Europe’s digital sovereignty. Ulrich Wilhelm, the director of the Bavarian Broadcasting Corporation (Bayerischer Rundfunk), was the first and strongest advocate of this idea. He expressed concern that “Europe is in danger of losing digital sovereignty over its defining values” (Wilhelm 15; translated by the author). Van Dijck, Poell, and de Waal (146) outlined a “value-centric design of the platform society”, which should realise “public values” such as safety, privacy, transparency, accuracy, democratic control, quality, accessibility, comprehensiveness, equality, inclusiveness, fair treatment, responsibility, and accountability (139–41). Hillje (133–60) proposed four elements for a “Platform Europe”: a European newsroom and a European news service, opportunities for citizens to participate, a cultural connection representing Europe's diversity and common “European Way of Life”, and apps for citizens to take action and interact. Another plan proposed the creation of a European infrastructure for public service media and other media, as well as for science, culture, and citizens (Kagermann and Wilhelm). What has been achieved until now? Not much. Several proposals have been made to create a European media platform. The Council for European Public Space, an NGO, has developed a draft for a decentralised platform for trustworthy news called “Delphi” (Pfeffer). The Public Spaces Incubator (PSI) brings together public service media from different countries to work together to develop platforms for better public dialogue. The PSI toolkit will be made publicly available as open-source software by 2027. The European Cultural Foundation develops and supports cultural initiatives that foster “belonging, solidarity, and democratic values—building connections across Europe and empowering communities to shape a shared future.” It presented the draft for European Digital Public Spaces back in 2020. France and Germany intend to expand their joint cultural television channel arte into a European media platform (Der Beauftragte der Bundesregierung für Kultur und Medien). In 2025, the Second German Television (ZDF) presented its plan for a public-interest-oriented Digital Public Open Space (Dogruel et al.). There are many plans, but it remains to be seen whether they can be successfully realised in future. The drafts for a European media platform largely leave open the question of which values they intend to achieve and how. Only smaller projects promoting European news exchange and discourse have been established so far. One such project is the press review euro|topics – European Press Roundup, which monitors European discourses and translates the main contributions from leading newspapers into five languages. This project was founded by the German Federal Agency for Civic Education (Bundeszentrale für politische Bildung, bpb) as early as 2005. A European Perspective (AEP) is a transnational European newsroom, launched by public service media in 2021. Its 23 member organisations from 17 countries exchange news and translate news using the AI-assisted EuroVox tool. In 2024, AEP launched YEP News (Your European Perspective), a multilingual news aggregator that reports on major European and global issues. Outline for a Common Good-Oriented European Platform for Journalism A compelling concept for such a platform is still lacking. While Twitter certainly opened up new possibilities for journalism, it was not primarily created to improve democracy. Therefore, simply copying it would not suffice. It would be better to first define the modules required for a European media platform that is oriented towards the common good. In line with the mission of public service media, such a platform could encompass journalism, education, advice, culture, and entertainment. This article, however, focusses on journalism, which contributes to the common good in two ways: by producing and disseminating news and comments, and by moderating public discourse. Unlike traditional mass media, digital platforms are not limited to the linear dissemination of news and comments. They also enable interactive communication, broad participation in the public discourse, and the archiving of verified news and justified opinions. Taking these digital capabilities into account, a matrix of journalistic platform modules can be developed that integrates dissemination, discourse, and archiving (table 1). These modules complement each other and are closely interconnected: news and comments distributed by the media provide ongoing opportunities for public discourse, during which their justification is questioned and clarified through argumentation. Validated news and opinions, along with their justifications, are stored in the archive and can be reintroduced into the process, serving as context for current events or providing argumentative support. However, they can also be corrected and supplemented themselves. Knowledge Assessment Journalistic intermediation Short-term: Production and dissemination News Comment Professional production and linear dissemination Medium-term: Public discourse Epistemic validation Opinion formation process Professional moderation (ensuring broad participation and deliberative quality of discourses) Long-term: Archiving Validated knowledge as context Documentation of opinion and its justification (pros and cons) Professional archiving and referencing Table 1: Modules of a journalistic platform The envisioned journalistic platform modules should connect three spatial levels: the local, national, and European. Yochai Benkler’s normative concept of an integrated networked public sphere, which he outlined back in 2006, is helpful here. The goal of this concept is to strike the right balance between openness and closedness in public discourse. Both are necessary, but also risky: openness brings participation and diversity, but also information overload, loss of news quality (disinformation), and rude discourse (hate speech). On the side of closedness, gatekeeping ensures news and discourse quality, but focussing attention on a small number of relevant topics (agenda-setting) can lead to a concentration of power and lack of diversity. According to Benkler, the tension between openness and closedness should be resolved by distributing specific tasks across the different levels of the public sphere and by the gradual processing of news and comments in different phases. This begins with a high degree of diversity in topics and related news and comments across numerous mini-publics at the local level, with strong citizen participation. This continues at the national and European level, mediated by journalistic selection and moderation. At the European level, exchanges between the national publics should be encouraged. At higher levels and in later phases, the publics merge and diversity in rational discourse is reduced when selection decisions are made about the relevance of topics, the accuracy of news, and the (better) justification of opinions. This narrowing of the focus in a bottom-up process should not be centralised or finalised. Rather than the “hard” selection decisions (gatekeeping) of traditional mass media, a recommendation-based approach and “soft” (revisable) selection process (gatewatching: see Bruns) should be adopted. This multi-level architecture helps to ensure that the concrete local experiences of citizens remain connected to the political decisions made at higher levels in distant capitals. Topics can be covered and discussed on platforms in the long term, with knowledge and opinions from the archive providing context. Of course, theories of democracy should not be the only normative benchmark for the European media platform. Additional modules are required to strengthen identity, community building, social cohesion, and connections between different lifeworld experiences (Bengesser). Steps Towards a Common Good-Oriented European Media Platform What steps are necessary for the design of such a European media platform? Digital transformation is an ongoing process of change, meaning that the conditions for realising democratic values are also perpetually changing (Coeckelbergh, Digital Humanism 3). This requires continuous learning and weighing up of new chances and risks. Appropriate learning environments include innovation labs (García-Avilés) and pioneer communities (Hepp and Loosen). This process of experimentation could be observed in the case of Twitter and is also currently evident in the field of generative artificial intelligence (Jungherr). Negative effects have become apparent, such as incorrect outputs, bias, unfairness, opacity, copyright violations, and environmental costs. Conversely, visions were developed on how to strengthen democracy with AI and how to democratise AI (Coeckelbergh, Undermines 70-119). There are already many AI applications that are conducive to democracy: LLM-powered chatbots can enhance news diversity (Heitz et al.), improve the quality of political discourse (Argyle et al.), and verify political information (Kuznetsova et al.). Pioneer communities such as the German AI for Media Network support systematic learning. An experimental approach is needed to exploit the opportunities and limits of digital technologies for democracy, following the concepts of “experimental democracy” by John Dewey and “piecemeal technology” by Karl R. Popper. Both authors recommended taking small, reversible steps to test new paths in democracy. In addition to the editorial development of a European media platform outlined here, the necessary institutional and legal frameworks must be created. If a new organisation is not established, existing public service media organisations should cooperate within the framework of the European Broadcasting Union (EBU), for example. Furthermore, a political consensus must be reached among EU member states. This will certainly be the greatest challenge. The rise of right-wing populist parties and the erosion of democracy in several EU countries is both the main reason for taking measures to strengthen the European public sphere, but also the biggest obstacle. Given this challenging situation, the only feasible approach is a gradual rollout of a European media platform, starting with a small number of countries and focussing on verified news as minimum consensus. The hope must be that the creation of a European public sphere will raise democratic awareness and promote European solidarity. Digital platforms can be useful in this respect; Twitter has demonstrated this potential early on. records.title: The problem with polarization research in an age of extremism
records.authors: Felipe Vilanova; Flavio Azevedo
records.abstract: "I have been gravely disappointed with the white moderate. I have almost reached the regrettable conclusion that the Negro's great stumbling block in his stride toward freedom is not the White Citizen's Counciler or the Ku Klux Klanner, but the white moderate, who is more devoted to "order" than to justice; who prefers a negative peace which is the absence of tension to a positive peace which is the presence of justice"-Martin Luther King, Jr., Letter from Birmingham Jail (1963) Over the past decade, political polarization has become one of the most studied topics in the behavioral and social sciences. A search for "political polarization" in the Web of Science database (conducted on 23 October 2025) yielded 13,387 results, and more than 60 per cent of which were published since 2020. During the same period, authoritarian and anti-democratic movements have gained strength across diverse contexts. A Friedrich-Ebert-Stiftung (2023) study reported that support for a dictatorship led by a "strong leader" in Germany increased, and endorsement of social-Darwinist statements such as "some lives are worthless" more than doubled compared with previous years. Similarly, the Leipzig Authoritarianism Study (Decker et al., 2024) reported renewed increases in xenophobia, chauvinism, and the downplaying of Nazism. In Germany, national reports indicate that extremist offenses have increased year after year (Reuters, 2024). Similar patterns are also observable in the United States and Brazil where not only national surveys reveal an increased openness to military coups and one-party rule (Pew Research Center, 2024a;2024b) but also extremists have attempted to overturn electoral outcomes by storming their respective congresses (European Parliament, 2023).Authoritarian, conservative, and reactionary networks have been among the principal drivers of the surge in distrust, conspiracism, and anti-scientific sentiment (Backhaus et al., 2023;Benegal et al, 2022;Cologna et al., 2025;Dakin et al., 2023;Pavlovic et al., 2022;Philipp-Müller et al., 2022;van Bavel et al, 2022;van der Linden, 2020;Vlasceanu et al., 2024;Voelkel et al., 2024). Coordinated reactionary movements couple conspiratorial and antiscientific narratives as a central element of their political strategy, which, in the recent decades, has been successful in undermining pluralist opponents, galvanizing reactionary followers, shifting blame away from authoritarian sources, and weakening democratic values and institutions (Ren et al., 2022). Through national and international political campaigns, these networks have attempted to replace societal trust and factual knowledge with alternative belief systems that frame them both as victims of ideological attacks and as opponents of a corrupt establishment against the "will of the people" (Golder, 2016;Mudde, 2007;Rothmund et al., 2020;2022;Van Hauwaert et al, 2018;2020). By portraying democracy and science as corrupt, elitist, or ideologically captured establishments, these actors erode public trust in civic society, empirical inquiry, and in the institutions that sustain both (van der Meer et al., 2026). Moreover, in framing pluralist democracy and scientific expertise as nefarious, they reframe their quest for political power and dominance as a project of "renewal" and "social progress".foot_0 This rather paradoxical-and populist (Golder, 2016;Mudde, 2007)-framing has been a potent tool spreading and legitimizing hostility towards pluralist democracy and its knowledge-based institutions. Opposition to democracy, science, and institutional expertise is therefore not an accidental feature of anti-democratic populism and authoritarianism, but its defining component (Capraro et al., 2026;Levitsky and Ziblatt, 2019;Sandel, 2022;Snyder, 2021;Stanley, 2020).These developments illustrate that contemporary polarization does not occur in a vacuum. Rather, it is embedded within a wider ideological shift towards authoritarianism marked by the normalization of violence, systematic dis/misinformation campaigns, and hostility toward scientific expertise (Azevedo and Jost, 2021;Roozenbeek and van der Linden, 2024;van der Linden, 2023;Van Dijck et al., 2018;Vilanova et al., 2025). Against this backdrop, the widespread assumption of the field that polarization is inherently detrimental warrants re-examination. Notably, most empirical studies conceptualize polarization either in ideological terms-typically as increasing divergence or clustering of citizens' attitudes along an ideological spectrum (Philipp-Müller et al., 2022)-or in affective terms, defined as intensified animus toward political outgroups coupled with ingroup favoritism (Iyengar et al., 2012). While analytically tractable, this approach is nonetheless conceptually naïve and methodologically too coarse for the current political moment. Polarization can reflect (i) agonistic democratic conflict-a constitutive feature of pluralist democracy in which adversaries contest values and policies while accepting democratic norms, rules, and outcomes (Mouffe, 2000)-or (ii) democratically corrosive conflict, in which political identity is asymmetrically organized and strategically exploited into distrustful camps and wielded to justify rule-breaking, delegitimizing of elections and pluralist institutions, and erosion of accountability (Somer and McCoy, 2019). Rather than reflecting a symmetric breakdown of civility, this form of dissension constitutes a well-documented, elite-driven pathway to democratic backsliding (Bermeo, 2016). This framing constitutes a tacit belief that social harmony and dialogue are the ideal state of democratic life, and political antagonism is a failure of civility. In the current moment of rising extremism, not all polarization is equivalent nor undesirable. Historical experience underscores this asymmetry. Normative appeals to civility and harmony, when applied indiscriminately, can obscure the moral distinction between domination and resistance-condemning confrontational opposition even in contexts where democratic survival or basic human dignity is at stake. Under conditions of systematic persecution, conflict is not a pathology of democracy but one of the few remaining mechanisms through which injustice can be resisted. Moreover, opposition between democratic and authoritarian values cannot be treated as symmetrical disagreement. When one side rejects pluralism, electoral legitimacy, or epistemic accountability, then 'reconciliation' and even 'civility' function less as neutral civic virtues than as asymmetric constraints, and they risk unilaterally disarming prodemocracy forces. Indeed, democratically corrosive conflict primarily disciplines democratic defenders while leaving anti-democratic actors free to escalate, delegitimize, and capture institutions. Under such asymmetric conditions, appeals to reduce polarization risk equating resistance to authoritarianism with intolerance.The assumption that polarization must be reduced carries profound epistemic and political consequences for social and political psychology and political science. It shapes research designs, variable operationalizations, and the normative interpretations of findings. Interventions aimed at reducing affective polarization, for example, often promote empathy and perspective-taking across ideological divides without considering whether the underlying attitudes sustain or undermine the very conditions that allow for democratic discourse and evidence-based reasoning (e.g., Gillissen et al., 2025;Santos et al., 2022;Tausch et al., 2024;Voelkel et al., 2024;Warner et al., 2020). When authoritarian and anti-scientific movements are gaining strength, such naïve depolarization efforts risk demobilizing both scientific communities and democratic publics at precisely the moment when active defense of evidence and reasoned inquiry is most needed. Safeguarding the norms that make civil society and empirical inquiry possible requires an explicit commitment to democratic rules, pluralism, and epistemic standards (e.g., electoral legitimacy, institutional accountability, and evidence-constrained claims-making). We therefore propose a distinction between democratic polarization-agonistic contestation among actors who accept multicultural pluralism, democratic institutions and election outcomes, civil and human rights, and epistemic accountability-and antidemocratic polarization, in which conflict is strategically mobilized to delegitimize opponents, erode institutional constraints, and normalize dehumanization, scapegoating, misinformation, antiscientific, and conspiratorial narratives as a route to political power. To clarify this distinction, we introduce a minimal framework specifying when political conflict remains within democratic bounds and when it begins to undermine them. This clarification is necessary because much of the polarization literature treats all forms of conflict as analytically comparable, regardless of their implications for democratic functioning.Under contemporary conditions of authoritarian resurgence, disinformation, and institutional erosion, the meaning of democratic conflict cannot be inferred from intensity, incivility, or ideological distance alone. Research treating polarization as presumptively pathological may misclassify democratic resistance as equivalent to anti-democratic escalation. Indeed, democratic politics is not reducible to civility, consensus, or the absence of conflict. In pluralistic societies, conflict is often unavoidable and sometimes necessary. Political disagreement commonly concerns collective priorities, the allocation of public resources, and the design of institutions that structure social life. But democratic disagreement does not extend without limit. It unfolds within a democratic framework that must secure equal standing, basic rights, and meaningful inclusion for all members of the polity. Polarization researchers must contextualize and interpret political conflict in light of the political reality, including stakeholders' commitments to pluralism, equal citizenship, collective welfare, equitable social and economic opportunities, and the maintenance of democratic institutions.This point is especially important because the boundary between "ordinary" policy disagreement and anti-democratic politics cannot be drawn by separating social and economic arrangements from questions of rights, recognition, and membership. Social and economic arrangements are not external to democratic inclusion: they help determine who has security, health, mobility, voice, and genuine access to collective life. When such arrangements systematically expose some groups to deprivation, precarity, premature death, or political marginalization while insulating dominant groups and concentrated economic power, they cease to be ordinary policy disagreements in any normatively innocent sense. They become mechanisms through which hierarchy is organized and reproduced. For this reason, conflicts over rights, recognition, and membership cannot be cleanly separated from conflicts over economic life, since the latter shape whether democratic citizenship is substantive or merely formal. When such inequalities are re-described as routine political disagreement, domination is recast as policy and anti-democratic projects can pass as normal democratic contestation.Accordingly, not all politically salient disagreements are democratically equivalent. Some conflicts occur within democratic bounds, even when they are intense and adversarial. Others target the very conditions that make democratic life possible. When political actors seek to deny full standing to opponents, restrict who counts as a legitimate member of the polity, erode rights protections, weaponize institutions, or degrade the epistemic conditions of public reasoning, the issue is no longer conflict within democracy alone. It is conflict over democracy's own normative and institutional basis. Under such conditions, domination can be redescribed as policy, exclusion can be redescribed as disagreement, and anti-democratic projects can pass as routine democratic contestation.To tentatively point out this distinction, Table 1 provides a heuristic framework for evaluating when political conflict remains consistent with democratic functioning and when it does not. It is not intended as a rigid classificatory scheme, nor does it aim to resolve ambiguities inherent to sociopolitical realities. Rather, it identifies a set of dimensions along which political conflict may be evaluated. The purpose of Table 1 is to make explicit why polarization cannot be evaluated solely in terms of distance, hostility, or civility, as it is often the case in the published literature. What should matter most, in our view, is the nature and kind of conflict being mobilized, by whom, under what institutional conditions, and toward what ends. Contestation over collective priorities, public resources, and institutional arrangements within a framework that protects equal standing, basic rights, and democratic inclusion.Mobilization directed at domination, exclusion, scapegoating, or the denial of full standing, often while being framed as ordinary policy disagreement.The key distinction is not between "material" and "symbolic" conflict, but between conflict within democratic bounds and conflict targeting democracy's normative basic tenets. Treating social and economic arrangements as if they were innocent or neutral background can obscure the existence of democratically corrosive conflict.Opponents are treated as legitimate adversaries within a shared political community, even amid deep disagreement.Opponents are cast as enemies, traitors, contaminants, or groups whose equal standing should be denied.In unequal systems, claims for equal inclusion are often re-described as divisive or extreme.Commitment to fair representation, meaningful participation, and peaceful transfer of power under substantively democratic conditions.Fraud claims without evidence, voter suppression, intimidation, rule manipulation, or other efforts to entrench minority rule.Procedural compliance alone is insufficient. Elections can be formally lawful yet substantively distorted by gerrymandering, disenfranchisement, or unequal access.Rejection of intimidation, vigilantism, and coercive force as tools of routine political competition.Endorsement, normalization, or strategic toleration of violence, threats, or paramilitary intimidation to secure political ends.Defensive resistance under conditions of authoritarian aggression should not be treated as equivalent to aggression in the service of domination.Disagreement proceeds with some commitment to evidence, accountability, policy evaluation, and truth-seeking institutions, even when values differ.Strategic disinformation, conspiracy narratives, epistemic nihilism, anti-scientific attitudes, or the systematic rejection of evidence when it constrains preferred outcomes.Democratic politics requires agreement and commitment to epistemic infrastructure. Accountable institutions for truth-seeking and policy assessment are necessary while not devolving into technocracy nor preaching technocratic infallibility. Preserves equal citizenship, equal protection, minority rights, opposition rights, and inclusive participation as non-negotiable conditions of democratic life.Treats the rights, recognition, safety, or participation of some groups as contingent, revocable, or subordinate to dominantgroup interests.Formal rights may coexist with substantive exclusion. The issue is whether institutions protect equal standing just formally or de facto. A democracy that protects formal liberties while permitting social and economic arrangements that systematically hollow out equal membership remains democratic only in a thin and unstable sense.Supports and materially sustains the institutions that enable accountability, including independent courts, watchdogs, civil society, electoral administration, and a genuinely free press.Defunds, captures, delegitimizes, or selectively weaponizes accountability institutions in order to avoid scrutiny or entrench power.The performative acceptance of democracy is too weak a standard. Democratic conflict must occur while all actors help sustain democratic accountability infrastructures.Clarifies genuine social conflicts, widens participation, increases accountability, and surfaces injustices that require political resolution.Accelerates democratic erosion, normalizes exclusion, immunizes power from scrutiny, and recasts hierarchy as ordinary disagreement.Whether conflict is agonistic depends partly on background power relations, not merely on tone or intensity. For one example, civil and political liberties cannot be exercised meaningfully in the absence of the social and economic conditions that make equal membership, voice, and participation materially possible.This framework indicates that polarization cannot be adequately evaluated solely in terms of attitudinal distance, hostility, or affect. By distinguishing between agonistic and corrosive forms of conflict, it helps account for why comparable levels of polarization may have different implications across contexts. This distinction, however, introduces challenges for classification and measurement. Simpler models may offer greater clarity, parsimony, and cross-context comparability, but these advantages often involve the omission of distinctions that are normatively and politically relevant. As a result, analytically distinct forms of conflict may be treated as equivalent. records.title: Geochemical Insights into Rare Earth Elements Distribution patterns in Granites of Nasarawa State, North-Central Nigeria
records.authors: Mohammed Salihu; Emmanuel Joseph; Adamu N. Baba-Kutigi
records.abstract: Purpose: To investigate the distribution of rare earth elements (REEs) in granites from selected locations within Nasarawa State, North-Central Nigeria, in order to evaluate their geochemical characteristics and assess their mineralization potential. Methodology: Fourteen (14) granite samples were systematically collected and analyzed using Instrumental Neutron Activation Analysis (INAA) at the Centre for Energy Research and Training, Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria, Nigeria. Trace element concentrations and REE patterns were examined, and geochemical discrimination diagrams were employed to determine tectonic settings and source characteristics. Findings: The trace element data show elevated concentrations of U (6.79 ppm), Co (64.81 ppm), Rb (266.89 ppm), Sb (2.04 ppm), Cs (43.83 ppm), and Ta (219.90 ppm) relative to Upper Continental Crust values, indicating moderate to extreme enrichment. REE patterns are dominated by light rare earth elements (LREE; average 58.44 ppm) over heavy rare earth elements (HREE; average 18.22 ppm). Geochemical discrimination diagrams indicate that the granites were emplaced in multiple tectonic settings, including syn-collisional, volcanic arc, and within-plate environments, and were primarily derived from the upper continental crust. Comparative analysis shows general depletion of most REEs, except for dysprosium (Dy), which exhibits elevated concentrations, suggesting potential Dy mineralization. Unique Contribution to Theory, Practice and Policy: This study provides baseline geochemical data for REE distribution in granites of Nasarawa State and contributes to the understanding of crustal evolution and tectonic settings in the region. It highlights the potential for dysprosium mineralization, offering practical insights for targeted REE exploration and resource development. The findings can inform mineral exploration strategies, guide investment decisions, and support policy formulation aimed at sustainable exploitation of REE resources in Nigeria.

records.title: Hunter-Gatherers with Smartphones
records.authors: Daniel Rosehill; Gemini 3.1 (Flash); Chatterbox TTS
records.abstract: Episode summary: The popular image of hunter-gatherers is decades out of date. We explore the reality of the world's last foraging societies, from their surprising health profiles to their strategic use of modern technology. Discover how groups like the Hadza use smartphones to sell honey and why others, like the Sentinelese, violently reject all contact, revealing a complex spectrum of adaptation and resistance in the 21st century. Show Notes The world's last hunter-gatherer societies defy simple categorization. They are neither noble savages frozen in time nor tragic figures on the brink of extinction. Instead, they represent a small but resilient slice of humanity navigating a deliberate and complex relationship with the modern world. **Health and Fitness: A Specialized Adaptation** Common perceptions of hunter-gatherers as supremely athletic are nuanced by recent science. While groups like the Hadza of Tanzania possess exceptional endurance and cardiovascular health—studies show remarkably low levels of heart disease—their fitness is highly specialized for their environment. A key finding颠覆s a major assumption: research indicates Hadza hunter-gatherers burn roughly the same total daily calories as sedentary Westerners, a phenomenon known as the "energy expenditure paradox." This suggests the human body adapts to high activity by conserving energy elsewhere, and that the *pattern* of consistent, varied, moderate movement is more critical than sheer calorie burn. Diet plays an equally crucial role. Obesity remains rare among these communities, strongly linked to diets high in fiber, complex carbohydrates, and lean protein, and virtually devoid of ultra-processed foods. Their leanness and health are a product of this synergy between activity and nutrition, highlighting a profound mismatch between our evolved physiology and modern lifestyles. **The Technology Spectrum: From Smartphones to Arrows** The binary idea of being either "cut off" or "assimilated" is obsolete. Remaining hunter-gatherer societies exist on a wide spectrum of contact and technological adoption, often using modern tools to reinforce traditional life. The Hadza, for instance, use mobile phones to coordinate honey-gathering expeditions or get better prices for goods, but not for social media leisure. Similarly, the Aka in Central Africa use phones for logistics and trade, while the Innu in Canada employ snowmobiles, rifles, and social media for hunting efficiency and cultural advocacy. At the far end of the spectrum are groups who actively enforce isolation. The Sentinelese of North Sentinel Island violently reject all contact, a rational response to historical trauma from disease and exploitation. In the Amazon, an estimated 196 uncontacted groups, many practicing foraging, face existential threats from logging, mining, and land invasion. Their isolation is a defense mechanism, but one that makes them politically vulnerable; reports warn half could be wiped out within a decade without urgent protection. **Redefining "Uncontacted"** The active, strategic choices these societies make force a redefinition of terms. Using a metal pot, a machete, or a GPS unit does not negate a hunter-gatherer identity. The core of that identity lies in a subsistence strategy based on foraging and hunting wild resources, coupled with mobility and specific social structures. When a society adopts a smartphone to sell honey or advocate for land rights while maintaining that core, it is not losing authenticity but demonstrating brilliant, selective adaptation. The story of contemporary hunter-gatherers is one of agency and resilience. It challenges us to move beyond romantic or doomed stereotypes and recognize these communities as active curators of their own future, navigating the pressures of the 21st century with a blend of ancient wisdom and strategic modern tool use. Listen online: https://myweirdprompts.com/episode/modern-hunter-gatherer-societies

records.title: Walk in our shoes: older homeless women's perceptions of the challenges of navigating streets and shelter life
records.authors: Judith G. Gonyea; Kelly Melekis
records.abstract: Introduction Older women experiencing homelessness (OWEH) have been a hidden or invisible population; however, with rising numbers globally, they are gaining attention. Our study examines what it means to be a woman in her 50s who is struggling financially and precariously housed in the United States. Although in their 50s, these women often experience accelerated aging and exhibit chronic health conditions comparable to those of housed women in their 70s and 80s. Lacking access to both public old-age benefits and family support, they often fall between the cracks of the nation's safety net system. While homelessness among women of reproductive age, including the role of gender-based violence in increasing their vulnerability, is now well documented, studies on the unique challenges faced by OWEH remain relatively limited. Research objective This study explores how daily life on the streets and in emergency housing shelters, a system historically designed for men (particularly younger men), affects the well-being of OWEH and their journey toward stable housing. The aim was to describe, from the perspectives of OWEH, how shelter environment, policies, and practices (including continual displacement to the streets) shape their daily lives, well-being, and pathways to stable housing. Of particular interest was gaining a deeper understanding of how navigating the traumas of homelessness and shelter living affects individuals' sense of dignity, self-worth, adaptive resources, and resilience. Methods This qualitative study involved 15 semistructured, private individual interviews, each lasting about 60 min, conducted by an MSW social worker. Eligibility criteria included being homeless for at least 1 month, being in one’s 50s, and being able to take part in an English-language interview. Using NVivo (qualitative research software), the interview audiotape transcripts were coded and analyzed using a multistep interpretative phenomenological approach to enable exploration of how OWEH make sense of what is happening to them (or the “lived experience') and their views (or “meaning making') of life and these experiences. Results Trauma was a universal experience, and almost all participants were coping with significant physical and/or mental health issues. Overall, participants perceived that shelter management and staff failed to fully understand the challenges women faced in rebuilding their lives, especially the interconnectedness of health struggles, societal bias against older women, and the social prejudice of people experiencing homelessness. Five superordinate themes were identified, highlighting how shelter physical and social environments contribute to OWEH's daily struggles and sense of disempowerment: (a) dehumanizing and stigmatizing treatment; (b) unsafe surroundings and hypervigilance; (c) harsh living conditions and declining physical and emotional health; (d) disempowering situations and loss of control; and (e) an absence of normalcy and stability. Conclusion This study contributes to our understanding of how emergency housing shelters create or exacerbate the challenges faced by OWEH and often result in disempowering. The findings suggest the importance of transforming both the physical and social environments of shelters, using trauma- and aging-informed approaches, to better support this growing population of OWEH in their pathway to stable housing.

records.title: Vitality and Vital Security: Socio-Philosophical Foundations of Resilience Formation in Critical Life Situations
records.authors: Igor Ryzhov; Petro Yashchuk
records.abstract: The article offers an interdisciplinary socio-philosophical, psychological, and anthropological analysis of vitality as an integrative category that characterises the capacity of individuals and social communities to preserve life potential, value-based orientation, and subjectivity under conditions of critical life situations. The methodological relevance of introducing the authorial concept of the vital-crisis situation is substantiated as an analytical framework for describing states in which intensive threats are combined with a deficit of coping resources, thereby significantly increasing the risk of loss of viability, autonomy, and subjectivity. It is demonstrated that vitality cannot be reduced to psychophysiological parameters of functioning, but rather constitutes a multidimensional anthropological phenomenon encompassing bodily, psycho-emotional, motivational, and moral-value components. Vitality is realised through the subject’s capacity to make responsible existential choices and to preserve dignity in boundary states characteristic of critical life situations. Boundary and vital-crisis states are interpreted as sensitive indicators of the level of vitality, since it is precisely under such conditions that the distinction between constructive and destructive modes of experiencing reality becomes most explicit, determining the preservation or erosion of subjectivity. On the basis of a synthesis of philosophical, psychodynamic, stress-related, and psychometric approaches, the theoretical preconditions for the operationalisation of vitality are clarified, and its interrelation with the phenomena of resilience, adaptive energy, and moral autonomy is explicated. The antivital consequences of deliberately destructive social influences are outlined, manifesting themselves in decreased life tone, erosion of value-normative orientations, and growing existential and social vulnerability. In conclusion, the conceptual integration of vitality with vital security is substantiated as a humanitarian and anthropocentric paradigm aimed at integrating individual life resources with legal, educational, psychosocial, and institutional mechanisms of support and prevention of degradation of the individual’s internal life potential. records.title: Evaluating Destination Competitiveness Through Dynamic Capabilities: A Systematic Literature Review of Qatar’s Sustainable Tourism
records.authors: Hale Özgit; Karima Chelihi
records.abstract: This study systematically reviews the evolution of Qatar’s tourism sector to evaluate the historical barriers impeding its development and the strategic initiatives deployed to enhance destination competitiveness. The research’s primary aim is to provide a theory-driven longitudinal analysis of Qatar’s tourism evolution, identifying systemic barriers and adaptive responses required for long-term sustainability. Grounded in the theoretical synthesis of Butler’s Tourism Area Life Cycle (TALC) and Dynamic Capability Theory (DCT), the research employs a systematic literature review (SLR) guided by the PRISMA framework, screening 4846 records to analyze 24 final studies. The findings reveal five primary structural and perceptual barriers: a price–value mismatch (luxury perception), regional political instability, cultural and regulatory constraints, environmental vulnerabilities, and gaps in tourist infrastructure. Utilizing DCT, the results demonstrate how the destination exhibited adaptive governance by sensing these barriers and seizing strategic opportunities—such as mega-event hosting and visa reforms—to partially transform its tourism system. These insights highlight that while created resources drive initial visibility, sustaining long-term competitiveness and sustainable growth relies on continuous institutional reconfiguration and socio-cultural alignment.

records.title: Prioritizing health and research needs of internally displaced populations in Mozambique: a policy and practice review
records.authors: Ivan da Costa Tomás Júnior; Alvaro Marcela Manhiça; Will Susse de Jesus Monjane; Paulo Salvador da Silva Tembe Júnior; Igor Paulo Ubisse Capitine
records.abstract: Internal displacement is an increasingly important public health and governance challenge, driven by the interaction of armed conflict, recurrent disasters, and climate-related hazards. Internally displaced persons (IDPs), who remain within national borders, often face persistent protection gaps, fragmented assistance, and disrupted access to essential services, challenges that are particularly pronounced in low- and middle-income countries in sub-Saharan Africa. Mozambique illustrates how historical patterns of conflict-related displacement intersect with contemporary crises linked to floods, cyclones, droughts, and renewed insecurity, resulting in repeated and protracted displacement. These dynamics generate cumulative health and social vulnerabilities among IDPs, including elevated risks of mental health disorders, malnutrition, poor maternal and child health outcomes, and infectious diseases, shaped by poverty, disrupted livelihoods, weak infrastructure, and constrained health-system capacity. This article presents a policy- and practice-oriented narrative review that synthesizes national evidence on internal displacement in Mozambique and critically situates these findings within global frameworks, international policy recommendations, and comparative contexts of displacement-affected areas. It examines the historical evolution of displacement dynamics and analyses their implications for health systems, governance, and research agendas. The review aligns with Mozambique's National Research Agenda in Human Health (AGISA) and assesses the Policy and Strategy for the Management of Internally Displaced Persons (PEGDI), identifying gaps in legal enforceability, integration of conflict- and disaster-related displacement, monitoring systems, and long-term resilience planning. Building on the Technical and Scientific Programme on Vulnerable Populations of the National Institute of Health (INS), Mozambique, this article proposes displacement-sensitive research and policy priorities to strengthen routine health planning, surveillance, participatory approaches, and multisectoral coordination. The findings underscore the need to move beyond short-term humanitarian responses toward sustained, evidence-informed strategies that recognize internal displacement as a structural determinant of health and embed displacement considerations within health-system strengthening, climate adaptation, and development planning in Mozambique.

records.title: Immunomodulatory Strategies for Managing Viral Infections in Solid Organ Transplantation: Progress and Challenges
records.authors: Amir Elalouf; Hanan Maoz
records.abstract: Solid organ transplantation (SOT) is a critical treatment for end-stage organ failure. Still, lifelong immunosuppression leaves recipients vulnerable to opportunistic viral infections, which can lead to severe complications such as graft dysfunction and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder. With emerging viral threats such as SARS-CoV-2 and arboviruses, alongside persistent challenges posed by CMV, EBV, and BKV, this review is timely in addressing the evolving landscape of post-transplant viral infections and their management. Recent studies highlight how immunosuppression impairs both innate and adaptive antiviral defenses, including diminished toll-like receptor signaling, dysfunction of NK cells, and disrupted T- and B-cell responses. Viruses exploit these deficits through immune evasion strategies, such as MHC-I downregulation and the production of immunosuppressive microRNA. Advances in management include antiviral prophylaxis, adoptive T-cell therapy, and immune monitoring, with emerging therapies like virus-specific T-cell infusions and complement inhibition showing promise. The findings underscore the need for personalized, organ-specific approaches to post-transplant care. Enhanced surveillance, vaccination strategies, and novel immunotherapies are critical in mitigating viral risks. Future research should focus on immune-risk stratification and the development of an adaptable therapeutic approach to enhance transplant outcomes in the face of evolving viral threats.

records.title: Rethinking Solitary Living in the True Shrikes (Family Laniidae): Territoriality, Cognitive Innovation, and Vulnerability
records.authors: Reuven Yosef
records.abstract: Solitary living is an evolutionarily widespread yet comparatively under-theorized social system, despite its occurrence across diverse animal taxa. Shrikes (family Laniidae) are small predatory passerines that combine raptorial behavior, strong territoriality, and predominantly solitary space use, making them a powerful model for examining the ecology and evolution of solitary living. Here, I synthesize published work on shrike behavioral ecology and explicitly link these traits to the costs and benefits of a solitary lifestyle. I argue that shrikes exemplify how solitary species can offset the absence of social buffering through cognitive innovation, finetuned habitat selection, and flexible yet tightly bounded sociality. I then compare shrike ecology to solitary mammals and reptiles, highlighting convergent patterns in resource dispersion, spatial memory, risk management, and juvenile dispersal. I further examine how anthropogenic pressures, such as habitat fragmentation, climatic instability, and urbanization, interact with solitary life histories and review evidence from management interventions in both European farmland and North American systems that demographic recovery is achievable but remains contingent on addressing broader land-use conflicts and sources of adult mortality. Finally, I outline five interconnected research priorities—spanning cognitive ecology, trophic interactions, movement ecology, genomics, and formal comparative analyses—that would move shrike research from its current observational foundation toward a more experimental, mechanistic, and phylogenetically informed programme. By reframing shrikes as a model taxon for solitary living, this review aims to integrate avian behavioral ecology into broader comparative frameworks of social organization, cognition, and resilience under global change.

records.title: Assessing retention of pandemic capacities from COVID-19 in humanitarian settings: A cross-sectional retrospective study of health workers in Honduras, Syria, and South Sudan
records.authors: Maryada E. Vallet; Husam Al Zuwayny; Christopher G. Kemp; Rose Lynn Cooper; Erin M. Sorrell; Gilbert Burnham
records.abstract: The global health security landscape remains critically vulnerable to emerging pandemic threats. Humanitarian settings face particularly acute challenges in health workforce preparedness and response capabilities. Humanitarian settings have traditionally been left out of global health security and other health system strengthening investments. There is also a significant gap in the literature around building sustained health worker pandemic capacities in these challenging contexts. This novel study measured the retention or ‘shelf-life’ of perceived COVID-19 training benefits for health workers around knowledge, skills, and confidence to face future infectious disease threats. The Dynamic Sustainability Framework was used for conceptual framing. The study spanned three distinct humanitarian settings: Honduras, Syria, and South Sudan. Employing a cross-sectional, retrospective self-assessment design, 129 primary healthcare and community level health workers were surveyed in March-April 2024. Participants self-reported pandemic capacities on five-point Likert ratings across three time points – retrospective recall for pre- and post-training, and for present status, which was on average three years after training. Results demonstrated substantial increases post-training in self-reported knowledge ( p < 0.001), skills ( p < 0.001), and confidence ( p < 0.001), and sustained or improved capacities at present (knowledge ( p < 0.01), skills ( p < 0.01), and confidence ( p < 0.001)). Despite low access to ongoing training, resources, and support, 84.3% of health workers reported feeling prepared to face emergent disease risks (COVID-19 or other). The results call for further exploration of the individual, training-related, facility, and contextual factors affecting the capacity retention. Due to study design limitations, these results cannot be attributed to the trainings or generalized to all health workers in these countries. Still, this research contributes critical insights into the potential sustained benefits of frontline health workforce pandemic capacity building in humanitarian settings. Since capacities were retained despite limited ongoing training and support, targeted, sustained investments become crucial to preserve and enhance health security in the most fragile health systems.

records.title: A Unified Digital Twin Architecture for Integrated Power Grid and Infrastructure Management
records.authors: Meihong Wang; Qingjia Yin; Yingshan Pan; Liang Zhang; Hong Li
records.abstract: INTRODUCTION: The increasing complexity of modern power grids, driven by the integration of distributed energy resources and dynamic operating conditions, presents significant challenges for stability assessment. Traditional stability analysis methods often fail to capture topological dependencies and nonlinear interactions among grid components, resulting in unreliable predictions. Furthermore, existing approaches such as static models and graph convolution networks lack effective node-level importance weighting, limiting their ability to distinguish between stable and unstable states. OBJECTIVES: This study aims to develop an advanced framework for power grid stability classification by integrating digital twin technology with Graph Attention Networks (GAT). The objective is to improve the modeling of inter-node relationships and enhance classification accuracy under complex grid conditions. METHODS: A digital twin-inspired graph model of the power grid is constructed, where nodes represent grid components and edges represent their interactions. A Graph Attention Network is employed to learn weighted inter-node dependencies using attention mechanisms, enabling effective differentiation between stable and unstable operating modes. The proposed framework is evaluated in an offline, simulation-based environment using the Smart Grid Stability dataset. RESULTS: Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, achieving an accuracy of 0.9640, precision of 0.9411, recall of 0.9607, F1-score of 0.9508, and ROC-AUC of 0.9958. Comparative analysis indicates that the proposed model outperforms conventional methods, including Artificial Neural Networks (ANN), Deep Neural Networks (DNN), and Random Forest, in overall classification performance. CONCLUSION: The proposed digital twin-inspired GAT framework provides accurate and reliable offline stability classification, significantly improving upon existing methods. However, challenges related to scalability for larger grid systems and real-time cyber–physical synchronization remain, highlighting important directions for future research.

records.title: “Trying to go at full speed with the handbrake on”: Living with persistent symptoms after COVID-19, a qualitative interview study
records.authors: Dilara Gülmez; Emelie Sarenmalm; Elena Nowacki; Emmanuel Dudoignon; Morgane Michel; Björn Peters; Lenka Vanek; Janosch Niknam-Saeidi; Amelie Kurnikowski; Justyna Siwy; Astrid Erber; Mariann Gyöngyösi; Ulrich Kropiunigg; Manfred Hecking
records.abstract: Abstract Background: Despite individuals experiencing a gradual reduction in persistent symptoms following SARS-CoV-2 infection, a subset remains at increased risk of death and health loss up to three years post-infection. Given prior evidence of gender-related disparities in acute COVID-19 outcomes and informed by survivorship concept, we examined psychosocial aspects of Long COVID by considering gender-related differences in participants’ narratives. Methods: In this multi-center qualitative study, 27 patients with persistent symptoms following acute COVID-19 and three primary caregivers were interviewed using a semi-structured interview guide across centers in Austria, France and Sweden. Qualitative analysis was informed by Charmaz’s constructivist grounded theory and stratified by self-reported gender. Results: The study cohort consisted predominantly of individuals previously hospitalized for acute COVID-19 assessed at a mean follow-up of 3.4 ± 0.6 years post-infection. Functional constraints coincided with shifts in self-concept prompting retrospective reflection and a search for reassurance predominantly among women; altered roles and responsibilities increased caregiver strain and heightened structural vulnerability in the context of prolonged recovery. Perceived neglect in healthcare prompted both women and men to engage in self-advocacy in aid- and health-management. Survival-oriented positive future outlooks and resilience following near-death-experiences were salient among men. Neglect of health needs was associated with a premature pressure to perform due to caregiving demands among women, and with prioritization of the breadwinner role and masculinity-linked stoic ideals of invulnerability among men. Conclusion: Both patient and caregiver narratives revealed intersecting challenges warranting holistic, coordinated care attentive to systemic barriers, social relations, and gender-related patterns.

records.title: Geoclimatic and Cognitive Shifts: An Analysis of Their Interrelationship in the Era of Global Crisis
records.authors: D. D. Stepanyuk; P. S. Seleznev
records.abstract: This article examines and analyzes the typology of global geoclimatic shifts, classifying the types of environmental and climatic changes that change the face of the planet. The authors identified 4 types of geoclimatic shifts, such as gradual climatic trends, extreme changes in weather conditions, turning points in the Earth’s system, and changes in biosphere and ecosystem regimes. The authors also consider global cognitive shifts that classify changes in human behavior, values, and collective psychology in response to the global crisis. The types identified by the authors are as follows: climate anxiety, environmental grief and the psychology of crisis, digital transformation and cognitive overload, changes in values, worldview, and moral principles. For each category in the article, the authors identified the key driving factors, their characteristics and the observed consequences for environmental stability, human health, food and water security, as well as the sustainability of infrastructure. The authors draw on modern scientific literature in the fields of the environment, behavioral sciences, cognitive sociology, and moral psychology. A key analytical contribution is the study of the effects of the interaction between geoclimatic and cognitive shifts. In the article, the authors analyzed how climatic stress factors — extreme heat, lack of resources, population displacement, and exposure to natural disasters — can increase psychological stress, change moral priorities, and transform institutional trust, while cognitive models such as increased risk, cascades of misinformation, and failures of collective action, in turn, can influence the results of mitigation and adaptation. In conclusion, the authors consider how these shifts interact with each other (for example, how climatic stressors cause psychological reactions or social changes), and also consider how such a typology can help in research, policy development, and political sustainability planning.
