records.title: Digital Transformation and Operational Excellence: The Role of Information Technology in Multi-Location Business Management
records.authors: Keya Karabi Roy; Gurpreet Kaur; Md Ali Azam
records.abstract: For organisations that have multiple locations, there is a need to be consistent, efficient and responsive, and this is where digital transformation is a strategic necessity. Integration of business processes, real-time communication and data-driven decision making across geographically distributed units are all enabled by information technology (IT), which is key to operational excellence. This paper aims to review and synthesize the current literature to understand the impact of digital transformation in improving operational performance in multi-location business environments. It delves into the role of enterprise systems, cloud computing, data analytics, Internet of Things (IoT) technologies, artificial intelligence (AI), and digital collaboration platforms in the process of standardisation, optimisation of resources, improvement of customer services, and agility of organisations. The review also emphasizes the strategic value of digital integration in enhancing the coordination of the supply chain, human resources management, performance tracking and monitoring, and decision-making, all of which allow organizations to better adapt to market conditions. Furthermore, the paper explores the key organisational, technological and human aspects that can impact digital transformation projects, such as leadership support, employee readiness, cybersecurity, investing in infrastructure, and managing change. The results show that, besides using advanced technologies, multi-location companies need to be able to properly connect their digital capabilities to their organizational strategy and business goals to become operational exemplary. The paper concludes that the advantages that an integrated digital ecosystem brings to an organisation are sustainable competitive advantages for organisations, as it provides them with operational visibility, better cooperation, less inefficiency and continuous innovation. The study adds to the current body of knowledge on digital transformation by offering a comprehensive view of the relationship between information technology and operational excellence in geographically distributed business operations.

records.title: When lecturers use GenAI: How EFL learners view lesson planning and materials development
records.authors: Kiki Juli Anggoro; Damar Isti Pratiwi; Norma Pawestri
records.abstract: This explanatory mixed-methods study examined how EFL learners perceive lecturers’ use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in lesson planning and instructional materials design within CALL environments. Data were collected from 410 undergraduate students in Thailand and Indonesia using a 29-item Likert-scale survey measuring learning value, engagement, and ethical concerns, along with attitudinal indicators of transparency and lecturer responsibility, and three open-ended questions. Quantitative analyses (descriptive statistics, correlations, ANOVA, and exploratory regression) showed that learners generally perceived GenAI-supported materials as useful and engaging, while also expressing strong ethical concerns about accuracy, fairness, and over-reliance. Learners with higher self-reported English proficiency and technology literacy reported greater learning value and engagement, whereas less prepared learners relied more heavily on teacher mediation. Qualitative findings indicated that students valued the clarity and structure of GenAI-supported materials but were concerned about generic output, misinformation, and depersonalization, and consistently emphasized the need for lecturer verification and transparency. Integration of both strands suggests that learner readiness shapes the extent to which students derive benefit from GenAI-mediated materials, while expectations for human oversight remain consistent across learner profiles. Unlike most studies that examine GenAI as a learner-operated tool, this study shifts attention toward GenAI as an instructional design resource used by lecturers and demonstrates how learners evaluate GenAI-mediated pedagogical decisions in EFL higher education.

records.title: Leveraging GIS-based multi-criteria analysis for flood-prone area detection in Nsanje District, Malawi
records.authors: Charles Bakolo; Lusungu Ngwira; Kennedy Nazombe; Veronica Immaculate Bukani; Ken Chapita; Devie Chilonga; Harineck Mayamiko Tholo; Chikondi Chisenga; Jabulani Nyengere
records.abstract: Flooding remains one of the most severe and recurrent natural hazards in sub-Saharan Africa, posing persistent threats to rural livelihoods, infrastructure, and environmental stability. In Malawi, the Lower Shire River Valley, particularly Nsanje district, is highly vulnerable to recurrent flooding due to climatic variability, land-use change, and geomorphological characteristics. Despite the growing availability of geospatial data, localized flood vulnerability assessments remain limited, constraining effective disaster preparedness and land-use planning. This study applied a Geographic Information System-based multi-criteria analysis using the Analytical Hierarchy Process to identify flood-prone areas in Nsanje district, Malawi. Five key spatial parameters were integrated: land cover, precipitation, slope, proximity to water bodies, and elevation. The datasets included Sentinel-2 imagery, CHIRPS precipitation records, Shuttle Radar Topography Mission digital elevation data, and official hydrological data. The weighted overlay analysis revealed that land cover and precipitation were the dominant determinants of flood susceptibility, accounting for 59.4 percent and 21.0 percent of the total influence, respectively. The resulting flood susceptibility map showed a pronounced north–south gradient in vulnerability, with the southern corridor exhibiting the highest exposure to flooding. Traditional Authority Nyachikadza emerged as the most critically affected area, with more than 1,500 residents situated in high-risk zones, whereas Traditional Authorities Malemia and Tengani displayed moderate levels of vulnerability. The findings indicate that the combined effects of land-use practices, rainfall intensity, and terrain configuration strongly influence flood susceptibility in Nsanje. This study provides a cost-effective and replicable framework for flood risk assessment in data-scarce environments. By leveraging freely available satellite data and open-source geospatial tools, it offers actionable intelligence to support disaster management, spatial planning, and community resilience in flood-prone areas. This approach contributes to the broader sustainability agenda by informing climate adaptation strategies that are aligned with national and global commitments to disaster risk reduction and Sustainable Development Goals. The five-factor model used here should be read as a first-order, operationally feasible approximation of flood susceptibility; geology, soil permeability, and drainage density were not incorporated and are discussed as an explicit limitation, and the precipitation criterion reflects cumulative seasonal totals rather than storm-scale rainfall intensity.

records.title: Projecting global soil moisture droughts under climate change: characteristics, agricultural exposure, and adaptation insights
records.authors: Sogol Moradian; Salem Gharbia; Fatimatuj Sonny; Ali Torabi Haghighi; Agnieszka Indiana Olbert
records.abstract: The intensification of global warming has increased the severity, frequency, and duration of extreme drought events, posing significant threats to agricultural stability. This study introduces a framework for assessing global agricultural drought impacts under climate change by integrating soil moisture data from 17 CMIP6 (Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6) models with statistical post-processing techniques. The framework utilises the high-resolution GLDAS (Global Land Data Assimilation System) reference dataset for bias correction and incorporates two SSP scenarios (namely SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5, where SSP stands for Shared Socioeconomic Pathways) to provide a comprehensive evaluation of future soil moisture-driven droughts. Performance metrics were applied to evaluate the accuracy of the climate models, and a non-parametric distribution was used to compute the SSMI (Standardised Soil Moisture Index) for past and future droughts using post-processed CMIP6 data. Statistical tests were conducted to validate the SSMI’s suitability for drought assessment. Future drought events were characterised by severity, intensity, frequency, and duration. An index, the Drought Exposure Index (DEI), was used to analyse drought exposure by overlaying land cover data, enabling the assessment of potential agricultural drought impacts under both SSP scenarios. The DEI ranges from 0 to 1, with higher values indicating greater drought exposure and agricultural vulnerability. Results indicate a clear intensification of soil moisture drought characteristics toward mid-century, particularly under SSP5-8.5, with longer drought durations and increased spatial extent across major agricultural regions. Agricultural vulnerability assessments identify regions most at risk, and continental analysis reveals pronounced drying trends in South America, southern Europe, South Asia, and parts of North America. The agricultural exposure assessment shows that cropland areas in these regions face substantially higher drought risk, with the global mean DEI increasing from 0.71 under SSP2-4.5 to 0.78 under SSP5-8.5 by 2050, reflecting a significant rise in exposure under the more extreme emissions scenario. These findings highlight regions where adaptation efforts are most urgently required. Ultimately, this work enhances understanding of the complex interplay between climate change and drought dynamics, offering actionable insights to support sustainable development. By identifying the most vulnerable drought-prone regions, this research provides critical recommendations for long-term soil moisture drought adaptation, sustainable water management, and climate resilience.

records.title: Numerical simulation of oil spill dispersion and weathering in the Alboran Sea: A case study of its North-Eastern Coast
records.authors: Asmae Nouayti; Soufiane Oubdil; Sara Ajmani; Safae El Aammouri; Payâgda Misaël Tarpaga; Lhoussaine Kammou; Mounaim Halim El Jalil; Mohammed Al-zharanie; Fahd A. Nasre; Ashraf Ahmed Qurtame; Ali Ait Boughrous; Nadia Lahrach
records.abstract: Accidental oil spills in the Alboran Sea represent a high-risk hazard because intense maritime traffic, semi-enclosed circulation, and sensitive Moroccan coastal ecosystems converge within a narrow coastal corridor. Operational-scale simulations for the Nador-Saïdia sector remain scarce, particularly for persistent heavy fuel oil and for the combined effects of mesoscale circulation, wind drift, Stokes drift, vertical mixing, and weathering. This study applies the OpenOil module of the OpenDrift Lagrangian framework to simulate a hypothetical release of 100 tons of heavy fuel oil (Generic Bunker C) offshore the Driouch coast (35.45° N, 2.95° W) over a seven-day (168 h) period, beginning on 02 July 2024 at 12:00 UTC. The model was forced with CMEMS Mediterranean physics fields, CMEMS Mediterranean wave data, and NOAA-GFS 10 m winds. The selected summer scenario represents a high-impact vulnerability case characterized by strong stratification, sea-breeze influence, peak beach-tourism exposure, and high ecological sensitivity of the Marchica Lagoon, Moulouya River estuary, and Cap des Trois Fourches. The simulations incorporated high-resolution meteorological and oceanographic forcing from CMEMS and NOAA-GFS. Results highlight the strong influence of mesoscale circulation patterns in the Alboran Sea, particularly the interaction between regional gyres, the Algerian Current, and local wind-driven drift. Lagrangian trajectories indicate a dominant east–southeastward transport, posing a direct threat to environmentally sensitive coastal areas. By the end of the simulation, 4,253 particles were stranded, corresponding to approximately 85.1 t of oil, while 747 particles remained active at sea, corresponding to approximately 14.9 t. Weathering was dominated by emulsification and viscosity increase, whereas evaporation remained limited to approximately 10–15% of the released mass and natural dispersion remained below 10%. The revised analysis indicates that high viscosity and density lower than seawater explain the long surface residence time of fresh Bunker C, while sedimentation risk becomes critical mainly in shallow, sediment-rich environments through oil-mineral aggregation. The study identifies priority coastal exposure pathways and provides management-relevant guidance for preparedness planning, including pre-positioning of response equipment adapted to viscous oils, rapid protection of lagoon inlets where feasible, and transboundary coordination between Morocco and Algeria.

records.title: Divergent trends in post-landfall decay of strong and weak tropical cyclones
records.authors: Chenxi Hu; Xinxin Sui; Dev Niyogi; Clint N. Dawson; Zong-Liang Yang
records.abstract: Abstract Tropical cyclone post-landfall decay strongly influences inland hazard exposure, yet most studies assume that environmental change affects storms of different intensities uniformly. Here we identify an intensity-dependent divergence in global trends of tropical cyclone post-landfall decay. Analyzing 885 observed events (1979–2024), we show that strong storms (≥29 m/s) now weaken 18.6% faster after landfall, whereas weak storms persist 14.5% longer inland. These contrasting trends arise from different environmental sensitivities. Weak storms respond primarily to thermodynamic factors, including sea-surface warming, enhanced atmospheric moisture, and increased oceanic influence along storm tracks, all of which favor prolonged inland persistence. In contrast, strong storms are more sensitive to dynamic and land-surface conditions, including faster translation speeds, increasing atmospheric stability, and drier soil, which collectively promote faster decay. Numerical experiments further demonstrate that weaker storms respond more strongly to thermodynamic enhancement, whereas stronger storms are more vulnerable to dynamic disruption. These results challenge uniform-response assumptions in tropical cyclone risk assessment, forging a dual-threat landscape: intensifying coastal impacts from faster-decaying strong storms alongside expanding inland risks from increasingly persistent weak systems. Our findings reveal pronounced intensity-dependent heterogeneity in tropical cyclones, urging refined hazard assessment and adaptation for vulnerable and unprepared regions worldwide.

records.title: Global Inflation After COVID-19 and Monetary-Policy Responses in Developing and Developed Countries
records.authors: Dr. Muhammad Irfan; Sundas Iftikhar; Dr. Waas Khan; Imran Ul Haq
records.abstract: This study examines the drivers of global inflation after COVID-19 and compares the timing, instruments, and effectiveness of monetary-policy responses in developed and developing countries. It adopts a quantitative, explanatory, and comparative panel-data design covering 2019–2025, with 2019 serving as the pre-pandemic baseline. Secondary data on consumer-price inflation, policy interest rates, exchange rates, economic growth, fiscal support, energy and food prices, external conditions, and governance are drawn from the International Monetary Fund, World Bank, Bank for International Settlements, and other official sources. The analysis combines descriptive trend comparisons with pooled ordinary least squares, fixed-effects, and random-effects models, including an interaction term to test whether monetary-policy transmission differs by development status. The findings indicate that post-pandemic inflation resulted from the interaction of supply-chain disruptions, reopening demand, expansionary fiscal and monetary policies, commodity-price shocks, and exchange-rate depreciation. Developed economies initially relied on very low interest rates, quantitative easing, and extensive fiscal support, then shifted to rapid rate increases and balance-sheet tightening. Developing economies often tightened earlier because of imported inflation, currency depreciation, capital outflows, and external-debt pressures. Although global tightening and easing supply constraints reduced inflation after its 2022 peak, disinflation was generally faster in developed economies. Developing countries experienced more persistent pressures because of import dependence, weaker currencies, limited fiscal space, and less effective policy transmission. The study concludes that monetary tightening is necessary but insufficient and should be complemented by fiscal discipline, credible institutions, supply-side reforms, food and energy security, reserve management, and targeted protection for vulnerable households. records.title: Station-specific thunderstorm forecasting using climate predictors with seasonal decomposition analysis in Bangladesh’s most vulnerable regions
records.authors: Mohammad Mahboob Hussain Khan; Amrin Binte Ahmed; Adisha Dulmini; Rawfun Nahin Kowbi; Dulsaba Azmain; Muhammad Abu Sufian; Md. Mahin Uddin Qureshi; Mustafizur Rahman; Rumana Rois
records.abstract: Thunderstorms pose significant threats to life, agriculture, and infrastructure in Bangladesh, particularly in the northeastern regions of Sylhet, Sreemangal, and Mymensingh. This study develops and rigorously evaluates localized thunderstorm frequency forecasting models for these high-risk stations using 40 years (1985–2024) of monthly data and thirty six modeling approaches encompassing classical time series (SARIMA/SARIMAX, ETS/ETSX), machine learning (ANN/ANNX, SVR/SVRX, XGBoost/XGBoostX), and deep learning (LSTM/LSTMX) architectures, applied to raw and seasonally adjusted (X-11, STL) data under both univariate and exogenous frameworks incorporating five climatic variables (temperature, relative humidity, cloud cover, rainfall, atmospheric pressure). Correlation analysis identified cloud cover ( r = 0.83–0.88), atmospheric pressure ( r = −0.79 to −0.85), temperature ( r = 0.77–0.79), and rainfall ( r = 0.74–0.78) as dominant meteorological drivers of thunderstorm activity. Seasonal pre-adjustment using STL substantially improved forecast accuracy, with STL-XGBoost achieving the lowest univariate errors (Sylhet: RMSE = 2.53; Sreemangal: 2.09; Mymensingh: 2.08). Inclusion of exogenous variables dramatically enhanced predictive skill with tree-based and kernel methods: STL-XGBoostX with climate predictors proved optimal for Sylhet (MASE = 0.22), while STL-SVRX with climate predictors was optimal for Sreemangal and Mymensingh (MASE = 0.17), representing over 80% improvement compared to univariate benchmarks. Seasonal forecasts (2025–2028) project peak monsoon activity reaching 100.5 frequency at Sreemangal and identify April–August as the critical preparedness window for these stations. This study provides the Bangladesh Meteorological Department with a validated, operational framework for station-specific thunderstorm frequency forecasting, demonstrating that explicit seasonal decomposition combined with tree-based ensemble and kernel methods offers robust accuracy for early warning systems. The methodology can be extended to additional stations and integrated with socio-economic data to enhance disaster preparedness and climate adaptation strategies for Bangladesh’s most thunderstorm-vulnerable communities.

records.title: Disaster, displacement, and distress: Earthquake intensity and persistent mental health effects in urban New Zealand
records.authors: Thoa Hoang
records.abstract: Abstract This study estimates the causal effect of spatially varying earthquake intensity on long-term mental health outcomes using linked administrative panel data on 236,856 adults in Greater Christchurch (2007–2019). Exploiting meshblock-level Modified Mercalli Intensity (MMI) variation as a continuous treatment in a difference-in-differences design with individual fixed effects, we find that each unit increase in MMI raises psychiatric medication use by 5.3% (0.051 medications per person-year), with effects persisting six to eight years post-disaster. Impacts are heterogeneous: point estimates are larger for adults aged 65 and older, those without tertiary education, and individuals with severe housing damage, with these differences confirmed by formal tests; effects are also directionally larger for women, though the gender gap itself is not statistically significant. Mediation analysis shows that employment disruption explains the effect among working-age adults but not among the elderly - the most affected group - pointing to unobserved channels such as social network disruption. Hospital admissions rise modestly (5.5%), confirming that exposure primarily generates mild-to-moderate distress. These findings call for differentiated recovery policies targeting labor market support for working-age adults and community-based interventions for older populations.

records.title: Deploying open-architecture infrastructure for critical zone monitoring: lessons from the environmental sensing and data network
records.authors: Boris Dessimond; Stephen M. J. Moysey; Char'Rese Finney; Rob Howard; Alex K. Manda
records.abstract: Introduction Characterizing Critical Zone processes requires high-frequency, spatially distributed environmental data. Environmental wireless sensing networks (WSNs) can meet this need, but few researchers currently implement this infrastructure themselves, instead relying on legacy data loggers that require manual data retrieval or commercial telemetry systems that are too often hindered by financial and logistical constraints, e.g., sensor lock in, proprietary data models, recurring cellular fees, and lack of programmatic data access (e.g., APIs). Yet advances in the Internet of Things (IoT) have made the deployment of WSNs more accessible than ever before. Understanding the current state of WSN technologies and documenting deployment cases is therefore important for broadening the use of environmental WSNs to both advance Critical Zone science and expand access to monitoring through participatory sensing. Methods We describe the Environmental Sensing and Data Network (ESDN), a multi-site infrastructure in eastern North Carolina that demonstrates a complete, off-the-shelf solution for distributed environmental monitoring. Combining LoRaWAN telemetry, a self-hosted ThingsBoard IoT backend, and cloud archiving, the ESDN integrates diverse legacy and modern sensors into a unified, interoperable data environment. Results Since its deployment in mid-2024, the network has expanded across contrasting urban, agricultural, and coastal wetland environments, growing to 110 deployed sensors and 14 communications gateways. These deployments successfully capture real-time processes across developed and natural landscapes, including surface-subsurface hydrologic coupling, saltwater intrusion dynamics, and urban stormwater responses. Cloud-based rule engines minimize power and computational loads on edge devices and enable real-time analytics, while the ESDN's open time-series APIs support data-driven workflows and artificial intelligence-ready applications. Discussion This paper both provides the current technology context for WSN deployment and an empirical demonstration as a blueprint for how open-source software and hardware tools can be used to deploy scalable, replicable, highly cost-effective, and analytically robust environmental sensing networks.

records.title: Multimodal Thinking with Renderable Programs
records.authors: Sunli Chen; Ding Zhong; Ziqiao Ma; Jiaxin Liu; Zeyuan Yang; Hao Zhang; Lie Lu; Joyce Chai; Chuang Gan
records.abstract: Current vision-language models (VLMs) excel at visual content understanding and text-based reasoning, yet their structure limits the advancement of incorporating images into the reasoning chain. Though Omnimodal models have made efforts in unifying text and image generation, they focus on visual tasks in the open-domain, lacking tractability due to rasterized or latent representations of images. We introduce SVGLM, a framework that uses scalable vector graphics (SVG) primitives to connect text and image in reasoning tasks. We exploit the duality of SVG as both image description and text instructions, yielding a more compact, interpretable solution to equip general VLMs with the capability of generating images within the reasoning process. We provide a large curated dataset of SVG-based image editing dataset, as well as the paradigm to tune open-source VLMs. Experiments on a mathematical reasoning benchmark demonstrate that SVGLM achieves strong SVG generation power as well as think-with-image intelligence. Our results highlight SVG as a suitable medium for building more robust digital domain agents, bridging the gap between text-based thinking and pixel-based images.

records.title: Application of Gröbner basis methodology to geometrically nonlinear axisymmetric circular isotropic plates
records.authors: T. M. Harrell; Y. J. Liu; J. Peddieson
records.abstract: Abstract This paper presents a systematic method for obtaining closed-form solutions to nonlinear engineering mechanics problems by combining weighted-residual approximations with Gröbner basis algebraic elimination. The proposed new approach begins with a weighted residual approximation technique of the governing nonlinear equations, such as Rayleigh–Ritz or Galerkin method, resulting in a coupled system of multivariate polynomial algebraic equations. Gröbner basis methodology is then used to transform the coupled system into an equivalent decoupled form that can, under certain conditions, be solved analytically. The novelty of the work lies in exploiting Gröbner basis techniques can be used as an enabling tool to derive closed-form solutions from nonlinear mechanics formulations that would traditionally be solved numerically. The methodology is demonstrated through the geometrically nonlinear analysis of axisymmetric circular isotropic plates based on Kirchhoff–von Kármán plate theory. Three representative boundary-condition cases are considered: clamped, simply-supported immovable, and simply-supported with an overhang. The Rayleigh–Ritz formulation generates the coupled polynomial equations that are symbolically decoupled using Gröbner bases and subsequently solved to obtain closed-form expressions for transverse displacement, stresses, moments, and shear forces. Results are validated against finite element solutions and show good agreement, with errors below 4% for large-deflection cases where linear theory becomes highly inaccurate. The resulting symbolic solutions retain the geometric, material, and loading parameters in explicit form, making parametric studies and design investigations significantly more efficient than repeated numerical simulations. The study therefore demonstrates the potential of a new general framework for deriving analytical solutions in many nonlinear structural mechanics that arise in several engineering applications.

records.title: Defending ecology and evolution in an age of democratic backsliding and environmental crisis
records.authors: Dennis L. Murray
records.abstract: Frontiers journals encourage editors to publish perspectives pieces that overview the field and chart the journal's future direction. In my role as Field Chief Editor for Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution, I deviate from traditional format by offering a dire warning and urgent challenge to researchers, students, educators, and policymakers across ecology, evolution, and environmental science. Recent events at the confluence of democratic backsliding, erosion of academic institutions, and declining environmental governance threaten to radically alter the state of the world as we know it and our ability to sustain vigorous research and influence future policy decisions. If left unchecked, these converging forces will not simply hinder progress but bolster the dismantling of scientific capacity required to confront ongoing environmental crises. We must brace for impact by forcefully protecting the foundation of acquired knowledge, maintaining productive and relevant research in areas of global importance, and disseminating findings and expertise broadly so they are recognized as vital contributions to society. Given current trends across many liberal democracies, these are not small tasks.The last eight decades witnessed a Golden Age of scientific discovery, with nations mainly in the Western world and led by the United States, supporting transformational research across virtually all scientific disciplines (Baker, 2014;Powell et al., 2017). Notwithstanding prominent global inequities, developed nations advanced countless discoveries propelled by computational and technological advances that were previously unimaginable and that now fuel innumerable benefits to human health and prosperity (Dong et al., 2016;Coccia, 2023;Wang et al. 2023). Ecology and evolution experienced remarkable breakthroughs during this period, combining theoretical, observational, experimental, and analytical approaches to deepen our understanding of organismal function, variation, and interactions with the environment (Krebs, 2006;Bonsall and Charlesworth, 2010). Notably, these advances went beyond mere academic inquiry and also informed environmental policy and conservation efforts, helping manage species and ecosystems in the face of global change (Carpenter et al., 2009, Kareiva andMarvier, 2012). Such contributions are vital in light of ongoing biodiversity loss and climate crises that will intensify in the coming decades (Bellard et al., 2012;Segan et al., 2016).Recent history shows that scientific discovery and innovation are most successful and impactful in liberal democracies, where evidence-based scholarship is valued and governments support academia by protecting the right to teach, investigate, and disseminate knowledge without interference or censorship (Cole, 2017;Whetsell et al., 2021). In these systems, governments allocate public funds for infrastructure, salaries, and research while honouring institutional autonomy over governance and curricula. In return, academic institutions train the next generation of skilled professionals, conduct research and scholarship in areas of pressing societal importance, and provide knowledge and expertise through various forms of professional or public service. Yet, despite that democratic nations were well-served by this arrangement for decades, its long-term stability is increasingly in doubt. Since the early 2000s, many democracies have faced structural, economic, and governance challenges that threaten their integrity and place them on a path of democratic regression (Waldner and Lust, 2018;Diamond, 2021). The rise of populist and neonationalist movements, often fuelled by economic anxiety, cultural grievance, and demographic change, has shifted political power toward more repressive and authoritarian styles of governance (Galston, 2018;Berman, 2021). As these movements gain traction, they erode a healthy democracy's key features, including support for academic institutions and evidence-based policy decisions (Mede and Schäfer, 2020;V-Dem Institute, 2025; Figure 1). Almost universally, such movements depict universities as out of step with public needs, training students with ill-suited skills, and conducting expensive, esoteric research (Motta 2018;Merkley, 2020). These narratives resonate with segments of society lacking post-secondary education, allowing attacks on academia to be framed as fiscal prudence and reining-in the elite class (Gideon and Hall, 2017;Mede and Schäfer, 2020;Gligorić et al. 2025).The anti-democratic playbook includes measures designed to limit academia's societal influence, including restrictions on institutional funding, constraints on self-governance and curricular autonomy, threats to tenure and employment security, and curbs on free expression (Cole, 2017;Fernandez et al., 2024; Figure 2). Repressive governments often target research that does not align with official priorities or ideology, including basic curiosity-driven inquiry and investigations aimed at strengthening environmental needs. For example, research addressing evolutionary biology, environmental protection measures, climate change impacts, and at-risk species conservation tends to be valued in functioning democracies but frequently delegitimized in more repressive regimes (e.g., Rydén et al., 2019;Menezes and Barbosa, 2021;Frizelle et al., 2025;Temple, 2025). Research defunding may be framed as austerity measures or fiscal reallocations, often directing funds toward politically aligned programs while leaving other disciplines underresourced. Even when research funding is maintained, it is often more restrictive or administered through cost-sharing partnerships with business or special interest groups, thereby reducing efficiency and weakening direct links between objective academic inquiry and societal advancement (Dziundziuk, 2024;Pandey et al., 2025). Concurrently, populist and authoritarian movements often promote science skepticism and diminish the role of expert knowledge in policy decisions (Schlaufer and Van den Dool, 2024). When combined with reduced transparency and restricted public access to information, these measures erode public trust in institutions and reduce engagement in policy processes (Hernández-Huerta and Inclán, 2025). Collectively, such strategies weaken the autonomy and influence of academic institutions and progressively decouple research activity from the broader societal needs it is intended to serve (Figure 2).An additional feature of democratic regression is that emerging regimes frequently prioritize economic growth over environmental protection and sustainability (Pentz et al., 2025; Figure 1). As the administrative state and public service are weakened or dismantled, environmental oversight and regulations are often removed, relaxed, or inconsistently enforced (Blum and Sellers, 2025), resulting in reduced environmental monitoring, declining quality standards, and diminished protection for sensitive habitats and at-risk species (Kates-Garnick, 2025; Meek and Börk, 2025;Shiffman, 2025;Orr, 2025). Activities such as basic research, monitoring, and assessment of species and ecosystems are particularly vulnerable, whether conducted directly by government agencies or through partnerships with academia and non-governmental organizations (Böhmelt, 2021;Halligan, 2021;Lockwood and Lockwood, 2022). Consequently, data on environmental baselines, human impacts, and mitigation strategies becomes less accessible (e.g., Dillon et al., 2019) while expert involvement in policy decisions is increasingly devalued, leading to weakened evidence-based environmental governance. Collectively, these losses activate a feedback loop promoting increased public detachment from environmental governance and policy, thereby reinforcing populist sentiments in society (Figure 2). It follows that losses in environmental research and policy in one nation can extend to other countries given the large spatial scale of many environmental problems and frequent need for coordinated scientific and regulatory responses (Steffen et al., 2015). Thus, ongoing and predicted increases in global biodiversity loss and climate change impacts place society in a perfect storm with far fewer scientific and regulatory guardrails.Democratic losses and related impacts on academia and the environment are well-documented in countries such as Hungary, Turkey, India, and Russia (Sundar, 2018;Ignatieff, 2023;Grigoriadis and Canpolat, 2024), but similar trends, often less overt, are present in nearly all major democracies worldwide. Over the past two decades, the majority of G20 nations, representing roughly 85% of global GDP, 75% of international trade, and 67% of the world's population, have exhibited signs of democratic regression (Diamond, 2020;Williamson et al., 2025), declining support for academic institutions (Fernandez et al., 2024;Lott, 2024;Hernández-Huerta & Inclán, 2025), and weakening environmental oversight (Pentz et al., 2025; see Supplementary Figure 1). Countries that recently signed international agreements to curb greenhouse gas emissions or expand land and water protection have quietly backtracked on their commitments (Lamb et al., 2020;Roelfsema et al., 2020;Roberts, 2024;Specht, 2025). In most cases, national priorities now emphasize economic growth and defence spending over support for higher education or environmental protection.These changes extend far beyond a simple rightward political shift. Even nations traditionally viewed as exemplars of liberal democracy, including my own country, Canada, classified as a "Full Democracy" (see Economist Intelligence Unit, 2014; 2024) and celebrated for freedom and environmental stewardship, have gradually slipped in measures of democratic performance and academic and environmental protection (see Savoie, 2019;Erl, 2020;Stockemeyer and Gaspard, 2025; Evidence for Democracy, 2025; Supplementary Figure 1). Indeed, Canada is increasingly reliant on private-public partnerships to support academic research (Canadian Association of University Teachers n.d.), which especially harms 'basic' research productivity because of its lessened link to revenue generation or societal benefit. Canada is increasingly supported by environmental policy outcomes with political rather than evidence-based motivations (Piper et al., 2022;Migone et al., 2024), imposes various forms of interference on government scientists working on environmental issues (Turner, 2013;Robertson et al., 2023), and has surprisingly weak environmental standards and governance (Cooke et al., 2016;OECD, 2017;Gibson et al., 2019;Ray et al., 2021). Canada's quiet backtracking on international commitments, such as the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, and its retreat from Paris Climate Accord targets, represent an insidious version of the overt assaults on environmental governance seen in less democratic nations.More dramatically and impactfully, the United States is in the midst of a slide into full-blown authoritarianism, with attendant erosion of its basic democratic, academic and environmental standards (Carrier and Carothers, 2025;Scholars at Risk, 2025) and uncertainty as to whether this trend will soon be reversed (Fernandez and Hutchens, 2025). Meanwhile, China's ascent as a global superpower offers little reassurance given its undeniable authoritarian structure and low rankings in key democratic and environmental metrics (Economist Intelligence Unit 2014; V-Dem Institute, 2025). Figure 1 and Supplementary Figure 1 synthesize these trends, illustrating how democratic backsliding is broadly associated with declines in academic freedom and environmental performance across regime types. Although some democratic nations retain the potential to provide global leadership on matters of democracy and the environment that are currently neglected by superpower nations, most face domestic challenges that limit their capacity to act forcefully. Thus, the global nature of current biodiversity and climate crises, transcending national borders and political regimes, will require unconventional responses if we are to avert a profoundly dark period in human history.A variety of strategies exist for resisting democratic regression and reversing authoritarian encroachment, and academics like Hannah Arendt, Bertrand Russell, and Timothy Snyder exemplify the long tradition of intellectual resistance to anti-democratic forces (Said, 1994). While such engagement has historically been more common in the humanities and social sciences, natural scientists tend to be less engaged and may encounter greater structural or reputational barriers to public advocacy (e.g., Rodrigues et al., 2023). Nevertheless, for researchers, educators, and policy specialists in ecology, evolution, and related fields, engagement should be viewed as necessary and may involve forming broad, sometimes unorthodox coalitions to strengthen democratic foundations and safeguard academic integrity and research, while simultaneously reinforcing public trust in institutions and evidence-based decision-making. The strategies outlined below are broadly applicable across disciplines and draw inspiration from humanities and social science research on best practices for countering democratic backslide and resisting authoritarianism (Acemoglu and Robinson, 2012;Snyder, 2017Snyder, , 2018;;Gamboa, 2022;Johnson et al., 2024;Bunce et al., 2025).Data purges and disinformation. Public data accessibility and integrity are at risk in declining democracies, with information from sources such as government environmental monitoring programs or partnerships with other entities being especially vulnerable. Authoritarian regimes tend not to adhere to FAIR (findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable) standards (O'Connor et al., 2019), and environmental datasets can be selectively removed or altered (Grigoriadis and Canpolat, 2024). Hungary ended longitudinal analysis of key air and water quality datasets while Turkey's repressions removed key personnel responsible for monitoring endangered species (Böhmelt, 2021;Halligan, 2021). These disruptions delayed critical biodiversity assessments and reduced data availability for global climate models, illustrating the broad consequences of data suppression and targeted academic repression on research continuity.In response to such actions, coalitions can work to protect public data, ensuring that datasets and findings remain broadly available in the future. This type of response is illustrated by the coalition of academics and non-governmental organizations who recently downloaded a variety of public datasets prior to their deletion from U.S. Government websites (Lucas, 2025, National Security Archive, 2025, Pacenza et al., 2025). records.title: Editorial: Learning for democracy
records.authors: Titus Alexander
records.abstract: The collection begins by revisiting foundational democratic theories and applying them to modern educational contexts. Yi-Huang Shih provides inspiration by revisiting John Dewey's ideas, framing democracy not just as a form of government but as a mode of associated living and communicated experience. Building on the conceptual nature of engagement, Helmut Heid, Michael Jüttler, and Tobias Kärner provide a rigorous conceptual analysis of student participation in the classroom, questioning whether and how these micro-level interactions serve as a legitimate basis for broader democracy education.Several papers examine the specific factors that drive or hinder student participation within higher education. Yang Lin and colleagues investigate the personal and institutional determinants of civic engagement, highlighting that student involvement is a product of both individual motivation and the institutional environment. This is complemented by the work of Ali Assad Watfa and Driss Ait Ali, whose research demonstrates the mediating effect of university citizenship promotion in transforming national loyalty into active student political participation.A significant portion of the Research Topic addresses how education functions in societies facing social fragmentation or the aftermath of conflict. In the context of intergroup tension, Devora Hellerstein and Mahmood Sindiani present "the roaming course," a method for fostering intergroup relationships among Arab and Jewish students within physical education teacher education, illustrating the power of shared physical activity in building democratic empathy. On a systemic level, Mohamed Yusuf Adan utilizes a "4Rs framework analysis" to explore the role of peace education in promoting social justice and sustainable peace in post-conflict societies, providing a structural lens for democratic reconstruction.Modern democracy also faces threats from within the digital and cultural spheres. Lucia Picarella examines the intersections of the digital society, specifically how "cancel culture" and "fake news" distort contemporary public discourse, presenting challenges for educators trying to foster rational democratic debate. In Chile, Jesús Marolla-Gajardo highlights the risks to democracy by analyzing the beliefs of teachers regarding the transmission of hate speech within teacher education, emphasizing the urgent need for pedagogical interventions against intolerance.The Research Topic also provides deep dives into specific regional challenges. Two papers focus on Indonesia: Sarbaini Sarbaini discusses the challenges and opportunities of enhancing civic education for nationalism in Indonesian higher education, balancing national identity with democratic values. Meanwhile, Rahmat Muhammad and colleagues offer an original research case study on rational choice and political imaging during legislative elections in East Luwu, providing empirical evidence of how democratic processes play out in resource-rich mining areas.A core theme emerging from these diverse studies is the need for more effective social models to drive change. Titus Alexander proposes that we view institutions as social models and 'dynamic theories'. This hypothesis suggests that social and political sciences can increase their impact by moving beyond observation and analysis to using research to actively inform and improve practice. Each paper in this collection explores different models of learning for democracy, whether for student participation in the classroom, intervening against hate speech, bridging differences through physical education or any of the other topics. The hypothesis proposes that scholars should work with practitioners to develop the working model itself, not just the conceptual theories about it, because every working model embodies a great deal of knowledge embedded in its infrastructure, norms, protocols, power dynamics, and relationships, as well as the beliefs and other mental models used to guide it (see Fig. 1). It argues that this can be seen as the social science equivalent of theories in the natural sciences. This approach suggests that learning for democracy is not a one-time educational event but a continuous process of theory, practice, reflection, research and evaluation, to continuously improve the model. It also recognises the importance of institutional support.In conclusion, the papers in this Research Topic demonstrate that while democracy is under pressure, universities and educators are developing innovative methods-from intergroup "roaming courses" to the "4Rs framework"-to strengthen it. The common thread is that learning for democracy must be an active, institutional priority that connects classroom participation with civic responsibility. By adopting dynamic social theories, the academic community can better equip the next generation to navigate digital misinformation, overcome social conflict, and revitalize democratic norms worldwide.

records.title: Learning from the past, building the future: AI in geotechnical engineering through the FOMLIG 2025 NextGen initiatives
records.authors: Mohammad Sadegh Farhadi; Alireza Duzandeh; Arianna Pucci
records.abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping engineering disciplines, and geotechnical engineering is no exception. The next generation of geotechnical engineers must not only learn to use AI tools, but understand where they come from, what assumptions they rest on, and where they may fail. This paper reports on three intertwined NextGen initiatives hosted at the 3 rd workshop on the Future of Machine Learning in Geotechnics (FOMLIG3 2025) in Florence, Italy. First, a Museum of AI showcased twenty landmark papers from Karl Pearson’s principal component analysis (1901) to GPT-3 (2020), tracing the historical foundations of modern AI alongside the intellectual heritage of Renaissance Florence. Second, a NextGen Student Competition challenged participants worldwide to predict shear wave velocity ( V s ) from piezocone penetration test (CPTu) data for offshore wind turbine foundation design, attracting 22 competing teams and six extended abstract presentations. Third, structured community exchanges captured practitioner and researcher perspectives on the challenges, opportunities, and future directions of AI in geotechnical engineering through open discussions. The perspectives gathered span data quality and physical modeling, education and skill development, ethics and governance, and industry practice and trust. Together, these initiatives offer a multidimensional portrait of AI adoption in geotechnical engineering and document the lessons learnt for the benefit of the broader community.

records.title: Unbounded inclusiveness and the ethics of bordering: domination, responsibility, and epistemic justice beyond the open/closed divide
records.authors: Jussi P. Laine
records.abstract: Contemporary border regimes operate through dispersed, technologically mediated, and externally delegated practices that exceed the traditional statist–cosmopolitan debate. This article argues that the central ethical problem is not simply whether states may exclude, but whether the practices through which bordering is organized can be justified to those who are subjected to them. Drawing on algorithmic governance, detention, externalization, and climate‑related displacement, it shows how contemporary enforcement produces domination, vulnerability, and epistemic exclusion that admissions‑focused theories struggle to capture. The article advances unbounded inclusiveness as a normative orientation that treats territorial membership as neither the sole source nor the natural limit of political responsibility. Responsibility instead follows the historical, ecological, economic, cultural, and political relationships through which bordering creates and distributes vulnerability. Unbounded inclusiveness is distinctive not because it advocates more open borders, but because it offers a standard for evaluating bordering practices wherever they occur. Those affected must be able to contribute to the knowledge on which such practices rest, challenge the power exercised over them, and hold institutions accountable for the responsibilities arising from their relationships. Epistemic justice and non‑domination are therefore not supplementary concerns but conditions of legitimate bordering. The article concludes by clarifying how this framework reorients border ethics towards the relational conditions through which contemporary bordering generates obligations and harm.

records.title: The Consensus and the Remainder: Comments on Four Views on Free Will, Second Edition
records.authors: Robert H. Wallace
records.abstract: In the second edition of Four Views on Free Will , John Martin Fischer, Robert Kane, Derk Pereboom, and Manuel Vargas have converged on a way of thinking about the free will debate that I dub “The Practical Consensus”. They agree, to varying degrees, that there are robust justifications for some moral responsibility practices even if we do not have libertarian free will. I agree too. But this revisionist-friendly way of thinking about the debate leaves a metaphysical remainder, a bit of thought and practice that resists forward-looking or otherwise anti-libertarian explanation. While this consensus should push Fischer and Pereboom towards free will revisionism, it leaves Vargas and all the authors—even Kane the libertarian—vulnerable in how they treat the remainder. I argue that metaphysical worries about “fundamental unfairness” remain, not as threats to the justification of moral responsibility practices, but as pressures on how those practices are expressed given our practical interests and self-understandings, even within single-tiered forward-looking responsibility systems that eschew basic desert. Though no view is unscathed, perhaps Fischer’s semicompatibilism turns out to be the most honest bookkeeper.

records.title: Polymers for Detecting or Protecting Against Chemical Warfare Agents: Recent Advances and Future Perspectives
records.authors: Xiaotong Yue; Tingting Wang; Aishuo Yu; Xiaopeng Li; Min Zhang; Xiaohui Zheng; Xinglan Wang; Yingru Li; Xiaoshan Yan; Li Li; Wei He
records.abstract: The persistent threat of chemical warfare agents (CWAs) drives the need for advanced detection and protective technologies. Polymers, with their tunable structures, ease of functionalization, and lightweight nature, have emerged as a versatile platform in this field. This review systematically summarizes recent progress in polymer-based materials for CWA sensing and protection, with emphasis on interaction mechanisms and structure–property relationships. In the realm of sensing, the working principles of polymer-based systems are rooted in electron transfer, hydrogen bonding, fluorescence quenching, and colorimetric response. Conductive polymers enable chemiresistive detection through charge transfer; hydrogen-bond acidic polymers provide selective recognition of organophosphorus agents; conjugated polymers exploit fluorescence quenching via the “molecular wire” effect; and polydiacetylenes offer visible color changes for naked-eye detection. Representative materials and their performance metrics are critically compared. For protection and decontamination, current polymer systems are designed around four synergistic mechanisms: barrier action, physical adsorption, filtration, and catalytic degradation. Barrier layers based on crosslinked networks or graphene/MOF composites suppress agent permeation while maintaining breathability. Porous polymers such as polymers of intrinsic microporosity (PIMs) and coordination polymers provide high-capacity adsorption through tailored surface functionality. Electrospun nanofiber membranes effectively filter aerosolized agents with low air resistance. Catalytic composites incorporating Zr-MOFs or single-atom catalysts enable hydrolysis of nerve agents and oxidation of blister agents under ambient conditions, with recent advances achieving self-buffering and solid-state operation. Despite significant advances, challenges remain in selectivity, environmental stability, and balancing protection with wearer comfort. Future directions point toward multifunctional systems that integrate detection, protection, and self-detoxification within wearable polymer platforms for next-generation chemical defense.

records.title: Mapping the gender attrition gap in academic psychology.
records.authors: Xinyi Zhao; Anna I. Thoma; Ralph Hertwig; Dirk U. Wulff
records.abstract: Women comprise the majority of students and early-career scholars in psychology, yet they are less likely to remain active in research over time. This pattern raises a central question: At what stages of academic careers do women disproportionately leave academia, and what factors drive their attrition? Using large-scale bibliometric data tracking 78,216 psychologists who began publishing between 2000 and 2014, we examine gender differences in research career attrition operationalized through publishing activity across the full trajectory from entry onward. Although women accounted for more than 60% of new entrants, they experienced higher attrition rates than men, with the gender gap peaking approximately 5 years after first publication. Early-career performance-particularly first-authored publications-was the strongest predictor of subsequent retention, whereas last-authored publications were most closely associated with continued activity at later-career stages. Collaboration patterns and institutional context also shaped career persistence, though less strongly than publication indicators. Notably, gender differences in research attrition persisted even after accounting for these career determinants, especially during early-career stages. These findings suggest that gender inequality in psychology is driven less by recruitment than by differential retention over time. Addressing early-career vulnerability may therefore be essential to achieving equitable representation in senior academic leadership within the discipline. records.title: Mutation-resilient RBD binding and host protection: Piperine for pediatric COVID-19
records.authors: Shu-wei Beh; Yu Heng Liew; Gideon Khoo; Lyn R Griffiths; Loo Keat Wei
records.abstract: COVID-19 presents an escalating threat in children, manifesting as persistent respiratory, neurological, and multisystem complications, alongside elevated risks of myocarditis, thromboembolism, and autoimmune dysregulation. Emerging Omicron subvariants, including BA.2, BA.2.86, and JN.1, exhibit pronounced immune evasion, undermining current therapeutics. Pediatric populations are particularly vulnerable due to immature immune and metabolic systems, and the safety profile of nirmatrelvir in this group remains inadequately characterized. Here, we identify piperine, alone or in combination with curcumin, as a dual-function, pediatric-compatible phytopharmaceutical. Molecular docking across B.1.1.529, BA.2, and a homology-modeled JN.1 receptor binding domain (RBD) demonstrated that piperine forms low-energy, structurally stable complexes (ΔG = – 8.46 kcal/mol), in contrast to nirmatrelvir (ΔG = – 7.20 kcal/mol), and consistently engages mutationally constrained RBM and core residues. Piperine retains robust binding even though structural analyses reveal that coordinated mutations (S371F, T376A, V445H, G446S, L452W, E484K, F486P) remodeled the β-sheets and α-helices of the RBD, which may affect ACE2 and antibody interactions. Complementary ADME and drug-likeness assessments further support its oral bioavailability and dietary suitability. Collectively, these findings position piperine, with or without curcumin, as a dual-action therapeutic, i.e., combining mechanistic antiviral activity through mutation-resilient RBD engagement with systemic protective effects. This strategy highlights its potential as a safe, diet-compatible adjunct to mitigate COVID-19 sequelae in children, offering a translationally relevant approach for variant-adapted pediatric care.

records.title: Voices on Fire: Narratives on Nurse Activism Amid Power Dynamics in the Philippines
records.authors: Gilbert D. Bernardino; Rufina Calub Abul
records.abstract: ABSTRACT This study explored the narratives of 10 Filipino nurse activists who transformed experiences of suffering, exploitation, and professional marginalization into organized resistance and advocacy. In the Philippine context, nurses continue to face poor working conditions, inadequate compensation, migration pressures, and political threats such as red‐tagging, yet little is known about how they navigate the shift from endurance to activism. Guided by narrative inquiry and informed by Foucauldian archeology and genealogy, the study examined interviews alongside position statements and news articles to uncover the emotional, social, and political dimensions of nurse activism. Findings revealed that mentors, early encounters with injustice, and formative acts of defiance shaped participants' entry into advocacy. Silence, hesitation, and institutional or familial disapproval also emerged as meaningful aspects of their experiences, reflecting the risks and sacrifices tied to public dissent. Participants developed heightened awareness of systemic inequities through volunteer work, the invisibility of nursing labor, and community‐based experiences, motivating advocacy for both fellow nurses and marginalized populations. Despite suppression, disillusionment, and migration pressures, participants sustained activism through research, education, alliance‐building, and community engagement, reframing activism as an extension of care and social accountability. The findings highlight activism as a gradual and evolving process shaped by courage, vulnerability, and persistence, with implications for nursing education, organizational advocacy, and health policy reform in the Philippines.

records.title: When Structure Conditions Memory: The Prospects for a South Korea-Japan Economic and Security Cooperation
records.authors: Daniel Lee; HyunJun Seo
records.abstract: This paper explores the prospects for South Korea-Japan economic and security cooperation beyond the politics of memory.It asks why institutionalized cooperation between South Korea and Japan has remained limited despite persistent strategic incentives.Existing research has often addressed this puzzle through a constructivist lens, emphasizing historical antagonism, mutual distrust rooted in collective memory, and domestic political constraints as primary obstacles to cooperation.This study, however, argues that the politics of memory operates less as a fixed independent cause than as a conditional intervening variable whose influence varies with changes in the surrounding strategic environment.Drawing on a structural realist framework, it theorizes that states divided by mutual suspicion may nevertheless move toward cooperation, not because historical reconciliation has been achieved, but because mounting external pressures make strategic coordination increasingly necessary.Methodologically, the study employs a qualitative comparative case study contrasting the relatively stable regional orders of the Cold War and early post-Cold War periods with the deteriorating strategic environment of the 2020s.It traces changes in structural conditions through peer-reviewed scholarship and, for recent developments, reports from research institutions and international organizations, together with reputable journalistic sources.The analysis focuses on intensifying great-power competition, tightening China-Russia-North Korea coordination, declining confidence in U.S. protection, and resulting economic and security vulnerabilities in Northeast Asia.The findings suggest that these structural pressures have reduced the capacity of historical antagonism to obstruct cooperation, making bilateral coordination more strategically attractive than under earlier regional conditions.Theoretically, this paper identifies the conditions under which strategic necessity may weaken the obstructive influence of historical antagonism.Practically, it suggests that Seoul and Tokyo may benefit from institutionalizing cooperation while structural incentives remain strong, thereby reducing the likelihood that future political disputes will again paralyze bilateral coordination.

records.title: Ensuring Macroeconomic Stability in Azerbaijan: Structural and Innovative Methods for Preventing Currency Crises
records.authors: Javid P. Safarov
records.abstract: DOI kodi: 10.52340/ekonomisti.2026.03.09 Annotation. his study examines the strategic evolution of macroeconomic management in the Republic of Azerbaijan, focusing on the protection of the national currency against exogenous shocks. The research introduces a “systemic triad” framework—comprising structural diversification, digital predictive signaling (AI/Big Data), and institutional-monetary regulation—to shift financial policy from reactive crisis management to proactive, multi-layered risk control. By analyzing the synergy between real-sector development (Agro-Industrial Complex, Middle Corridor, IT services) and advanced analytical monitoring, the paper provides a comprehensive roadmap for insulating the national economy from global volatility. The findings advocate for a robust, high-tech architectural approach that mitigates the risks of "Dutch disease," maximizes the efficiency of state reserves, and establishes a foundation for stable, long-term economic growth. Keywords: macroeconomic stability, currency crisis, Azerbaijan, manat, Central Bank (CBAR), SOFAZ, structural diversification, agribusiness (APC), Big Data, predictive monitoring, Early Warning Systems (EWS). 1. Introduction In the age of post-industrial change, escalating economic fragmentation, and significant volatility in worldwide financial markets, the challenge of maintaining macroeconomic stability assumes a fundamentally new aspect for nations characterized by a small, open, and resource-driven economic framework. The historical experience of Azerbaijan\\\`s financial system distinctly shows that national macroeconomic indicators are strictly influenced by global super-cycles in the hydrocarbon market. Exogenous terms of trade shocks, conveyed via international trade channels, have an immediate, significant, and uneven effect on the nation\\\`s balance of payments, the structure of the domestic foreign exchange market, and thus, on the exchange rate stability of the national currency—the manat. Declining energy prices reveal the fragility of the monetary system to "Dutch disease" effects, drastically decreasing foreign currency supply amid a surge in speculative demand from economic actors, propelled by expectations of devaluation. The conventional set of macroeconomic regulation instruments, historically employed by the Central Bank of the Republic of Azerbaijan (CBAR) and the government, has depended on responsive mechanisms. These comprise extensive direct actions in foreign exchange auctions, regulatory limitations on the open currency positions of commercial banks, and strict sterilization techniques of the money supply via CBAR short-term notes. The primary institutional constraint in this system is the State Oil Fund of the Republic of Azerbaijan (SOFAZ), which performs fiscal equalization and absorbs surplus petrodollars via fixed allocations to the state budget. Nevertheless, amidst the unparalleled surge in cross-border financial movements and the digitization of financial services, the straightforward "firefighting" response strategy is diminishing in its overall effectiveness. Persistent reduction of gold and foreign exchange reserves to uphold a fixed exchange rate can deplete the country\\\`s liquid assets and only preserve structural deficiencies without tackling the underlying issues that create the system\\\`s weakness. As a result, there is a crucial necessity for a basic shift in Azerbaijan\\\`s macroeconomic policy towards proactive (anticipatory) management. The research objective tackled in this study concerns discovering the ideal synergy among foundational long-term changes, contemporary analytical techniques, and functional regulatory mechanisms. This study presents a comprehensive, innovative conceptual framework for macroeconomic security, where technological advancements, monetary policy tools, and the growth of Azerbaijan\\\`s real non-oil sector are considered not as separate institutional trends, but as functionally interconnected components of a cohesive state strategy aimed at preventing currency crises. This study aims to offer a theoretical and practical basis for developing a complex, three-part model to guarantee the enduring sustainability of the national financial landscape. Achieving this objective involved addressing several systemic issues: examining the development of theoretical frameworks for currency crises within resource-dependent economies; creating a conceptual framework for the interplay of protective strategies; and elaborating on the potential of three main aspects of the preventive framework: Structural Methods ("The Foundation"): Focused on the essential diversification of the real economy (high-tech agriculture, transportation routes, IT service exports, and import substitution in the light industry) to create a self-sufficient inflow of foreign currency not reliant on the commodity cycle. Innovative-Technological Methods ("The Signaling System"): Incorporating Early Warning Systems (EWS) into the CBAR framework, employing Big Data and AI technologies, for real-time predictive detection of market irregularities and agent sentiments. Institutional-Monetary Methods ("The Fire Extinguishers"): Showcasing the traditional, collaborative operational response toolkit of the CBAR, Ministry of Finance, and SOFAZ (interventions, adaptable liquidity management through the interest rate corridor, fiscal guidelines) for prompt market stabilization amidst short-term variations. The suggested integrative method enables the transformation of the analytical framework from reactive management to proactive risk mitigation, guaranteeing accurate safeguarding of state resources and fostering stable conditions for the Republic of Azerbaijan\\\`s long-term economic development. 2. Anatomy of Macroeconomic Sustainability: A Systemic Triad of Methods for Protecting the National Currency To maintain the enduring stability of the national currency and shield the macroeconomic framework from harmful external disturbances, regulatory authorities must avoid depending on disconnected or partial instruments. The contemporary financial environment, defined by immediate international information exchange and significant capital movement, necessitates the establishment of a sophisticated, intricately tiered defense mechanism. In this research, this system is envisioned as a comprehensive architectural framework—a "macroeconomic edifice." The building\\\`s strength and adaptability are guaranteed through the clear demarcation and concurrent synergistic collaboration of three essential categories of approaches: structural, innovative-technological, and institutional-financial. Every category of methods possesses its own timeline for implementation, a distinct target of impact within the economy, and carries out a unique, essential role in maintaining the stability of the manat. 2.1. Structural Methods as the "Foundation of the Building" Structural methods represent the basis of all macroeconomic stability. The object of their influence is the real sector of the economy. These methods are aimed at fundamentally changing the proportion of national production, diversifying the export basket, developing non-oil sectors (agribusiness, transport logistics corridors, high-tech sectors, etc.) and implementing a rational import substitution program. According to the macroeconomic estimates of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), Azerbaijan\\\`s non-oil sector showed high resilience to external factors, recording growth dynamics of 9.1% during active macrostructural changes, and then maintaining a stable benchmark of about 6.2% within the medium-term trend [1]. In our architectural metaphor, construction methods serve as the basis for load-bearing and fire resistance. When a country\\\`s economy relies solely on raw material exports, buildings have weak foundations and are susceptible to subsidence when global commodity prices fall. On the contrary, the diversified real sector is forcibly exporting high-profit, high-value-added products under the national brand of \\\`\\\`Made in Azerbaijan,\\\`\\\` thereby physically creating an autonomous channel for foreign currency inflows and dispersing it among various sectors. The main economic function of the Fund is to provide long-term guarantees of natural surplus or balance of payments, thereby reducing the fundamental vulnerability of states to exogenous shocks. However, structural reform is an inertial process that requires large-scale investment and time (3 to 10 years to see results). 2.2. Innovative-Technological Methods as the "Digital Signaling System" While their structural foundations are strengthened and modernized, financial markets face daily risks from speculative attacks, hidden capital flight, and demand shocks. Securing the system requires innovative technological methods that are integrated into the central bank\\\`s analytical and supervisory circuits. They rely on digital technology, big data analytics, and predictive models. The need for such predictive tools is driven by the rapid development of the internal trading space. records.title: Leveraging Artificial Intelligence for Climate Change Mitigation in Africa: A Sustainable Approach
records.authors: Ogunade Josiah Ayodele
records.abstract: As climate change intensifies environmental and socio-economic vulnerabilities across Africa, there is a growing need for innovative, scalable solutions to support climate resilience. This study critically examines the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in enhancing climate adaptation and mitigation efforts on the continent. Employing a qualitative, multi-source research methodology, the paper synthesizes academic literature, institutional frameworks, and applied case studies to assess the integration of AI into environmental monitoring and resource management systems. Particular emphasis is placed on the use of machine learning and remote sensing technologies to support real-time data analysis, land-use classification, water resource management, and early warning systems. The Enhancing National Climate Services (ENACTS) program is analyzed as a leading case, demonstrating how the fusion of satellite and groundbased data can significantly improve climate services in sectors such as agriculture and public health. The paper also identifies critical challenges—including data scarcity, inadequate infrastructure, limited technical capacity, and ethical risks such as data privacy and algorithmic bias—that hinder the effective deployment of AI. In response, the study offers strategic policy recommendations to strengthen climate data infrastructure, promote cross-sector collaboration, and build human capital in AI and climate science. The findings underscore the importance of African-led innovation, ethical governance, and context-specific solutions in ensuring that AI contributes meaningfully and equitably to sustainable development and climate resilience.

records.title: Leveraging on Artificial Intelligence Technology in Boosting Cassava Production in Nigeria: The Gains and Constraints
records.authors: IGBUNU, Richard Oghenerume
records.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology is reshaping agricultural landscape globally by employing data-driven, efficient, and scalable production methods. Nigeria, as the world’s largest producer of cassava, faces persistent challenges like low yield per hectare, pest infestations, climate variability, and inefficient farming techniques. This study focuses on the potential of AI technology to exploit and enhance the nation’s agricultural potentials and productivity. The study decisively examines the application of AI in cassava production in Nigeria, focusing on its gains and constraints. It adopted ways to addressing the critical challenges like climate variability, scarce access to digital farming techniques, and the need for sustainable practices. Using a descriptive and analytical approach based on secondary data from FAO, NBS, IITA, and recent scholarly publications, the study explores AI-driven technologies such as precision agriculture, machine learning, remote sensing, and automation. Findings from the study reveal that AI technology application in cassava production can significantly improve productivity, optimize resource utilization, and reduce post-harvest losses. However, adoption can be constrained by high costs, poor infrastructure, low digital literacy, and weak policy frameworks. This paper investigates how AI technology can be employed to achieve the mass production of cassava in Nigeria, while critically examining the associated gains or benefits and constraints.

records.title: Nanorobots-Assisted In Vivo Computational Methodology for Tumor Lesion Exploitation and Lesion Boundary Exploration
records.authors: Shaolong Shi; Zeyuan Xu; Jiawei Zou; Weiqi Liu; Qiujun Huang
records.abstract: An innovative in vivo computational model that reframes the challenge of early tumor detection as an optimization problem has been developed recently. In this scope, the tumor lesion is viewed as the optimal solution that to be found by the computing agents (i.e., nanorobots). The tumor-triggered biological gradient field provides the information for the real-time path planning and fitness evaluation of nanorobots. The main emphasis of previous work has been on engineering tumor-targeting methodologies that address the challenges imposed by in vivo biological conditions. In this paper, we investigate the issue of tumor lesion exploitation by controlling the motion of nanorobotic swarm, which aims to enhance the operational efficiency of nanorobots deployed for tumor lesion identification. Thus, an exploitation approach about the settings of nanorobots moving direction and step size is developed. Furthermore, inspired by the spontaneous motion property of nanorobots, we propose cooperation and competition mechanisms to overcome the challenge of lesion boundary exploration in this paper. Some computational simulations are performed to validate the efficacy of this novel methodology.

records.title: Application of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Algorithms to Monitor Drinking Water Pollution in Arid and Semi-Arid Regions: A Review
records.authors: Saadu Umar WaliWali
records.abstract: In arid and semi-arid regions, water pollution poses a significant threat to environmental sustainability and public health due to the limited availability and high vulnerability of water resources. Traditional methods for monitoring water quality often struggle to address the unique challenges of these regions, including sparse data collection and delayed response times. This review explores the application of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) technologies in enhancing water pollution monitoring in these environments. By leveraging advanced data analytics, real-time processing, and predictive modelling, AI and ML offer promising solutions to overcome the limitations of conventional monitoring techniques. The review highlights the key causes and sources of water pollution in arid and semi-arid regions, such as agricultural runoff, industrial discharge, and inadequate waste management. It examines current monitoring practices and their constraints, providing a foundation for understanding the potential benefits of AI and ML. Successful case studies from diverse regions demonstrate how these technologies can improve environmental monitoring efforts' accuracy, efficiency, and timeliness. Future directions include the integration of multisource data, the development of real-time and predictive monitoring systems, and the use of autonomous technologies. However, these advancements come with challenges related to data quality, computational resources, and ethical considerations. Privacy, equity, transparency, and the environmental impact of AI technologies must be addressed to ensure that AI-driven solutions are effective and responsible. In conclusion, AI and ML represent transformative tools for enhancing water pollution monitoring in arid and semi-arid regions. While offering significant potential for improving environmental management, their successful implementation requires careful consideration of ethical, social, and technical factors to balance technological advancement and sustainable environmental stewardship.
