records.title: Digital Transformation of Food Microbiology: Artificial Intelligence, Biosensors, and Smart Monitoring Systems
records.authors: Ömer Faruk Yeşil
records.abstract: Food microbiology is moving from episodic, laboratory-centered testing toward connected systems that can detect, interpret, and anticipate microbial hazards across food production and distribution. This transition is being driven by the convergence of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), biosensors, computer vision, spectroscopy, predictive microbiology, Internet of Things (IoT) infrastructure, and digital-twin concepts. The value of these technologies lies not in replacing reference microbiological methods, but in shortening the interval between sampling, evidence generation, risk interpretation, and corrective action. AI can extract patterns from images, spectral fingerprints, sensor signals, molecular data, and environmental measurements; biosensors can convert biological recognition into rapidly measurable signals; and connected monitoring architectures can place these outputs within dynamic process and supply-chain contexts. Recent studies demonstrate progress in deep-learning-based microbial identification, machine-learning-assisted biosensing, non-destructive hyperspectral and volatile sensing, smartphone-enabled field analysis, and predictive models that integrate temperature, pH, water activity, and other determinants of microbial behavior. However, translation from proof-of-concept studies to routine food control remains constrained by matrix effects, limited external validation, data drift, small or unrepresentative datasets, inconsistent reporting, device interoperability, cybersecurity, and uncertain regulatory pathways. This chapter examines the principal components of digital food microbiology, emphasizes their integration into practical food-safety workflows, and proposes a validation-oriented perspective for responsible deployment. The emerging paradigm is therefore best understood as augmented microbiology: conventional culture and molecular reference methods remain essential, while digital tools add speed, continuity, predictive capacity, and decision support.

records.title: An Overview of Anti-Islanding Protection Schemes in PV-Based Microgrids
records.authors: Mateo Beus; Nino Nikić
records.abstract: The increasing integration of distributed energy resources (DERs), particularly photovoltaic (PV) systems, is transforming modern power systems and introducing new challenges for protection, reliability, and stability. The transition toward smart grids with bidirectional power flows has significantly changed the operating conditions under which protection systems must perform. Among the key challenges associated with DER integration is unintentional islanding, in which a DER or a group of DERs continues to energize a portion of the distribution network after disconnection from the main utility grid. If not detected and cleared within the required time, islanding may pose risks to personnel safety, power quality, equipment, and system stability. This paper presents a comprehensive review and critical analysis of islanding detection methods for PV and inverter-based DER systems, including passive, active, hybrid, and communication-based techniques. The methods are evaluated with respect to detection speed, the non-detection zone (NDZ), false-trip behavior, power-quality impact, implementation complexity, cost, and adaptability to different inverter and grid conditions. Particular attention is given to multi-inverter systems, weak and converter-dominated grids, communication and cybersecurity, and standardization and benchmarking challenges. Based on the identified limitations and research gaps, future research directions are discussed, with emphasis on AI/ML-based detection, adaptive protection, grid-forming inverters, multi-inverter coordination, PV–battery systems, weak-grid and low-inertia networks, and experimental validation. The review highlights the need for adaptive, coordinated, and intelligent islanding protection frameworks capable of ensuring reliable detection in increasingly complex inverter-dominated power systems.

records.title: The management paradigm transformation in pharmacy: from traditional models to the use of digital technologies
records.authors: I. V. Bondarieva; V. V. Malyi; O. Yu. Rohulia; N. G. Malinina
records.abstract: The relevance of the study is due to the impact of digitalization and crisis factors on the pharmaceutical sector, which determines the need for a theoretical rethinking of the modern management paradigm in pharmacy. Aim. To theoretically substantiate the evolution of the management paradigm in pharmacy, identify the main stages of its transformation, and systematize the characteristics of the contemporary digital management model of pharmaceutical organizations. Materials and methods. The information base for this study was compiled from regulatory and strategic documents (WHO, Ministry of Health of Ukraine) and scientific publications for 2015–2026, retrieved from Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, and Google Scholar using keywords related to digitalization and management in pharmacy. The study used systemic, structural and functional, comparative, and historical-logical methods, as well as generalization and scientific abstraction. Results and discussion. Six stages in the evolution of the management paradigm in pharmacy, such as administrative-functional, economic-market, strategic, process-oriented, patient-centered, and digital stage, have been systematized. It has been substantiated that each subsequent paradigm does not eliminate the previous one, but transforms and integrates its managerial tools in accordance with changing conditions in the pharmaceutical sector. The transition from managing resources, functions, and operations to managing end-to-end processes, relationships, data, digital platforms, as well as ecosystems, has been identified. The transformation of managerial functions from periodic planning, control, and experience-based decision-making towards dynamic forecasting, real-time monitoring, predictive analytics, automation, and data-driven decision-making has been demonstrated. The social-pharmaceutical dimension of the digital paradigm has been substantiated, within which the digital transformation contributes to improving the accessibility and quality of pharmaceutical care, strengthening patient-centredness, and increasing the social efficiency of pharmaceutical organizations. The need to combine technological efficiency with risk management, cybersecurity, human capital development, and digital resilience has been determined. Conclusions. Digitalization is defined as a systemic transformation of the management paradigm that provides the transition from a predominantly hierarchical and reactive model to an adaptive, process-oriented, network-based, platform, and data-driven management model. Further research should focus on developing methodological approaches to assessing the digital maturity and digital resilience of pharmaceutical organizations, identifying appropriate KPIs, and studying their relationship with the quality of pharmaceutical care and social effectiveness.

records.title: Debt maturity structure, corporate governance, and hostile takeover threats: half a century of evidence
records.authors: Pattanaporn Chatjuthamard; Pornsit Jiraporn; Pandej Chintrakarn
records.abstract: Exploiting a takeover-threat measure that is less directly subject to managerial choice than firm-chosen governance provisions and a large sample spanning more than half a century, this study examines the association between hostile takeover threats and corporate debt maturity structure. Drawing on the hostile takeover index that has been widely used in the literature and a sample covering the period from 1964 to 2020, we investigate whether variation in takeover threats is associated with differences in firms’ debt maturity choices. We find that firms facing greater hostile takeover threats tend to rely more heavily on short-maturity debt, a pattern consistent with, although not demonstrating, the view that takeover threats and short-term debt may serve as complementary governance mechanisms that enhance outside monitoring and constrain managerial discretion. These associations remain robust across firm fixed-effects regressions, propensity score matching, entropy balancing, and instrumental-variable specifications. We also find that the association between takeover threats and shorter debt maturity is stronger among highly levered firms but weaker among firms with greater profitability, larger cash reserves, and higher capital expenditures. Because our design mitigates but does not eliminate endogeneity and alternative explanations, we interpret the evidence as a robust conditional association between hostile takeover threats and firms’ debt maturity policies rather than as causal evidence.

records.title: Beyond Principlism: A Cosmopolitan and Care Ethics Approach to One Digital Health
records.authors: Cristian Moyano-Fernández; Jon Rueda; Janet Delgado; Irene Gómez-Franco; María Victoria Martínez-López; Ana Toledo-Chávarri; Alice Rangel-Teixeira; Angel Puyol
records.abstract: Abstract This article examines the limitations of principlism in addressing the ethical challenges posed by One Digital Health. While principlism remains influential in bioethics, digital health, and global health policy, we argue that it is insufficient to capture the relational, data infrastructural, and multispecies dynamics shaping the threats to One Health. Using antimicrobial resistance as a paradigmatic case, we show that One Digital Health governance is shaped not only by distributive ethical concerns but also by structural asymmetries in data visibility, digital infrastructure, and epistemic inclusion across human, animal, and environmental domains. These asymmetries reveal a key limitation of principlism: although it articulates abstract commitments to justice and equity, it lacks the conceptual and operational resources to explain how inequalities are produced and reproduced in digital systems. To address this gap, we propose an integrated framework that combines the ethics of care, cosmopolitanism, and a FAIRER-based account of data governance. Ethics of care foregrounds situated vulnerability and relational interdependence; cosmopolitanism extends moral responsibility across global and multispecies scales; and FAIRER operationalizes these commitments within digital infrastructures and data systems. The antimicrobial resistance case study shows that this approach provides a more comprehensive account of One Digital Health governance by linking lived practices, global responsibilities, and data infrastructures. We conclude that addressing One Health threats through digital transformation requires moving beyond principle-based reasoning toward relational frameworks that integrate global commitments with contextual sensitivity.

records.title: Microplastics and Human Health: Exposure Pathways, Contributive Roles, and Mitigation Strategies
records.authors: V. Anjali; K.A. Prasad; K. Balasubramani; M. Ramkumar
records.abstract: The sophistication of human life with the inventions and infrastructure development that followed the industrial revolution has one unintended consequence—plastic pollution. Their exponential growth, accumulation in all the environmental systems, persistence and low rate of decay have made them unique polluters of this century, to which no wise management practices and mitigation strategies are known currently. The micro/nano sizes of plastic debris not only concerned in the natural environment; they also possess emergency risks to human health. Through an extensive literature search, we retrieved a total of 4583 records from the Scopus database appeared in last decade (2016–2025). By adopting PRISMA guidelines, we selected 932 literatures for extensive scoping review of the exposure pathways and mechanistic evidence linking microplastics to human health. The review has synthesized the evidences on microplastics contamination of external and internal human systems and traced the occurrence, types, abundance, distribution, and modes of transportation and bioaccumulation reported in the literature. The dominant mode of microplastics transport includes ingestion, followed by inhalation, dermal contact, and injection. Translocation of microplastics through circulatory systems within the human body endangers vital organs including brain and placental tissues, raising concern about potential systemic health risks. Review and examination of the microplastics exposure to humans with reference to the relative vulnerabilities of various organs revealed that, the gastrointestinal tract-digestive system, followed by liver-hepatic system, kidney-renal system, lungs-respiratory system, brain and nerves-the nervous system, reproductive system, cardiovascular and circulatory system, skin-integumentary system and lymphoid organs and tissues-immune system are all prone to microplastic-nanoplastic contaminants and are subjected to various levels of threats. Owing to their bioaccumulation capacity, slow rate of decay and persistence in almost all the media, effective mitigation/management strategies are yet to be devised and their effectiveness in tackling the menace is validated. With about 50 primary types of polymers, producing over 60,000 formulations, at an approximate rate of 8% increase every year, result in an alarming rate of plastic refuse in natural environments, often unmanaged is a looming threat to environmental systems and ecological niches. Addressing this situation requires urgent, policy initiatives, and microscale management practices, that include plans and strategies for source reduction, environmental intervention, legal and mandatory management/reuse/recycle practices at microscale.

records.title: Low Pay, High Risk: The Nursing Pay Gap in Italy as a Systemic Health Policy Vulnerability
records.authors: Ippolito Notarnicola; Rosario Caruso; Sara Carrodano; Serena Caponetti; Gennaro Rocco; Alessandro Stievano
records.abstract: Background The nursing workforce is a key determinant of health system resilience, quality, and sustainability. In Italy, nurses receive significantly lower salaries compared to the OECD average, and the country has one of the lowest nurse-to-population ratios in Europe. This study examines the Italian nursing pay gap as a systemic vulnerability in health policy, with implications for the National Health Service's (NHS) capacity to deliver safe and continuous care. Methods This study follows a descriptive policy analysis approach integrated with comparative data analysis. Salary and workforce data were obtained from Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) datasets (2015–2024) and complemented with national and international institutional sources. The analysis was guided by Walt and Gilson's Policy Triangle and the Nursing Theory of Complex Adaptive Systems (NTCAS). Results Italy reports an average nursing salary of approximately USD 48,000 (PPP), about 21% lower than the OECD average, and a density of 6.2 nurses per 1,000 inhabitants compared with 9.4 internationally. In the selected country comparison, higher salary levels co-occurred with higher nurse density, while the policy analysis identified persistent constraints in remuneration, career development, workforce planning, and retention. Theoretical interpretation frames the pay gap as a systemic variable with potential consequences for quality, safety, and equity. Discussion The Italian pay gap reflects structural weaknesses in workforce governance rather than an isolated issue. Limited career pathways, migration, and workforce shortages further increase system vulnerability. Conclusion Addressing the nursing pay gap is a strategic priority to strengthen retention, reduce inequalities, and ensure the long-term sustainability of the NHS.

records.title: Jukun-Tiv Crises and Economic Development in Wukari Local Government Area of Taraba State Nigeria
records.authors: Awudu Ishaya GANI
records.abstract: Ethnic conflicts remain a persistent challenge in many societies, particularly in Africa, where historical grievances, political competition, and resource struggles fuel tensions. Nigeria, with its vast ethnic diversity, has frequently experienced violent inter-group rivalries, notably between the Jukun and Tiv ethnic groups in Wukari Local Government Area, Taraba State. This study examines the impact of the Jukun-Tiv crises on economic development in Wukari, employing Donald Horowitz's ethnic conflict theory as a theoretical framework. The study utilized a descriptive survey research design, collecting data through questionnaires and interviews from a sample of 400 respondents, with 388 valid responses analysed. Findings reveal that recurrent ethnic conflicts have significantly disrupted economic activities, particularly agriculture and trade, leading to loss of livelihoods, destruction of property, and stunted economic growth. The dominance of farmers and traders among respondents emphasised the economic vulnerability of the region to ethnic violence. Furthermore, the study highlighted how political and economic contestations exacerbate tensions, with local elites often manipulating ethnic identities for political gain. The study recommends inclusive governance, economic empowerment programmes, and robust conflict resolution mechanisms as essential strategies for fostering sustainable peace and economic development in Wukari LGA.

records.title: Frequency Stability Assessment and Synthetic Inertia in Low-Inertia Power Systems: A Comprehensive Review
records.authors: Jennifer Ugochukwu Njonu; Boyi Jimoh; Mohammed Musa; Sulaiman Haruna; Bashir Musa Umar; David Enemali Abah
records.abstract: The rapid integration of inverter-based renewable energy sources (RESs), particularly solar photovoltaic (PV) and wind power, has significantly reduced the rotational inertia traditionally provided by synchronous generators, creating unprecedented challenges for frequency stability in modern power systems. Reduced system inertia results in higher rates of change of frequency (RoCoF), deeper frequency nadirs, and increased vulnerability to disturbances, necessitating advanced frequency assessment and synthetic inertia solutions. This paper presents a comprehensive review of frequency stability assessment methods and synthetic inertia techniques for low-inertia power systems. First, the fundamental principles of frequency dynamics, inertial response, and the impact of renewable energy penetration on system inertia are discussed. Subsequently, recent advances in deterministic and probabilistic frequency stability assessment methodologies are reviewed, followed by a critical evaluation of virtual synchronous machines, droop-based virtual inertia, model predictive control, battery energy storage systems, grid-forming converters, and intelligent control strategies for synthetic inertia provision. A comparative analysis of existing studies highlights their methodologies, performance metrics, advantages, and practical limitations. The review further identifies key research challenges, including uncertainty modeling, adaptive inertia allocation, converter operational constraints, computational complexity, and real-time implementation. Finally, future research directions toward uncertainty-aware frequency assessment, adaptive synthetic inertia, artificial intelligence-assisted control, and resilient converter-dominated power systems are discussed. This review provides a comprehensive reference for researchers and power system engineers developing reliable frequency stability enhancement strategies for future renewable-dominated electricity networks.

records.title: Artificial Intelligence–Driven Precision Agriculture Systems: Engineering Frameworks for Climate-Resilient Food Production
records.authors: Olumayowa Iyanda; Oluwadare Oyebode; Iretiayo Adelaiye; Ayomide Afolabi
records.abstract: Climate change, soil issues, water scarcity, and the increasing need for food worldwide mean we need smart farming systems that can manage resources flexibly. Old farming methods used the same inputs and simple rules for decisions. AI can help us manage resources better by adapting and optimizing them as we deal with complex environmental factors. This paper looks closely at AI-powered precision agriculture systems designed to make food production more resilient to changing weather. The authors reviewed research from 2021 to 2026 in agricultural engineering, computer engineering, and environmental systems. The authors examined how machine learning, deep learning, reinforcement learning, computer vision, robotics, and IoT sensors are used for predicting crop yields, spotting diseases, improving irrigation, managing nutrients, and automating field tasks. Our analysis shows that hybrid deep learning models (CNN-LSTM) are better than single models for predicting crop yields over space and time. Reinforcement learning algorithms are also better at adjusting irrigation cycles when weather is unpredictable. Using edge computing for system design reduces delays and improves real-time decision-making compared to traditional cloud-based systems. However, there are still big challenges with understanding how AI models work, having enough diverse data, ensuring cybersecurity, setting common standards, and making these systems affordable, especially in developing countries. To tackle these problems, we suggest a framework that combines AI analysis, distributed sensor networks, adaptive controls, and climate risk assessments. The authors provided critical insights into essential research gaps and outline a technological roadmap towards achieving sustainable, resilient and intelligent agricultural systems.

records.title: Quantum-Enabled Video Intelligence for Sustainable Post-Harvest Systems: A Static Image Classification Feasibility Study
records.authors: Theebiga Vicknarajah; Kanagasabai Thiruthanigesan; Aruna Kumara; Thiruchchelvan Nagarathnam
records.abstract: Global food security faces a critical challenge from post-harvest losses, which exacerbate economic instability and environmental degradation. As agricultural systems strive for sustainability, the limitations of classical computer vision in handling high-dimensional, real-time data become increasingly apparent. This chapter provides a comprehensive examination of Quantum-Enabled Video Intelligence (QVI) as a transformative solution for modern post-harvest management. This study describes the basic principles of quantum machine learning (QML) and quantum sensing. Also, it demonstrates how the above-mentioned quantum technologies can be exploited to enhance classical computations in applications such as visual analytics for defect, ripeness, and quality grading. Using this methodology as a first step for a complete video stream deployment, we benchmark the QVI architecture on static image classification of produce classes as a performance baseline before temporal video extension. The discussion bridges theoretical quantum frameworks with practical agricultural applications, exploring a hybrid quantum-classical architecture designed for efficiency and scalability. Key topics include the proposed integration of hyperspectral and video data with quantum algorithms in future deployments, reducing energy consumption in sorting facilities, and the potential for minimizing chemical waste through precise anomaly detection. Furthermore, the chapter addresses the current technological barriers, hardware requirements, and the roadmap for integrating quantum solutions into existing supply chains. By synthesizing current research with future projections, this work offers researchers, practitioners, and policy-makers a strategic understanding of how quantum technologies can drive the transition towards zero-waste, sustainable post-harvest systems aligned with global development goals.

records.title: A national framework for strengthening public health laboratory preparedness and resilience in Jordan: advancing health security, One Health, and early warning capacity
records.authors: Dalia Kashef Zayed; Tasnim Abu Al Khair; Ruba A. Al-Smadi; Mohammad H. Gharaibeh; Tareq L. Mukattash; Adel Belbiesi; Ala'a B. Al-Tammemi
records.abstract: National laboratory systems are central to epidemic intelligence, early detection, and implementation of the International Health Regulations. In Jordan, substantial diagnostic capacity exists, but laboratory functions remain distributed across institutions and sectors, with persistent challenges in governance, quality systems, biosafety and biosecurity, workforce capacity, referral arrangements, and data interoperability. In 2023, Jordan undertook a national laboratory mapping using a multi-method approach comprising review of 226 national and international documents, 20 key-informant interviews, and 23 field visits covering 27 laboratories in four governorates. Findings were analyzed thematically using the LABNET framework and reviewed through a national multisector stakeholder validation process. Building on these findings and the subsequent endorsement of Jordan's National One Health Laboratory Strategic Plan 2026–2030, we propose an implementation-oriented framework for strengthening the national laboratory system. The framework is organized around five interdependent pillars: governance, legislation, and strategic direction; a coordinated national laboratory network; quality management, external quality assessment, and accreditation pathways; workforce competency development and retention; and digital transformation with multisector One Health information exchange. Rather than establishing new parallel structures, the framework is intended to connect and strengthen existing capacities while preserving the statutory and technical mandates of participating sectors. A phased roadmap for 2026–2030 translates these pillars into operational priorities and links them to cross-cutting enablers, including sustainable financing, biosafety and biosecurity, cybersecurity, equity, emergency preparedness, and monitoring, evaluation, and learning. The framework is prospective and has not yet been evaluated as an integrated intervention. Its value will therefore depend on implementation fidelity and prospective assessment against defined baselines. If effectively operationalized, it could strengthen referral performance, diagnostic reliability, reporting timeliness, multisector risk assessment, and the use of laboratory intelligence for early warning and coordinated response. Although developed for Jordan, the framework offers a context-adaptable model for countries seeking to strengthen laboratory resilience through phased, multisectoral, and One Health–oriented reform.

records.title: Editorial: Non-timber forest products: from sustainable harvest to market innovation
records.authors: M. Anjaly Shanker; Payel Ghosh; Sandeep Singh Rana
records.abstract: Forests perceived primarily as timber source, is a major contributor in fueling industries from construction and paper production since many decades. This narrow perspective blocks the immense diversity of forest resources and also of what they provide. There is an undervalued and vast portfolio of Non-Timber Forest Products (NTFPs) under the shadow of this approach, with a status reflected as non-traditional, secondary, nonwood or minor products. Non-Timber Forest Products (NTFPs) including fruits, nuts, medicinal plants, honey, latex, resins, and ornamental foliage-represent a vast group which were historically harvested by subsequent human population for their use and trade (Hazari et al., 2023). These products contribute to the livelihood and wellbeing of the population living in and near to the forest, catering them with the food, medicine and other material inputs along with the source of income and employment. There is a growing interest towards different attributes of NTFPs during the last 10-20 years owing to their contribution to rural development and ecological balance. This mounting interest of NTFPs can be articulated into three main reasons. One among them is the early discussed contributions of these resources to the livelihood and economic welfare of the populations (Rosenfeld et al., 2024). The second among the reasons is their contribution to sustainable forest management. The harvesting of these non-timber products is less ecologically invasive and destructive than the harvesting of timber and other forest products, maintaining the balance and sustainability. Other reason is the growth in perceived value of tropical forest owing to the increase in commercial harvesting of NTFPs. This would lead to the increased incentive to preserve the forest reserve than their conversion to forest agriculture land or for livestock. This classifies NTFPs as natural resources that represents both livelihood security and conservation (de Mello et all., 2020). A study on the pattern of NTFPs management in Ayubia National Park, Pakistan displays that more than 50% of the population of the villages were involved in the collection of NTFPs and most of them involved in the process were women. The study also emphasizes the contribution of these NTFPs towards the food security of these populations with an extra monetary benefit accounted in the form of NTFP trading in nearby cities (Zaman et al., 2023).The global demand of NTFPs in international markets is aligned with the consumer pressure for organic, ethical and naturally sourced products. In different regions of South Asia, Africa and the Amazon basin, NTFPs play an integral role in managing food security and cultural identity and serves as a backbone of their financial operations (Shackleton & De Vos, 2022). With the demand flowing from multiple industries like cosmetic, oil plants etc, they are positioned as commodities with high economic, social and ecological value. Highly valued market profile tends to create a control over local collective systems of NTFPs forest resources leading to uncontrolled, destructive usage of resources and also burden the poor local users. The existing undervaluation on NTFPs related policies has created research gaps, weak market infrastructure and limited institutional support. This resource miscalculation curbs fair market accesses, value-addition opportunities and also effects the certification process. Similar is the issue with aggressive market pressure and over commercialization of NTFPs (Ahamad et al., 2022). Hence, considerable attention should be given to the edge among conservation and development of NTFPs for making the market global trade more compensable and stable to the consumers. This editorial situates NTFPs within the broader discourse on sustainability and innovation, urging forests to be seen as hubs of diverse, renewable, and culturally rich resources. By exploring sustainable harvest, market integration, innovation, and policy support, it highlights NTFPs as catalysts for resilient green economies that nurture both people and planet.As previously stated, there is a significant benefit aligned with less ecological invasive harvest operations of non-timber forest products. The basic idea aligned with this indigenous collection or harvesting procedure is to prevent overexploitation of forests and thereby safeguarding the availability of resources every year. The sustainable harvesting practices of NTFPs revolve majorly around long guided traditional knowledge more than structured operational flowcharts. Native and rural population follows methods involving seasonal resource calendars, rotational product collections and spiritual doctrines. Seasonal collection of NTFPs revolve around low impact harvesting techniques like selective hand-picking, careful tapping for resins, and evading the overharvesting of reproductive structures (Ticktin, 2015). Proper collection techniques ensure the minimal disruption of surrounding or adjacent soil layer and associated vegetation. This approach aligns ecological sustainability with consistent annual economic benefits for local populations utilizing these NTFPs. For example, the harvesting of Brazil nuts in amazon basin is done without distressing the wild trees (Afonso, 2022). This operation method safeguards the forest canopy, upholds wild life habitats and strengthening the biodiversity. The nuts are allowed to fall naturally to the ground where they are gathered by the local collectors. The gathered product is a recognized income source owing to global market demands, linking sustainability with livelihoods (Pandey et al., 2016).Similar is the case of gum arabica or acacia gum which is basically a sap collected from acacia trees. The parent tree is not affected by the sap collection procedure, maintaining the tree canopy and wild harmony (Paramanik & Bhattacharyya, 2021). The product collected is widely used in food, pharmaceuticals and cosmetic industries, providing higher value to the end product. This pattern is further demonstrated across a wide range of examples.Seasonal plucking of tendu leaves commonly used in traditional cigarette ensues seasonal plucking of leaves preserving parent tree health (Kumar, 2017). These resources provide vital seasonal income for millions of indigenous harvesters particularly women, thereby enhancing local livelihoods. Along with the plant-based NTFPs such as fruits, leaves etc, the animal-based products also play a crucial role in forest economies. Examples like lac resin, bushmeat in certain African regions (Tiwari et al., 2021;Ingram et al., 2025). Lac resin is the secretions from insects that live in host trees and is used to produce shellac, widely used in varnishes, polishes and even in food coatings (Thombare et al., 2020). In Central and West Africa, bush meat acts as a major source of protein and income among the different groups. It positively contributes towards food security of these communities without largescale ecological distribution (Ingram et al., 2025). Similar is the case with shells and feathers collected for handicrafts, ornaments and cultural practices supports the local artisans through regulated harvesting and maintaining biodiversity (Simard et al., 2018). The opportunity that these NTFPs provide to the livelihood is more than imaginary. Mahua (Madhuca longifolia) flowers one of the common NTFPs of India, is projected to comprise 10 million tribal gathers during the flowering period and generates a seasonal income of around 2000-4000 INR per household. Also, the seed oil obtained from this Madhuca longifolia, serves both nutritional and industrial applications. Mahua seed oil is used in rural cooking and also as feedstock in biodiesel production, highlighting the economic gain to the gatherers involved in NTFP management (Chakrabarti & Dutta;2026). While these sustainable practices ensure the accessibility of resources without much ecological impact, long term dependence on these supplies create vulnerabilities. To complement this, the communities and researchers have altered into followed pattern of domestication and cultivation of NTFPs. The study on Nilgiris Biosphere Reserve highlights the efficiency of producer collectives in establishing the nurseries foe honey plants, silk cotton and medicinal species by integrating the traditional seed knowledge with the modern cultivation practices (Global Alliance for Green and Gender Action, 2024). The community-based domestication of Allanblackia trees in Ghana also highlights the successful integration of this oilseed species into agroforestry systems, reducing reliance on wild harvesting while supplying raw material for food and cosmetic industries (Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, 2023). These farmer cooperatives cultivating Allanblackia in Ghana support over 10,000 smallholder households explaining the multifaceted gains associated with sustainable management of NTFPs. By incorporating forest products into agroforestry, this strategy secures supply chains, protects wild ecosystems, and boosts local economies.Non timber forest products represent a high valued global industry which has direct influence on local and national economies. However, the economic structure of NTFPs remains decentralized and consents to substantial revenue flow to the rural sections. As the trade flow of these resources occurs mainly across localized markets, the total macroeconomic value of NTFPs stays lowballed. The economic importance of these resources lies not only on immediate subsistence but also on their profound capacity in integrating different commercial sectors and managing broader markets. At a domestic level, NTFPs primary contribution is towards food security and economic stability of indigenous population. Wild fruits, mushrooms, tubers, and honey supplement diets with essential nutrients, while medicinal plants reduce dependence on costly pharmaceuticals. To illustrate, Singh et al., (2025) has highlighted the significant contributions of shitake mushroom to human health and wellbeing of indigenous and forest dwelling communities. These mushrooms are rich in key compounds like lentinan, ergosterol, eritadenine and antioxidants underlining their potential as an antioxidant source, boosting immunity and controlling the risk of chronic diseases like cancer, heart disease etc. They have the power of controlling poverty, nourishment etc by replacing the staple diets, securing healthcare, investment in education and also changing the income distribution. From a broader perspective, collectors earn money from the sale of different type of products; collecting food in the form of fruits, nuts, tubers etc, acquire wood as energy source, collecting palm leaves and stem as thatch and construction poles, and also gathers wild foliage as ornamental decoration Even when all forest products aren't sold, they still save households money by providing items they would otherwise have to buy. The assortment and trade of commercial NTFPs deliver supplementary income to the household and acts as a potential barrier against climate irregularities, economic instability and crop failures.Further, secondary links in NTFPs supply chain generates employment to the individuals who are involved in trade as well as processing. The primary financial draw of NTFPs is that they generate high revenue with low capital investment and minimum input or resource. Collection process is known to be labour intensive but doesn't require fertilizers, pesticides, machinery or much of scientific information. This makes them approachable to marginalized groups, including women and landless labourers, who can contribute in value chains with limited resources. As collection and handling of NTFPs entail minimum formal education and investment, the entry barrier to this economy is remarkably low. This again ensures the cash flow serving as an operative tool for poverty alleviation (Bagal et al., 2023). Another distinct economical advantage of NTFPs is its gender-based division of labour and distribution of income. While most of the men labour is concentrated on timber and large-scale agriculture, the value chain of NTFPs is solely surrounded around rural women. Women included in financial course of household reported a different pattern of money redistribution concentrating nutrition, child welfare and community development. Hence, strengthening NTFPs market contributes to the internal distribution of wealth empowering vulnerable demographic groups along with an increase in the total economic condition.The market dynamics of NTFPs are extremely imperfect, random and undesigned. Rural operations involved the presence of a middle men to whom the harvesters or collectors will be selling their NTFPs. These middle men are local trades who buy the product in low values and thereby passing on a low profit margin to the harvesters.Fairer price distribution and elimination of middleman promote the economic stability of the source communities and also the other market stakeholders. Another approach for ensuring economic stability is to formalize producer networks and thereby guaranteeing gender inclusion, avoiding exploitative intermediates and fairer prices. The producer collective in Nilgiris biosphere reserve was successful in creating branded NTFPs products like soaps, baskets, food items etc substantiating bargaining power and fixed prices (Global Alliance for Green and Gender Action, 2024). Modern economic strategies involve shifting the value addition to the community level. Value addition always remains crucial in increasing the returns from NTFPs. Introducing basic minimal processing methods like sorting, grading, drying etc will enhance the quality and fetch high process to the rural cooperatives (Dou et al., 2023). A study based on Central India proposed the economic edge in selling the processed goods like oil, balms and other food products from small scale processing units of mahua flowers and chironji seeds. A study on comparative analysis on drying of West Indian cherry, displays that the drying methods involved were effectual in maintaining nutritional and functional profile of the fruit. This underscores the potential of this cherry variety for application in functional food and nutraceutical, which would be challenging without the followed preprocessing method (Das, 2025). These centres reduce post-harvest losses by 25% and improve quality control, while diversification into multiple product lines strengthens household incomes by 20-30% (Bhattacharya & Anjali, 2025). Supplementary to direct sales, NTFPs promotes broader economic diversification by cross bridging forestry with other commercial sectors. Incorporating value chains in NTFPs and integrating them into general agribusiness network will generates secondary economies around product handling, cold storages, quality certification, transport and distribution (Sheppard et al., 2020). Further more The cultural tradition of forest foraging has fuelled new tourism markets throughout Europe and Asia. Guided excursions, culinary forest trails, and harvest festivals now allow regions to profit from their woodlands while keeping them protected. Editorially, the economic dimensions of NTFPs reveal their transformative potential (Bachi & Carvalho-Ribeiro, 2023). They are not peripheral supplements but strategic assets that can drive inclusive growth, empower women, and diversify rural economies.Even though the collection and marketing of NTFPs ensure ecological, economic and social balance, there are several bottlenecks that effect the smooth functioning of this system. First and foremost, would be the issue of overexploitation of these natural resources. Collectors and other stake holders face pressure to gather and distribute the products early and in elevated quantities owing to the market demand. This would precede to practices like over collection of fruits or seeds or flowers, stripping off too much of the bark, collecting immature products etc which will abuse the resources. These practices ascribed to substantial economic income, lack of proper handling, extraction technique, poor resource management and lack of structured guidance would affect the long-term viability and survival. Menggala et al., (2019) reported the direct remarks on C. burmannii production techniques and their impact on forest conservation. The clear cutting and slash-burn technique in the production of cinnamon has equally contributed to deforestation and sustainability as intensive harvesting and posed a significant threat to the biodiversity. Loss of habitat is posing a significant pressure on meeting the demand of increasing consumer base of NTFPs. Rapid deforestation, increasing agricultural lands and expanding urban areas leads to shrinkage of natural forest spaces automatically effecting the biodiversity present. This loss on biodiversity accelerates climate change by destroying the very ecosystems that naturally absorb and store carbon. Extreme weather events, changing rainfall patterns, floods, rising sea levels, intense heat waves and long droughts disrupts natural season cycles of the forest. These climate shifts influence the quality and quantity of forest products like in agricultural land produce.Another critical issue associated with NTFPs is the local or middle men in the trade-offs. One major thing that fuels this condition is the geographical weakness of remote areas for most forest dependent population. This acts as a constraint in accessing the broader markets and thereby limiting the commercialization of NTFPs. Local traders exploit this condition by keeping the higher share of the product to themselves and leaving the collectors with minimum returns (Bele et al., 2015). This issue is enflamed by the lack of proper equipment, money, machinery, cold storage facilities etc in the rural areas and lack of their knowledge among the indigenous population. Furthermore, sustainable management of NTFPs relies majorly on effective governance. Studies illustrate that engaging multiple stakeholders in decision-making process ensures fair access and benefits to the local residents, which positively influences the forest (Gideon, 2018). Similarly, handing local communities' control over these resources safeguards their livelihoods and benefits in reinstating nature (Gosling et al., 2017;Dash et al., 2016;Dao et al., 2016). Democratic, community-led governance models play a bigger role in transforming devolved forest management into sustainable livelihood strategies, as highlighted by Prateek and Divy (2024). By combining local Gram Sabhas, indigenous collectors gain critical market access, avoiding exploitative intermediaries and locking higher-value, fair trade prices. records.title: Editorial: Public health challenges in post-Soviet countries during and beyond COVID-19, volume II
records.authors: Antonio Sarria-Santamera; Ida Liseckiene; Natalya Glushkova; Yuliya Semenova
records.abstract: On January 30, 2020, the WHO Director-General accepted the recommendation of the Emergency Committee and declared the novel coronavirus outbreak (2019-nCoV) a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC)(1). Post-Soviet countries (PSC) faced significant challenges during the COVID-19 pandemic. As for many other countries, the pandemic was the first experience of such magnitude for Ministries of Health (MoH) since the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991. Therefore, many MoHs in the PSC lacked the necessary infrastructure, protocols, and staff to manage such events. However, while public health systems in many developing countries elsewhere are subpar, PSC inherited systems based on the Semashko model that were undergoing reforms to varying degrees (2). This factor proved critical to countries' capacity to respond to the pandemic, as public health emergency response systems had not been updated since Soviet times. These limitations are especially evident in the lack of progress in incorporating upto-date methodologies of disease surveillance and laboratory testing. As a result, the COVID-19 pandemic became a system shock that challenged the readiness of public health emergency response capacities. While it is clear that PSCs were not ready (as in many developed countries), it is not clear whether the MoHs in these countries have learned their lessons and strengthened their capacities to face the next pandemic.The COVID-19 pandemic had devastating impacts on public health, leading to the inaccessibility of health services for many people in need, catastrophic healthcare expenditures, and premature deaths. The countries experienced a shortage of facilities and medical professionals, a shortage that was particularly pronounced due to earlier reductions in hospital beds. Resources proved to be insufficient due to a severe shortage of essentials like medicines, diagnostic tests, and personal protective equipment, particularly during the peak period (3,4).Researchers from the region investigated aspects of public health systems such as a shift towards private healthcare. The example of Kazakhstan gives an interesting perspective for readiness as its healthcare system was based on the Soviet-era system, and the private healthcare sector was almost non-existenthttps://www.frontiersin.org/journals/publichealth/articles/10.3389/fpubh.2025.1608557/full (6). However, in the decade preceding the pandemic, healthcare shifted towards a higher number of private healthcare facilities. Thus, the pandemic required the government of Kazakhstan to mobilize both public and private healthcare providers to address the dramatic increase in patients. Although private hospitals were not originally adapted to manage large-scale infectious disease outbreaks, they adjusted by setting up COVID-19 units, at the cost of considerable business disruptions due to decreased patient flow and financial constraints.The pandemic exacerbated many prior challenges in the healthcare system of PSC, including issues of trust and violence against healthcare workers: up to 38% of healthcare professionals experience some form of violence in the workplace (7). The COVID-19 pandemic brought not only increased workloads and burnout, but a threat of violence from patients and family members (8)(9)(10). Moreover, the pandemic has eroded the societal respect traditionally given to healthcare workers (11): in Moldova, almost half of the violence aimed at healthcare workers primarily involved verbal threats; the COVID-19 pandemic increased concerns about workplace violencehttps://www.frontiersin.org/journals/publichealth/articles/10.3389/fpubh.2025.1560096/full. COVID-19 infection brought new attention to chronic diseases, including cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes mellitus. While these diseases traditionally affect older populations, their prevalence among younger populations is increasing (12). Moiynbayeva et al. (13) forecast a rise in cardiovascular disease and stroke prevalence in Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, and Turkmenistan. This is concerning, as patients with chronic diseases were at a higher risk of severe complications and death from COVID-19 (14)(15)(16).The pandemic's demographic effects were significant worldwide, though different countries reacted differently to lockdowns, declining birth rates, reduced in-person communication, fear of COVID-19, and other issues. Karibayeva et al. ( 17) report no long-term effect on birthrate in Kazakhstan, which might suggest a limited effect of the pandemic on life. However, long-term studies on birthrate and reproductive health are needed, as some studies suggest that COVID-19 infection might have long-term effects on the reproductive system, including hormonal disturbances that can affect regularity of the menstrual cycle, ovulatory function, and receptivity of the endometrium (18). Data from United States suggests that the COVID-19 pandemic has worsened existing health disparities and disproportionately affected racial and ethnic minorities (19). As reported by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, segregated ethnic groups have experienced higher rates of infection, hospitalization, and death compared to other populations (20). These findings were corroborated by European studies (21,22), which report that people living in segregated, lowincome neighborhoods were affected by disproportionately higher rates of COVID-19 infections. One of the other vulnerable groups are older adults, particularly 65 and over, who were at the higher risk for severe complications and death from COVID-19 and thus requiring improved access to healthcare services for both acute and chronic conditions (23). A survey of 1,503 Lithuanians aged 65 and overhttps://www.frontiersin.org/journals/publichealth/articles/10.3389/fpubh.2025.1504049/full reports that the primary reasons for nonutilization of healthcare services included fear of COVID-19 infection for 1 in 6 respondents. These studies provide further support for the view that the COVID-19 pandemic had a significant effect on healthcare systems worldwide, limiting access to routine healthcare and exacerbating inequalities in access to healthcare (25).Health-related behaviors in older adults were also affected during and after the COVID-19 pandemic: in Lithuania, there was a decrease in physical activity, face-to-face communications, and an increase in remote communication in older adults in Lithuania. Factors like education, income, age, residence, and health status affected these outcomes, suggesting that a differential approach is needed for mitigating negative outcomes from the pandemichttps://www.frontiersin.org/journals/publichealth/articles/10.3389/fpubh.2024.1504193/full.While the WHO declared the end of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2023, populations across the world were reminded of dangers posed by fast spreading and deadly viruses. Public attention to emerging viruses was at all time high during and several years after the pandemic, but the challenges associated with managing a large epidemic are still potentially there. While thousands of research papers were dedicated to the COVID-19 pandemic, much lesser attention is given to lessons learned from the pandemic, or state of readiness in case of another worldwide outbreak of infectious disease.One of the significant challenges in PSC during the pandemic was undiagnosed infection. The potential undercount of overall cases has been estimated to be by 55-60% by official statistics (27), although managing the COVID-19 pandemic may have also decreased healthcare systems' ability to surveil and report other infectious diseases https . COVID-19 pandemic also brought new attention to hygiene among different population groups, including children (29,30): the majority of school children in Karaganda region, Kazakhstan, showed appropriate hand hygiene practices, though only one-fourth of the students washed hands after contact with a sick friend. Therefore, to reduce the spread of infectious disease among school children, public health interventions should focus on behavioral reinforcement in addition to education, including habit formation techniques and peer modelinghttps://www.frontiersin.org/journals/publichealth/articles/10.3389/fpubh.2025.1593579/full. Overall, studies from the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic exposed gaps in the PSC public health capacity and pandemic preparedness, reflect on risks associated with health delivery services, violence against health workers, and population behavior, as well as the impact of COVID-19 on the intersection of chronic and infectious diseases.However, the studies were predominantly cross-sectional designs and data on long-term public health impacts or the persistent effects of the COVID-19 pandemic or comparison of health systems pre-and post-pandemic period are lacking. Globally, lessons from the pandemic have emphasized the need for comprehensive health policies that strengthen national health systems on the foundations of public health and universal health coverage, focusing on the management and prevention of both chronic and infectious diseases while maintaining a strong emphasis on population health behavior, especially among vulnerable populations. Countries should determine and expand national pandemic preparedness plans to prevent and respond to newly emerging infectious diseases.

records.title: Dark tourism: concepts, practices, ethical challenges and future research
records.authors: Wondemsew Mesafint Kebadie
records.abstract: Purpose This review paper critically synthesizes contemporary scholarship on dark tourism, integrating conceptual foundations, visitor motivations, management practices, ethical dilemmas, sustainability challenges, and emerging research directions. It aims to advance a coherent understanding of responsible dark tourism development through an interdisciplinary lens. Design/methodology/approach A systematic critical literature review of peer-reviewed literature published between 2000 and 2025 examined on tourism, heritage, psychology, ethics, cultural studies, and sustainability research. Through an iterative thematic synthesis, the literature was organized into four interconnected dimensions. These dimensions informed the development of an integrated conceptual framework for contemporary dark tourism scholarship. Findings The review reveals that dark tourism is not inherently exploitative; its ethical and social implications depend on governance, interpretation, stakeholder engagement, and management practices. Visitor motivations extend beyond morbid curiosity and include education, remembrance, identity formation, and moral reflection. Ethical concerns about commodification, authenticity, and digital representation underscore the need for inclusive governance and community participation. Sustainable dark tourism development requires historical sensitivity and the integration of triple bottom line principles. Research limitations/implications As a conceptual review based on secondary sources, the proposed framework requires empirical validation across diverse cultural and institutional contexts using qualitative, quantitative, and mixed-methods approaches. Originality/value This paper advances dark tourism scholarship by proposing an interdisciplinary framework linking conceptual debates to ethical governance, sustainability, destination management, and emerging technologies. By synthesizing fragmented literature into a coherent theoretical perspective, the study offers practical guidance for destination managers and policymakers. It identifies priority research areas, including postcolonial dark tourism, Global South perspectives, terrorism-related tourism, digital memorialization, virtual reality, and responsible governance.

records.title: Evaluating laboratory cyberbiosecurity capacity in Morocco: development and pilot implementation of the cyber self-laboratory assessment tool (Cyber-SLAT)
records.authors: Alexander G. Linder; Vanessa Grégoire; Larbi Baassi; Sanae Lemrabet; Erin M. Sorrell
records.abstract: Introduction Cyberbiosecurity, the discipline addressing risks at the convergence of biological research and digital infrastructure, has advanced conceptually but remains largely untranslated into laboratory practice, and empirical assessments of laboratory‐level cyberbiosecurity capacity in low‐ or middle‐income countries (LMICs) remain rare. Methods The objective of this study was to develop and pilot the Cyberbiosecurity Self‐Laboratory Assessment Tool (Cyber‐SLAT), which integrates a new cyberbiosecurity domain of 57 questions into an existing, validated biorisk management self‐assessment instrument, yielding a bilingual (English/French) tool of 258 questions across six domains that span risk evaluation, planning and management, infrastructure and systems, and incident response. The Cyber‐SLAT was piloted across seven Moroccan laboratories representing five institutional types, using an implementation‐driven design that combined virtual training, structured self-assessment, quantitative gap analysis, a review of corrective actions, and a two-day in-person capacity‐building dialogue that included the national cybersecurity authority. Results While traditional biorisk management functions were generally operational, the cyberbiosecurity domain contained the highest concentration of gaps of any domain assessed (53 of 129 identified problem questions). Two universal gaps, which no laboratory could affirm, and 12 critical gaps were identified related to cyberbisoecurity, with 12 of these 14 severe gaps (86%) addressing operational rather than technical capacities. These findings suggest that the principal barrier for laboratories entering the cyberbiosecurity domain is operational rather than technical, and that operational foundations must be established before technical safeguards can be effectively implemented or sustained. The assessment process was accompanied by a cross-functional dialogue between laboratorians and information technology personnel and established direct linkages between the laboratory community and national cybersecurity governance. Discussion This pilot provides, to our knowledge, the first application of the full Cyber‐SLAT in North Africa, and adds to a small but growing evidence base on laboratory cyberbiosecurity capacity in resource‐constrained settings.

records.title: Characterization and pollution assessment of surface water in the Ziz Basin, southeastern Morocco
records.authors: Aziza Lamchaimech; Khadija El-Moustaqim; Youness Kouchane; Yousef Hahou; El Houssaine Ouharba; Jamal Mabrouki
records.abstract: Surface-water resources in arid and semi-arid regions are increasingly vulnerable to climatic variability and anthropogenic pressures, including urban expansion, wastewater discharge, agricultural activities, and inadequate waste management. In southeastern Morocco, the Ziz Basin is an important water-resource system, particularly because it is connected with the Hassan Addakhil Dam. Understanding the spatial distribution of water quality and identifying the main pollution sources are essential for protecting these resources and supporting sustainable water management. This study aims to assess the physicochemical and environmental conditions of the surface waters in the Ziz Basin by analyzing monthly water samples collected during two separate 12-month monitoring periods, in 2016 and 2022, at 7 sampling stations. The results showed that the surface waters in the Ziz Basin were contaminated. The pollution is of domestic origin and threatens the basin’s water quality. The study methodology utilized principal component analysis of physicochemical parameters to categorize the sampling stations into two types. Upstream of the Hassan Addakhil Dam, stations were characterized by high dissolved oxygen levels and lower values for other parameters, whereas downstream stations showed higher COD, BOD5, total phosphorus, and phosphates. Physicochemical parameters were analyzed using standard methods to assess basin pollution control. Results indicated minimal spatiotemporal variation in pollution, although pollution levels increased significantly during the rainy season. In conclusion, this study highlights the importance of monitoring and managing water quality in the Ziz Basin, particularly regarding the impacts of urban pollution. The findings suggest the need for effective measures to mitigate the anthropogenic impacts on the region’s environment.

records.title: Open innovation for sustainable urban transformation in Kazakhstan's monotowns: integrating digital transformation, ESG governance, and urban-territorial resilience
records.authors: Marina Abikayeva; Rajasekhara Mouly Potluri; Assem Omarkozhayeva; Zhibek Omarkhanova; Danagul Tleuzhanova; Gulden Zholdayakova; Olga Yanovskaya
records.abstract: Resource-dependent monotowns face interconnected urban sustainability challenges arising from economic concentration, environmental degradation, technological dependence, infrastructure pressures, demographic change, and institutional vulnerability. Addressing these challenges requires an integrated approach to sustainable urban transformation that combines digital innovation, environmental responsibility, social inclusion, and urban resilience. This conceptual study develops an integrative framework explaining how open innovation can connect digital transformation and ESG-oriented urban governance to strengthen the resilience and sustainability of Kazakhstan's monotowns. Using a qualitative conceptual approach, the study synthesizes academic literature, international policy documents, and Kazakhstan's national strategic documents through thematic analysis to identify seven interrelated themes and inform the proposed framework. The present study is intentionally theory-building and conceptual and does not claim empirical validation of the proposed relationships. Drawing on Regional Resilience Theory, Evolutionary Economic Geography, Open Innovation Theory, the Quadruple Helix Model, and sustainability governance, the framework conceptualizes monotowns as resource-dependent urban-regional systems in which government, industry, universities, and communities jointly shape sustainable transformation. The framework identifies digital infrastructure, smart technologies, data-enabled governance, knowledge exchange, collaborative innovation, institutional adaptability, human-capital development, and ESG-oriented governance as interconnected mechanisms supporting sustainable urban infrastructure, environmental resource management, economic diversification, social inclusion, and resilient urban development. Open innovation is positioned as the bridging mechanism through which digital and sustainability transitions can be coordinated across urban stakeholders. The study contributes to sustainable cities research by integrating innovation ecosystems, digital transformation, ESG-oriented urban governance, and urban-territorial resilience within a place-sensitive framework. The framework also provides policy directions to advance SDG 11 and support inclusive, environmentally responsible, technologically enabled, and resilient transformation of resource-dependent monotowns.

records.title: Digital Twins and Simulation Technologies in Service-Oriented Supply Chains
records.authors: Thinh Gia Hoang; Nam Hai Vu
records.abstract: This chapter examines how digital twins and simulation technologies can enhance service-oriented supply chains by improving visibility, decision-making, resilience, and service performance. It explains the conceptual foundations and evolution of digital twins, emphasizing their role as continuously updated virtual representations of physical service processes, supplier networks, and customer interactions. The chapter further discusses how simulation methods, including discrete event simulation, agent-based modelling, system dynamics, and hybrid approaches, support operational planning, demand responsiveness, partner network visibility, disruption management, and continuous performance improvement. Drawing on industry examples and prior research, it also identifies key implementation barriers at organizational and industry levels, including leadership commitment, workforce readiness, data governance, interoperability, cybersecurity, standardization, and scalability.

records.title: Digital Servitization in Service-Oriented Manufacturing Through Dynamic Capabilities and Supply Chain Transformation
records.authors: Thinh Gia Hoang; Tien Tran Thuy Dang
records.abstract: This chapter examines how Industry 4.0 technologies reshape servitization and service-oriented manufacturing within digitally transforming supply chains. While digital servitization is often associated with technologies such as IoT, artificial intelligence, cloud platforms, analytics, and digital twins, the chapter argues that technology adoption alone is insufficient to generate service-oriented performance. Drawing on service-dominant logic, business model innovation, supply chain integration, socio-technical systems thinking, and dynamic capabilities theory, the chapter develops a theory-informed model explaining how manufacturers sense digital service opportunities, seize them through Industry 4.0-enabled service offerings, and reconfigure supply chain relationships around lifecycle value creation. The model is applied to an anonymous industrial equipment manufacturing case that illustrates the transition from product sales and reactive maintenance toward predictive maintenance, remote diagnostics, lifecycle service agreements, and recurring service revenue. The chapter contributes by positioning digital servitization as a capability-driven supply chain transformation and highlights practical conditions related to data governance, supplier readiness, customer trust, cybersecurity, and service-oriented performance measurement.

records.title: Integrating character education and student well-being: A comparative review for elementary schools
records.authors: I Made Pustikayasa; Dedi Kuswandi; Agus Wedi; Nurlyta Virlyani
records.abstract: This study examines how character education can be positioned as a foundation for student well-being through a structured narrative comparative review of Indonesia, Singapore, and Vietnam. Scholarship was identified through targeted searches of peer reviewed journals and academic books, complemented by reference list screening, and supported by selected policy and organizational documents. Evidence was extracted on key constructs, proposed mechanisms, and school practices, then synthesized through SDT guided comparative thematic analysis. Findings are organized into four analytic domains: curriculum, classroom pedagogy, learning space/school climate, and digital governance. The evidence base is uneven: Singapore’s literature more consistently foregrounds well-being initiatives, Indonesian studies emphasize need supportive pedagogy, and Vietnam’s sources are more strongly oriented toward child protection and legal or regulatory frameworks. Across contexts, well-being, oriented character education appears most plausible when curriculum intentions are enacted through need supportive teaching that fosters autonomy, competence, and relatedness and is reinforced by safe learning environments. Leadership routines, governance, and digital safeguards (privacy and cybersecurity) shape implementation conditions. Conclusions are presented as bounded propositions; future research should test them using primary school evidence in each context
