records.abstract: This deposit accompanies the survey "Cybersecurity of Smart Residential Solar Energy Systems". It contains a replication of the structured, PRISMA-informed literature search on which the survey rests, together with the code that produces it. The funnel counts reported in the article are those recorded for the original search of 3 August 2026. The record-level output of that run was not preserved, and the state of the OpenAlex index cannot be pinned to a past date without a paid plan. What is deposited here is therefore a re-execution of the same twelve queries and the same screening and eligibility rules, carried out on 25 August 2026, so that the procedure can be inspected and repeated rather than taken on trust. The archive holds the retrieval and screening code, the 2,040 raw records of the replicated run, the screening and eligibility decision for every one of those records, the per-query hit counts, and the match of each cited study against the replicated result set. A README states the stage-by-stage comparison between the original and the replicated funnel, and it states explicitly what does not follow from these numbers. Coverage figures as of 21 September 2026: of 95 cited peer-reviewed journal and conference papers, 50 appear in the replicated result set, 49 matched by DOI and 1 by normalised title. Of the remaining 45, ten predate the 2020 to 2026 search window and thirty-five lie inside it but were returned by none of the twelve queries.

records.title: Enhanced resilience of demand response under hybrid disruptions in renewable- and storage-rich integrated energy systems: A safety-filtered multi-agent deep reinforcement learning framework
records.authors: Reza Sepehrzad; Nima Khosravi; Hadi Vatankhah Ghadim; Jeremy Watson; Hamid Reza Abdolmohammadi; Mahdieh S. Sadabadi
records.abstract: Demand response (DR) in renewable- and storage-rich integrated energy systems (IESs) must remain economically reliable and physically executable despite renewable and load uncertainty, volatile prices, and cyber disruptions affecting sensing and communication. Existing approaches commonly separate market scheduling, distributed control, cyber resilience, and feasibility enforcement, creating a gap between day-ahead commitments and real-time delivery. This paper proposes a unified market-to-execution framework based on large language model (LLM)-guided multi-agent deep reinforcement learning (MADRL). The framework coordinates electrical and thermal loads, renewable generation, battery and thermal storage, and multi-energy conversion resources through cyber- and uncertainty-aware observations, adversarial and domain-randomized training, and conditional value-at-risk regularization. The LLM is used only as a bounded supervisory layer that interprets structured operating conditions, prioritizes inter-agent coordination, and supports repair decisions; executable actions remain generated by the MADRL agents and are projected onto a feasible operating region defined by device, storage, comfort, network, and power-quality constraints. The framework is assessed under nominal, uncertainty-only, attack-only, and combined-stress regimes involving false-data injection, denial-of-service, and communication delay. Under combined stress, DR delivery remains within 93.8–96.4%, while operational violation rates remain within 1.2–2.3%. The results further show progressive rather than abrupt performance degradation, stronger economic and downside-risk performance than advanced learning-based baselines, and adaptive reallocation of flexibility toward more controllable storage-supported resources as stress increases. The main finding is that reliable market delivery under cyber-operational stress is achieved through the coordinated interaction of risk-aware distributed learning, bounded supervisory guidance, and feasibility-preserving execution rather than through any single control component.

records.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Transformation in Smart and Sustainable Infrastructure Systems
records.authors: Marjan Sultana Nuha
records.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and digitalization are rapidly transforming the planning, operation, maintenance and management of critical infrastructure. Planning, operation, maintenance and management of critical infrastructure is changing with Artificial Intelligence (AI) and digitalization. The review covers energy, transportation, water, building, and urban infrastructure sectors, focusing on predictive maintenance and forecasting, anomaly detection, adaptive control, digital twins, asset management, and resilience planning, highlighting the potential and limitations of AI and machine learning (ML) applications in these fields. AI's forecasting capabilities help with load balancing in electricity systems and the integration of renewable energy, while intelligent transportation systems enhance traffic management, safety, and infrastructure condition monitoring. AI is being used in water systems for leak detection, water quality monitoring, and drought forecasting, while in building applications, it's used for energy optimization, predictive control, and equipment fault detection. The review also explores cross cutting data quality, sensor reliability, interoperability, cybersecurity, human oversight, governance, ethics and regulatory compliance requirements. Although significant technology advancement has been realized, implementation is limited by existing legacy infrastructure, disparate data systems, limited technical capacity, funding and procurement barriers, cybersecurity, and demos from research and into large scale operating deployment. Special emphasis is placed on the concept of explainable AI, human in the loop decision making, risk based asset prioritization and ongoing model validation as ways to provide public accountability and reliability. Future directions are: climate adaptive infrastructure management, digital twins, edge computing, advanced remote sensing, continual and federated learning, dynamic network modeling, and hybrid human AI decision systems.

records.title: Digital Twins for Nuclear Reactor Monitoring and Operational Intelligence: A Systematic Scoping Review
records.authors: Veska Gancheva
records.abstract: Digital twins (DTs) are increasingly proposed for nuclear-reactor monitoring, diagnosis, prediction, control, and decision support, but the maturity of reported systems is difficult to compare because DT realization, physical anchoring, synchronization, adaptation, validation, real-time execution, and trustworthiness are often conflated. This systematic scoping review maps substantive DT research for nuclear fission reactors and nuclear power plants using a strict substantive-DT definition and a multidimensional evidence-coding framework covering DT realization, physical anchoring, adaptation, validation, real-time capability, and trustworthiness. Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and IEEE Xplore yielded 845 database records and 590 unique records after deduplication. A multi-pass title/abstract workflow classified 182 records as Include, 397 as excluded from the primary-study stream, and 11 as Uncertain, yielding 193 reports sought for retrieval. Despite iterative multi-source retrieval attempts, 96 reports could not be retrieved. One additional Uncertain conference report was linked to an already retained journal report and was not treated as an independent report; 96 retrieved reports underwent primary full-text eligibility assessment. Seventy-one retrieved and eligible peer-reviewed primary reports met the inclusion criteria. Of these, 44/71 (62%) were Tier A implemented or integrated DT systems. Physical anchoring ranged from P0 simulation-only realization (39/71, 55%) to P3 operating-reactor or plant evidence (9/71, 13%); within P3, four reports used retrospective/offline operating data and five demonstrated live or near-live reactor/plant linkage. Validation evidence comprised 40/71 reports (56%) with development-linked validation (V1), 26/71 (37%) with separated empirical or benchmark validation (V2), and 5/71 (7%) with prospective, challenge-based, or independently confirmed validation (V3). Adaptation was limited: 51/71 reports (72%) demonstrated no adaptation (A0), 3/71 (4%) episodic or intermittent recalibration (A1), 5/71 (7%) online state synchronization/estimation (A2-S), 12/71 (17%) online parameter/model adaptation (A2-P), and none met the A3 criterion. Computational real-time capability was supported in 42/71 reports (59%), whereas integrated real- or near-real-time execution was demonstrated in 27/71 (38%); live physical-data ingestion, explicit recurring physical-to-digital synchronization, and automatic DT-to-physical actuation were demonstrated in 11/71 (15%), 5/71 (7%), and 1/71 (1%), respectively. Hybrid modelling was the dominant paradigm (34/71, 48%). Trustworthiness was asymmetric: calibration and robustness/OOD assessment were much more common than uncertainty quantification, explainability, cybersecurity, traceability, human oversight, or demonstrated regulatory readiness. A targeted data audit identified only four reports linked to clearly open and reusable benchmark or downloadable resources. Family-aware, quality, physical-evidence, temporal, and data-access sensitivity analyses did not materially change the central conclusions. Nuclear-DT maturity is best understood as multidimensional; future progress requires staged physical validation, bounded adaptive synchronization, trustworthy decision support, reproducible data/model provenance, and independent deployment-oriented validation.

records.title: Dynamic coupled control with closed-loop robustness for reconciling adaptability, safety, and real-time performance under production line condition switches
records.authors: Yansheng Chen; Jiulin Song; Jie Li; Zhonghao Liu; Yuning Xie; Hao Xu
records.abstract: Context Light industry production lines are characterized by frequent dynamic condition switching, heterogeneous task portfolios, and deeply interconnected equipment. Their intelligent upgrading imposes competing demands for algorithmic adaptability to varying conditions, security against cyber threats, and real-time responsiveness for critical tasks. These three objectives are inherently in conflict, and existing approaches largely address them in isolation, lacking a unified mechanism to reconcile their trade-offs under dynamic operation. Objectives This paper aims to develop a coupled control and robustness assurance framework that jointly optimizes adaptability, safety, and real-time performance under dynamic operating conditions, while maintaining end-to-end robustness across both routine condition switches and extreme fault scenarios. Methods We propose a closed-loop "sensing–decision–execution–feedback" architecture driven by real-time operating-condition prediction. Multi-source perception (sensors, PLCs, MES) feeds an LSTM-based condition forecaster, whose outputs guide dynamic weight allocation among the three objectives. The optimal trade-off point is solved via an adapted NSGA-Ⅲ algorithm under production-line constraints. A hierarchical adaptation strategy tailors control parameters for heterogeneous equipment (PLC/DCS, industrial robots, sensors). Lightweight security primitives (SM3, AES) and a priority-deadline hybrid scheduler are integrated to keep overhead within millisecond bounds. A robustness feedback module continuously monitors performance and triggers re-optimization when deviations are detected. Results Experiments on electronic assembly and food processing lines show that our system achieves a 96.3% adaptability success rate, a security response time of 7.2 ms, and a key-task latency of 38.2 ms under dynamic conditions—meeting the ≤50 ms deadline with 99.2% satisfaction. Under simultaneous multi-device failures, the core-task interruption rate drops to 15%, a 75% relative reduction over the traditional scheme, with anomaly recovery within 80 ms. Conclusion The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively reconciles the adaptability--security--real-time trade-off through dynamic coupled control and closed-loop robustness feedback, offering a practically deployable solution for intelligent production-line upgrades in complex, time-varying industrial environments.

records.title: Preparing pre-service teachers to understand and address cybersecurity challenges and promote digital citizenship in resource-constrained educational contexts: the role of 21st-century skills and technological knowledge
records.authors: Lebohang Mahlo; Agnes Chigona
records.abstract: The availability and use of affordable mobile technologies offer significant opportunities for teachers to integrate technologies in their teaching, particularly in resource-constrained contexts. However, the availability and affordability of these digital tools do not guarantee their effective use. Their use also exposes teachers and learners to cybersecurity risks, and how well pre-service teachers (PSTs) are prepared to deal with those risks cannot be assumed. This study examines how PSTs are prepared to understand and address cybersecurity challenges and to promote digital citizenship in resource-constrained educational contexts. Preparation is examined along two dimensions: the 21st-century skills that PSTs demonstrate and the technological knowledge (TK) they acquire. This study was guided by the Cybersecurity Curriculum Framework, which integrates Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK), Digital Citizenship, and 21st-century skills. A qualitative approach was used. Open-ended surveys were completed by 357 PSTs, from which ten information-rich responses were selected for in-depth analysis, and a further 11 PSTs took part in a focus group interview. Participants from two universities included 1st- to 4th-year students enrolled in the Intermediate, Senior, and Further Education and Training (FET) phases. The findings revealed that preparation was uneven across the competencies the framework requires. Critical thinking, media and ICT literacy, and social responsibility were consistently evident in participants' accounts, whereas problem-solving, collaboration, creativity, and leadership were not. PSTs were therefore prepared to understand cybersecurity challenges but not to address them, and to value digital citizenship but not to promote it. TK combined with evaluative skills produced a protective form of digital citizenship, while the generative and collective skills needed for empowered, future-ready practice were not in evidence. Institutional, curricular, and contextual factors further constrained PSTs from acting as digital citizens. This study contributes to Initial Teacher Education (ITE) institutions by enabling them to design modules that prepare PSTs to understand and address cybersecurity challenges, especially those that affect learners, and to promote digital citizenship by deliberately developing the 21st-century skills and TK that such preparation requires, rather than relying on awareness-raising alone..

records.title: Challenges of ICT Usage among Academic Staff in University of Uyo, Nigeria
records.authors: Ngozi U. Nwonye
records.abstract: The integration of Information and Communication Technology (ICT) in Nigerian universities has introduced transformative changes to education and communication, yet significant barriers impede its optimal utilization. This study investigates these challenges within the University of Uyo, employing a mixed-methods approach. A structured survey was administered to 317 academic staff, utilizing stratified random sampling to ensure representation across faculties. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and thematic analysis. Findings reveal that inadequate infrastructure (mean = 3.85, SD = 0.42), high internet costs (mean = 3.78, SD = 0.65), and limited digital literacy (mean = 3.48, SD = 0.70) are critical obstacles to ICT adoption. Additional challenges include frequent power outages, insufficient training programs, and cybersecurity concerns. These barriers disproportionately affect rural areas, exacerbating the digital divide. Recommendations emphasize the need for robust investments in ICT infrastructure, including high-speed broadband and reliable power supply, alongside subsidized internet costs and targeted digital literacy training. Collaboration between government, private sectors, and academic institutions is essential for implementing scalable solutions. The study highlights the importance of addressing these systemic issues to bridge existing inequalities, improve academic productivity, and enhance familial communication. Future research should focus on sector-specific and culturally relevant strategies to overcome ICT challenges and foster inclusive educational practices in Nigerian universities. These interventions are critical for realizing ICT's transformative potential in academia and beyond.

records.title: DIGITAL TOOLS FOR ENSURING THE ECONOMIC SECURITY OF ENTREPRENEURIAL ACTIVITY IN CONDITIONS OF SYSTEMIC CRISIS
records.authors: N. Tanasiienko; L. Bushovska; S. Hrebinska
records.abstract: The article examines the role of digital tools in ensuring the economic security of entrepreneurial activity under conditions of systemic crisis, characterized by high uncertainty, dynamic risks, increasing digital dependence, and growing cyber threats. The purpose of the study is to systematize digital tools for ensuring economic security, determine their functional purpose and impact on the main components of enterprise security, and substantiate an approach to their comprehensive integration. The study considers digital security provision as an integral component of the enterprise’s overall economic security system aimed at protecting economic interests, information and digital resources, ensuring business continuity, and increasing adaptability to crisis impacts. Digital tools are systematized according to their functional purpose, including monitoring and data collection, analytics and forecasting, early warning, cybersecurity and information protection, digital trust and identification, digital management and coordination, and business continuity and resilience. The functional capabilities of artificial intelligence, Big Data, digital platforms, Early Warning Systems, and cybersecurity tools are determined. Their role in monitoring, risk assessment, threat forecasting, early warning, decision-making, and response is substantiated. It is proposed to consider digital tools as interconnected elements of a unified digital cycle «data → analysis → forecast → warning → decision → response», which contributes to reducing the time between threat emergence and managerial response. Based on the generalization, four interrelated functional roles of digital tools are proposed: analytical, preventive, protective, and adaptive. The analytical role involves transforming large data sets into an information basis for managerial decisions; the preventive role focuses on risk forecasting and early threat detection; the protective role provides counteraction to digital, information, and related economic threats; the adaptive role ensures operational adjustment of business processes, continuity, and recovery under crisis conditions. It is concluded that the effectiveness of digital economic security provision depends not on the number of implemented technologies, but on their functional integration and ability to transform data into timely managerial decisions. Further research should focus on developing methods for quantitative assessment of digital security

records.title: CONCEPT AND IMPLEMENTATION OF JARIMAH TA'ZIR IN CONTEMPORARY ISLAMIC CRIMINAL LAW
records.authors: St. Hadijah Wahid; Muh. Bambang Taufik; Muh. Ilham Azis; Jusri Mudjrimin; Nur Qalbi
records.abstract: In the contemporary era, social dynamics and the emergence of new forms of crime require Islamic criminal law to remain adaptive. Unlike hudud and qishash, which are textually prescribed and relatively rigid, jarimah ta'zir offers regulatory flexibility based on the authority of the ruler (ulil amri) to realize the public interest (maslahah). This study aims to provide an in-depth analysis of the fundamental concept, criteria for determining sanctions, and the dynamic implementation of jarimah ta'zir within the context of modern Islamic criminal law. This study employs a qualitative method using library research. It adopts normative-juridical and philosophical approaches by analyzing primary and secondary legal sources related to contemporary fiqh jinayah. The findings show that contemporary ta'zir is no longer limited to classical physical punishments such as flogging but has evolved into forms of administrative and financial sanctions, including fines, as well as restrictions on liberty that are considered more relevant to human rights. The determination of ta'zir sanctions is based on the principle of flexible legality, the level of harm and impact caused by the offense (mudharat), and a rehabilitative orientation (tadzib). In modern implementations, such as those applied through the Aceh Qanun and legal codifications in several Muslim countries, ta'zir has demonstrated its potential to serve as a bridge between classical Islamic l aw and modernity, particularly in responding to cyber, corporate, and financial crimes. In conclusion, jarimah ta'zir possesses considerable legal elasticity and constitutes a major instrument of Islamic criminal law for remaining relevant, solution-oriented, and oriented toward justice amid changing times.

records.title: Social isolation, loneliness, and unsafe behavior in the digital environment
records.authors: T.N. Berezina; T.A. Finogenova; M.M. Simonova
records.abstract: Context and Relevance. The relevance of the study is determined by the increasing digitalization of society and the specific psychological mechanisms of online decision-making. In conditions of uncertainty social isolation and loneliness become factors that determine human behavior and can contribute to the adoption of unsafe decisions. Goal. Analysis of the psychological determinants of unsafe behavior in the digital environment and identification of the role and place of social isolation and loneliness among these determinants. Study hypothesis: we assume that the causes of unsafe behavior may be related to factors such as social isolation and loneliness, may be caused by them, may be intensified, transformed, or acquire a different meaning under their influence. Materials and methods. Method: systematic analysis. Data source: search on the Google Scholar and ResearchGate platforms; publications posted in the Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, and eLIBRARY.RU databases were selected. Data extraction: 46 articles were selected. The author’s model of unsafe behavior was used for interpretation. Results. Unsafe behavior is defined as the performance of actions that deviate from established rules, procedures, and safety measures. The digital environment is replete with specific risks, factors of which include emotional loneliness (which leads to suspicious acquaintances, unsafe relationships, sexual harassment, violence and aggressive attacks, phishing, sexting, fraud, material damage, and theft of personal data); social loneliness (which results in cyberbullying, fraud, involvement in illegal activities, social engineering, material damage, and theft of personal data); and social isolation in the workplace (which causes safety violations, downloading of unsafe software, infection with computer viruses, and material damage). Young users in the online environment are more likely to encounter cyberbullying, trolling, aggression, sexual harassment and internet addiction; adults are most vulnerable to information security threats in the workplace and to the compromise of corporate data; older people, as a rule, become victims of cybercrimes of a socio‑economic nature. The protective role of other people in reducing the risks of unsafe behavior has been confirmed (meeting the need for communication, warning about danger, seeking external help). The role of subjective loneliness as a direct predictor of unsafe behavior in the digital environment is not clearly confirmed: the causes of unsafe behavior in the digital environment may also include the level of self‑control, attachment type, tendency to be persuaded, cognitive impairments (more common in older people), rather than loneliness; unsafe virtual relationships rarely translate into reality; loneliness can stimulate creative self‑realization in the digital environment. It is predicted that new risks in the digital environment will emerge, dependent on social isolation and the experience of loneliness; it is assumed that they will be associated with the emergence of digital interlocutors and the development of communication with chatbots. Conclusions: The relationship between social isolation and loneliness and the digital environment is ambivalent: on the one hand, social isolation and loneliness can act as factors provoking various forms of unsafe behavior in the online environment, and on the other hand, the online environment can perform a compensatory function, providing the opportunity for social interaction and the experience of social inclusion and significance.

records.title: Ten pillars for responsible and ethical AI adoption in Lebanon’s health sector
records.authors: Francois Fadell; Lina Khatib; Walid Ahmar; Abir Alame; Kyaw Myint Aung; Elie Klimos; George Assaf; Lina Abou Mrad; Audine Salloum; Mirjam Messo; Jordi Martin Domingo; Ibrahim Makdessi; Abdulrahman Merkbawi; Fadl Khaled; Abdul Rahman Al-Bizri; Razi El-Hage; Fadi Alame; Ziad El-Khatib
records.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into healthcare systems globally, including diagnostics, predictive analytics, and public health surveillance. AI adoption is increasing, yet fragile and resource-limited settings face distinct ethical and legal challenges. Lebanon provides a complex case: since 2019, the country has experienced economic collapse, workforce migration, rising non-communicable diseases, and sustained refugee influx, alongside rapid digital expansion. In 2026, the Ministry of Public Health launched the National Digital Health Transformation Strategy (2025–2030), recognizing AI as a potential lever to strengthen services and rebuild public trust. However, national ethical and legal standards specific to healthcare AI remain underdeveloped. In this perspective report, we present AI opportunities, legal gaps, and ethical risks within Lebanon’s fragmented public–private system. AI offers potential benefits in clinical decision support, public health surveillance, workforce support, and medical education. Yet algorithmic bias, data protection weaknesses, regulatory ambiguity, and unclear liability expose patients and professionals to uncertainty. Lebanon currently operates within a regulatory gray zone, as existing healthcare system and data laws predate machine-learning-based decision systems. Drawing on international ethical frameworks and pluralistic moral traditions, we propose an ethical containment strategy grounded in human dignity, accountability, transparency, and equity. We outline ten pillars, including human-led decision-making, sector-specific governance within the Ministry of Public Health (MOPH), bias containment, strengthened data protection and cybersecurity, clarified legal responsibility, professional training, participatory oversight, and lifecycle evaluation. Ethical containment does not resist innovation; rather, it seeks to ensure that AI strengthens resilience and trust instead of amplifying systematic vulnerabilities. The credibility and acceptance of AI in Lebanon will depend more on the strength of its ethical and institutional frameworks than on the sophistication of the technology itself.

records.title: Agricultural and Agribusiness Law
records.authors: Theodore A. Feitshans
records.abstract: This textbook provides a comprehensive introduction to the key concepts of agricultural and agribusiness law in the United States, offering an accessible guide for students and professionals alike. The fully revised and updated edition addresses significant legal developments, including changes in trade, taxation, water law, intellectual property, and animal law. Reflecting a growing number of farms in financial distress, new materials on workouts and debt relief, including Chapter 12 of the U.S. Bankruptcy Code, have been added. A new chapter explores the emerging legal landscape surrounding industrial hemp and marijuana production. The text also reflects the absence of a comprehensive farm bill since the 2018 Farm Bill and examines the legal and policy impacts of the Trump and Biden administrations. In an era where legal information is increasingly accessible online, the book delves into the challenges posed by cybercrime and misinformation, equipping readers to discern reliable sources from unreliable ones. Designed for students with little or no legal background, the text helps readers identify legal issues that may require professional consultation. Each concise chapter focuses on a specific legal topic relevant to agriculture and agribusiness, covering both federal law and illustrative examples of state law. In addition to foundational topics such as contracts, property law, and estate planning, the book addresses contemporary issues like organic certification, genetically engineered crops, and food safety. It highlights the broad scope of agricultural law, extending beyond farming to include agribusiness professionals who provide services, inputs, and act as intermediaries between farmers and consumers. Additional online resources are provided, including quiz questions for each chapter and PowerPoint slides. This textbook is essential for students of agriculture and land-based services with little or no legal background, as well as those studying agribusiness. The book also serves as a useful reference for agricultural professionals.

records.title: AI TRANSFROMATION IN E- COMMERVE: UNLOCKING BUSINESS OPPORTUNITIES FOR SUSTAINABLE GROWTH
records.authors: Ms S. BABITHA THARANI
records.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming e-commerce from a transactional digital channel into an intelligent, predictive, personalized, and increasingly automated business ecosystem. Machine learning, natural language processing, computer vision, recommender systems, generative AI, predictive analytics, and AI agents are changing how firms attract customers, manage operations, optimize supply chains, develop products, and make decisions. This paper examines how AI transformation can unlock business opportunities while contributing to sustainable growth. The study adopts a conceptual literature-based approach and synthesizes recent research on AI-driven business models, e-commerce, consumer behaviour, digital transformation, sustainability, and responsible AI. Eight major opportunity areas are identified: intelligent customer experience, AI-enabled marketing, predictive commerce, smart supply chains, intelligent logistics, AI-supported innovation, opportunities for small businesses, and agentic commerce. The paper argues that AI transformation can support sustainable growth through productivity and economic resilience, resource efficiency and environmental performance, and responsible customer and stakeholder value creation. However, privacy concerns, algorithmic bias, cybersecurity threats, workforce disruption, AI-generated misinformation, digital inequality, vendor dependence, and the environmental cost of computing may weaken these benefits. A conceptual framework is proposed linking AI capability, organizational readiness, customer value, operational intelligence, innovation capability, responsible governance, and sustainable growth. The study concludes that successful AI transformation requires a shift from technology adoption to responsible strategic integration.

All rights reserved. Description EQUILIBRIUM OS™ is a proposed technical architecture for an AI-enabled intelligence and decision-support layer for energy, water, compute, infrastructure integrity, resource stress, cybersecurity, and governance-constrained critical infrastructure. The architecture is founded on a central systems principle: The infrastructure that powers intelligence must itself be intelligent, resource-aware, resilient, constraint-aware, verifiable, and auditable. EQUILIBRIUM OS™ treats critical infrastructure not as a collection of independently optimized assets, but as a coupled cyber-physical system in which energy, water, compute capacity, infrastructure condition, resource stress, security state, service continuity, and governance constraints may interact dynamically. The Version 1.0 Public Technical & IP Freeze defines an integrated architecture intended to support: State estimation Uncertainty representation Forecasting Scenario analysis Constraint-aware optimization Critical-service prioritization Cyber-physical resilience Governance-safe decision controls Digital-twin analysis Verification Auditability Decision lineage Controlled future implementation research The architecture explicitly separates prediction, optimization, recommendation, authorization, and execution. A computational recommendation does not automatically constitute an executable command. Safety, policy, authorization, verification, human oversight, and audit controls remain distinct architectural concerns. 1. Core Systems Architecture The canonical operational sequence is: Sense → Estimate → Predict → Constrain → Optimize → Verify → Act / Recommend → Audit → Recover The system represents infrastructure conditions through a multidimensional state model covering, as applicable: Energy Water Compute Infrastructure Integrity Resource Stress Security State Governance and Safety Constraints A general dynamic representation is: xₜ₊₁ = F(xₜ, uₜ, dₜ, θₜ) + wₜ with an observation relationship of the form: zₜ = H(xₜ) + vₜ where system state, control inputs, disturbances, model parameters, process uncertainty, and observations are represented explicitly. Decision-making is formulated as a constraint-aware optimization problem, rather than as unconstrained numerical maximization: minᵤ J(u; x, ŷ, σ) subject to: gₕ(u,x) ≤ 0 h(u,x) = 0 u ∈ U The architecture distinguishes among hard constraints, service-continuity constraints, resource-risk constraints, efficiency objectives, and policy preferences. Where hard constraints cannot simultaneously be satisfied, the architecture is designed to return an infeasible or degraded-mode condition rather than manufacture an apparently feasible solution. 2. Eight Integrated Technical Engines 2.1 EQUILIBRIUM OS™ — Master Technology & IP Architecture Defines the system-of-systems architecture for resource-aware, resilient, and auditable critical infrastructure. The master architecture establishes: Canonical system architecture System-state representation Decision contracts Constraint hierarchy Interface architecture Reference data structures Requirements traceability Verification strategy Audit and decision-lineage concepts Separation between recommendation and execution authority The master architecture provides the integration layer through which the remaining technical engines interact. 2.2 Equilibrium State Engine™ Provides a framework for state estimation, uncertainty representation, and equilibrium-distance assessment. The engine addresses: Multidimensional infrastructure state Equilibrium reference states Observed versus estimated state Uncertainty and data-quality representation Robustness rules Estimator contracts Numerical reference testing Degraded and failure conditions Verification of state outputs A computationally estimated state is not treated as ground truth merely because it is numerically detailed. 2.3 Cross-Infrastructure Optimization Engine™ Addresses coupled multi-resource optimization across energy, water, compute, and infrastructure capacity. The architecture supports: Multi-objective optimization Hard and soft constraint classes Service continuity Resource-risk constraints Scenario-based optimization Rolling-horizon decision procedures Feasible-set construction Fallback strategies Solver failure handling Verification before publication of a candidate decision A lower-priority objective may be sacrificed where necessary to preserve higher-priority constraints. Numerical benchmarks contained in the release are reference methodologies and validation structures, not claims of field performance. 2.4 Critical-Service Priority Engine™ Provides explicit modelling of critical services under scarcity, dependency, and competing infrastructure demands. Service requirements may include: Criticality class Minimum service level Dependency relationships Maximum interruption duration Recovery target Uncertainty Authorization class Permissible degradation modes Dependency propagation occurs before discretionary prioritization. Scarcity allocation is designed to protect declared continuity requirements before allocating residual capacity according to explicit policy and fairness rules. The architecture recognizes that a mathematical priority score is not inherently morally or socially neutral and therefore preserves policy, authority, and audit information alongside numerical ordering. 2.5 Cyber-Physical Resilience Engine™ Connects cyber integrity, physical operating state, and bounded response authority. The architecture addresses: Security-state representation Trust gating Threat modelling Cyber-physical coupling Resilience state transitions Verification Degraded operation Response boundaries Failure modes Security assurance considerations A cyber anomaly may affect confidence, constraint posture, and permissible response classes rather than being treated as an isolated cybersecurity event. Security conditions can therefore influence operational decision validity while maintaining explicit authorization and verification boundaries. 2.6 Resource Stress Forecasting Engine™ Provides uncertainty-aware forecasting of: Energy stress Water stress Compute demand and capacity stress Infrastructure stress Resource availability Disturbance scenarios Forecast objects may include: Forecast horizon Target variable Point estimate Intervals, quantiles, or scenarios Model version Training-data window Feature provenance Calibration diagnostics The architecture supports scenario generation for conditions including: Demand spikes Water restrictions Grid constraints Equipment derating Resource shortages Security incidents Evaluation structures include appropriate forecasting error measures, interval coverage, calibration, false-alarm behaviour, and decision-oriented evaluation. 2.7 Governance-Safe Decision Layer™ Provides the architectural boundary between optimization and execution. records.title: Cybernetics, the Anthropocene, and education: student learning in conjunction with AI
records.authors: David R. Cole; Pegah Marandi
records.abstract: This article develops a speculative and empirically inflected account of how university students are learning in conjunction with artificial intelligence (AI). It brings together three interlocking fields: cybernetics, the Anthropocene and education. Cybernetics is central because the communicative and control processes through which students engage AI for research, writing and study raise fundamental questions about agency, authorship and the capacity to think otherwise within machine-mediated capitalism. The Anthropocene provides a second axis of analysis, naming the planetary consequences of human technological development, economic acceleration and ecological damage. Education forms the third axis, because universities are key sites in which these cybernetic and Anthropocene dynamics are materialised through everyday practices of study, assessment and writing. The article combines philosophical analysis with empirical data from education students learning with AI. These data are organised as “data portals”: analytic thresholds that interrupt, extend and test the conceptual argument. Drawing on Deleuze’s transcendental empiricism, the article argues that students do not encounter AI as an external tool alone, but as part of a wider student-AI-university assemblage. The article concludes that agency persists in this assemblage, but is increasingly modulated by feedback, acceleration, assessment pressure, economic precarity and machinic cognition.

records.title: Mobility-aware service migration and two-timescale task offloading for distributed edge computing in open RAN
records.authors: Amin Mohajer; Abbas Mirzaei; Babak Nouri-Moghaddam; Ali Ghaffari; Xavier Fernando
records.abstract: This paper proposes a mobility-aware two-timescale orchestration framework for distributed edge computing in Open Radio Access Networks, where user mobility, handover events, service migration, task offloading, and radio–compute allocation are jointly considered. The framework exploits the functional separation between the Non-Real-Time RAN Intelligent Controller (Non-RT RIC) and Near-Real-Time RIC to coordinate decisions over different temporal scales. At the slower timescale, the Non-RT RIC analyzes historical traffic, regional load, and predicted mobility flows to generate service-placement guidance, resource envelopes, and migration-aware control parameters. At the faster timescale, a Near-RT RIC xApp performs handover-coupled task offloading, service migration, bandwidth allocation, and edge-computing assignment using instantaneous channel, queue, mobility, and resource states. A graph-contextual representation is further employed to capture neighboring-region congestion, available capacity, and mobility transitions, enabling scalable inter-region coordination. The resulting stochastic optimization formulation incorporates communication, computation, and migration delays together with resource, queue-stability, and service-continuity constraints. A hybrid actor–critic learning mechanism with centralized training and decentralized execution is adopted to obtain feasible mobility-aware orchestration policies for dynamic multi-service Open RAN edge environments.

records.title: The more you automate, the less you see: Hidden pitfalls of autonomous AI scientists
records.authors: Ziming Luo; Atoosa Kasirzadeh; Nihar B. Shah
records.abstract: The rapid rise of autonomous AI scientists marks a paradigm shift in scientific discovery by automating the research lifecycle. Yet their rushed development has outpaced critical oversight, leaving key workflow decisions dangerously unscrutinized. We present a much-needed systematic analysis of open-source AI scientist systems, investigating four primary pitfalls: inappropriate benchmark selection, data leakage, metric misuse, and post hoc selection bias. Through controlled experiments that isolate each pitfall, we find systematic vulnerabilities across two representative open-source systems. Crucially, we find that these flaws are largely invisible at the level of the final manuscript, suggesting that current manuscript-centric peer review paradigms are fundamentally insufficient for ensuring the integrity of automated research. We further propose mitigation strategies and demonstrate that access to full workflow artifacts (log traces and code) enables more effective auditing. Our findings suggest that journals, conferences, and researchers should move beyond manuscript-only evaluation toward process auditing the end-to-end workflow artifacts of AI scientist systems.

records.title: Designing for Who Actually Shows Up: A SIGNAL Framework for Online Adult Learners in Cybersecurity and Information Technology
records.authors: Chad Whistle; Mayyada Al-Hammoshi
records.abstract: Online adult learners pursuing cybersecurity and information technology credentials represent one of the fastest-growing student populations in American higher education, yet the frameworks institutions use to support their success were not designed for them. This population, disproportionately drawn from the 41.9 million Americans who hold some college credit but no credential, arrives workforce-embedded, time-constrained, and skeptical of institutional systems that previously failed to serve them. Existing persistence models grounded in traditional student integration theory inadequately account for the behavioral patterns, motivational structures, and credential expectations that define this learner. This paper proposes the SIGNAL Framework (Skills-based credential architecture, Integrated AI-informed analytics, Goal-proximate pedagogy, Nontraditional adult learner persistence, Alignment with labor market demand, and Lifelong learning pathway design), a population-specific student success model for online adult learners in cybersecurity and IT. Drawing on learning analytics research, the stackable credentials literature, and the emerging skills-based hiring landscape, SIGNAL addresses the structural mismatch between how institutions measure and support persistence and how this population actually learns. Institutional implications and a targeted research agenda are discussed.

records.title: Digital ecosystems and supply chain resilience in manufacturing: the mediating role of supply chain complexity in technology-driven operations
records.authors: Aamir Rashid; Rizwana Rasheed
records.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine the association between digital ecosystems and supply chain resilience in manufacturing firms, with particular attention to the statistical mediating role of supply chain complexity. It addresses the limited understanding of how digital technologies, including AI, IoT, and cybersecurity, operate collectively rather than in isolation. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on the resource-based view (RBV) and dynamic capability view (DCV), the study employs a quantitative research design using survey data from 732 managerial and supervisory respondents working in manufacturing firms in Mississippi, West Virginia, and Arkansas. Structural equation modeling (SEM) using AMOS is applied to test the proposed relationships. Findings The results indicate that digital ecosystems are positively associated with supply chain resilience, with cybersecurity exhibiting the strongest association with the Digital Ecosystem construct. Supply chain complexity shows a positive but comparatively smaller association with resilience and the statistically significant indirect relationship is consistent with partial mediation. Research limitations/implications The study is limited to manufacturing firms in selected U.S. states, which may affect generalizability. Future research could explore cross-industry and cross-country contexts and examine additional mediating or moderating mechanisms. Practical implications The findings suggest that managers should consider investing in integrated digital infrastructure, prioritizing cybersecurity capabilities and using data-driven technologies while proactively managing the complexity of digital transformation. Originality/value This study advances a systems-level understanding of digital ecosystems in supply chains by showing that integrated digital capabilities, rather than isolated technologies, are positively associated with resilience in complex operational environments.

records.title: Technology readiness of internet of things systems for mine safety using LoRa technology and LoRaWAN networks alongside related wireless architectures in a systematic scoping review
records.authors: Robin Alberto Acuña Benites; Jimmy Aurelio Rosales Huamani
records.abstract: Abstract This systematic scoping review assesses the technological maturity of Internet of Things (IoT), LoRa and Long Range Wide Area Network (LoRaWAN), and related wireless architectures for mine-safety applications published from 2021 to 2025. Guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR), the documented review corpus comprised 50 studies for qualitative synthesis; 40 had sufficient evidence for coding with an operational Technology Readiness Level (TRL) adaptation informed by ISO 16290:2013, and 10 were retained as contextual qualitative evidence. The structured TRL evidence synthesis is concentrated at TRL 3–6, includes one TRL 7 operational demonstration, and contains no reviewed academic study with sufficient TRL 8–9 evidence. The preserved aggregate operating-context distribution reports underground mining as predominant (32/40), with applications in environmental monitoring, worker safety, localization, connectivity, and energy management. LoRa and LoRaWAN were treated as distinct implementation layers. Long-term validation, interoperability, cybersecurity, certification, maintenance, and economic viability were inconsistently reported. These are gaps in the reviewed academic literature, not evidence that advanced or certified systems are absent from industry.

records.title: Digital Service Quality, Sharia Compliance, Security, and Financial Literacy on BSI Customer Loyalty
records.authors: Fajri Chandra Herputra; Aga Nugroho Saputro; Reni Anggun Perdani; Miranda Hotmadia Tanjung
records.abstract: The rapid evolution of financial technology requires Islamic banks to synchronize operational excellence with religious integrity to maintain a competitive advantage. Despite significant sector growth, fostering sustainable loyalty among the younger generation of digital natives remains a primary challenge due to the existing gap between Sharia identity and functional digital utility. This quantitative research study surveyed 211 active digital banking users of Bank Syariah Indonesia residing in the Java region predominantly within the Jakarta Metropolitan Area (Jabodetabek) and its surroundings. Data collected via purposive sampling were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling to evaluate the framework of system functionality, cybersecurity, and religious adherence. Findings reveal that digital service quality and robust security frameworks significantly and directly enhance customer retention. Surprisingly, strict adherence to religious principles does not exert a direct influence on loyalty, revealing a pronounced attitude-behavior gap among consumers. However, this relationship is fully transformed through the mediation of Sharia-based financial literacy, which emerges as the most powerful determinant of long-term commitment and spiritual attachment. It is concluded that functionality and values must coexist; technical reliability acts as a prerequisite, while financial literacy serves as the critical bridge to achieving spiritual loyalty. Strategic recommendations emphasize prioritizing advanced threat detection and interactive digital education tools to secure trust and mitigate risks among the sensitive younger demographics

records.title: Autonomous Mining Trucks: A Review of Deployment, Technology Architecture, Operational Benefits and Emerging Challenges
records.authors: Joshua Whajah; Baah Bossman Effah; Jossiah Whajah; Gilbert Etiako Djanetey
records.abstract: Autonomous mining trucks are driverless haul vehicles that transport ore, waste rock and overburden without an onboard operator. They have become one of the most consequential technology transitions in modern surface and underground mining. This paper reviews the current state of autonomous haulage systems (AHS), with attention to deployment growth, functional architecture, sensing and perception stacks, path planning and fleet management strategies, and demonstrated operational outcomes. Global adoption has accelerated sharply: the operating fleet on surface mines rose from roughly 2,080 units in mid 2024 to more than 3,830 units by July 2025, an 84% increase in twelve months, led by iron ore, copper, coal and oil sands operations across Australia, Chile, Peru, Canada and China. Reported gains include productivity improvements of up to 30%, operating cost reductions of about 20%, safety related incident reductions of approximately 50%, and utilization improvements of up to 20% relative to conventional manned fleets. Rio Tinto autonomous trucks operate approximately 700 hours per year more than conventional units and are associated with load and haul cost reductions on the order of 15%. Beyond these gains, the paper examines outstanding challenges in perception under dust, fog and non line of sight (NLOS) conditions, cybersecurity of highly connected cyber physical systems, workforce transitions, and the integration of autonomy with the emerging generation of battery electric and trolley assisted haul trucks. The review synthesizes evidence from peer reviewed journals, industry publications, corporate disclosures on autonomous mining technologies, and identifies interoperability, ecosystem level intelligence, cyber secure V2X communications and human–robot collaboration as the priority research directions for the next decade of automation in mining.

records.title: Development of a master of science in digital health program at Muhimbili University of Health and Allied Sciences, Tanzania: a mixed-methods curriculum development study
records.authors: Felix Sukums; Linda Simon Paulo; Yoktan Thadeo; Mpanga Paul; Samwel Mndima; Juliana Mbuke; Rebecca Chaula; Junior Kaskazi; Amani Anaeli; Obadia Nyongole
records.abstract: Background The rapid expansion of digital technologies is transforming health systems and creating increasing demand for a workforce with competencies in health informatics, data science, artificial intelligence (AI), cybersecurity, digital health governance, and implementation. However, digital health training remains fragmented in many low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), including Tanzania. This study describes the systematic, evidence-based process used to develop an MSc Digital Health program at Muhimbili University of Health and Allied Sciences (MUHAS), Tanzania. Methods A mixed-methods curriculum development approach was undertaken, comprising document review and benchmarking, a quantitative stakeholder survey, qualitative interviews with alumni of the MSc Health Information Management program, and a stakeholder consultative workshop. Nine higher-education and competency-framework sources were reviewed to identify gaps and emerging competency domains. A structured survey was administered to 48 stakeholders purposively selected from government, non-governmental, private-sector, and start-up organizations. Qualitative data from alumni interviews and open-ended survey responses were analyzed thematically using manual coding by two independent coders. A two-day consultative workshop involving 22 stakeholders from academia, professional associations, non-governmental organizations, government, and clinical practice reviewed and validated the proposed curriculum. Results Benchmarking demonstrated substantial variability in digital health curriculum content, with no single program comprehensively covering all priority competency domains. Stakeholders identified AI and machine learning (48.0%) and big data and analytics (41.7%) as prominent emerging technology competencies, while data science and predictive analytics, health information systems and interoperability, cybersecurity and data privacy, and epidemiology and biostatistics were also emphasized. Overall, 81.3% of survey respondents considered digital health competencies highly important to their organizations, while 89.6% indicated willingness to employ MUHAS MSc Digital Health graduates. Qualitative findings emphasized five priority areas: advanced computing and emerging technologies; applied health data science and analytics; health systems architecture and interoperability; experiential learning and program delivery; and governance, cybersecurity, leadership, and professional ethics. Workshop participants endorsed the proposed curriculum and recommended stronger practical learning, field attachment, innovation-oriented projects, and alignment of course content with emerging workforce needs. The resulting program was structured as a two-year, full-time MSc Digital Health program with three specialization tracks: Digital Health Leadership, Digital Health Systems Development, and Health Data Science and AI. Conclusion The MUHAS MSc Digital Health curriculum was developed through an iterative, evidence-informed, and stakeholder-driven process that integrates multidisciplinary digital health competencies with practical, implementation-oriented learning. The approach provides a potentially adaptable model for curriculum development in LMIC settings. Future evaluation should assess program implementation, graduate competencies, employment outcomes, employer satisfaction, and contribution to national digital health transformation.

records.title: The dropshipping market: transforming the risk environment
records.authors: Gul'nara Efimovna Chernobaeva
records.abstract: An analysis was conducted of the current risks faced by participants in the dropshipping market in the context of the transformation of e commerce and the growth of digital platforms. The relevance of the study is substantiated; the steady growth of the global dropshipping market, its professionalization, and the simultaneous increase in the complexity of the risk environment faced by both entrepreneurs and end consumers are noted. The key categories of risks characteristic of the current stage of the dropshipping market’s development have been identified and systematized, and the directions for developing effective risk management strategies have been determined. An analysis was conducted of scientific publications, industry analytical reports, data from international and Russian research companies for 2020–2025, as well as practical recommendations from platforms and services operating in the field of dropshipping. Seven main categories of risks were identified: logistical, quality related, legal, financial, marketing, image related, and technological. It has been shown that these groups of risks are closely interconnected and cannot be considered in isolation. Special attention is paid to shifting the focus from a formal classification of risks to a subjective one, within which the key sources of risk events are suppliers, cybercriminals, and buyers. It has been established that the risks associated with the unreliability of suppliers have the greatest impact on the stability of a dropshipping business, as they simultaneously provoke logistical, quality, financial, and reputational losses. The main areas of risk management have been systematized, including supplier verification, technological and legal protection, customer service, and financial security. The results obtained can be used in developing comprehensive risk management strategies for dropshipping companies and in adapting business models to modern market conditions.

records.title: Atoms and Geography: The Paradox of North Korea’s Security
records.authors: Baruna Kumar Behera; Shri Ritesh Kumar Pradhan
records.abstract: The relationship between geography and nuclear weapons remains insufficiently explored within contemporary security studies. While technological advancements have transformed the nature of warfare, geography continues to shape states' perceptions of vulnerability, strategic options and security behaviour. This article examines the nexus between geographical constraints and nuclear deterrence through the case of North Korea. Drawing upon geopolitical thought, realist and neo-realist theories of international relations and contemporary scholarship on nuclear deterrence, the study develops the concept of the "Geo-Deterrence Paradox." The concept posits that geography indirectly influences nuclearization by generating perceptions of strategic vulnerability, which encourage states to pursue nuclear weapons as instruments of survival. However, while nuclear capabilities may enhance security for individual states, their proliferation contributes to broader systemic instability. Using qualitative analysis and a case study approach, the article argues that North Korea's nuclear programme is best understood not as an irrational expression of ideological aggression but as a strategic response to a challenging geopolitical environment characterized by limited strategic depth, powerful neighbouring states and persistent external threats. The findings suggest that geographically constrained states are more likely to view nuclear deterrence as a rational security strategy. The study contributes to contemporary debates on nuclear proliferation by demonstrating that geography remains a critical variable in understanding state behaviour in the nuclear age and continues to shape the balance between deterrence and insecurity in global politics. Keywords: Nuclear Deterrence, Geopolitics, North Korea, Security Dilemma, Geo-Deterrence Paradox, Strategic Vulnerability

records.title: Artificial Intelligence Related Sentiments and Perceptions on Federated Social Networks: A Computational Text Analysis
records.authors: Sadettin Demirel
records.abstract: This study aims to examine public perceptions of artificial intelligence (AI) on federated social networks, specifically Bluesky and Mastodon. While existing research focuses on centralized platforms, a significant gap exists regarding AI perception within decentralized networks. This study addresses this gap through computational analysis of AI related posts in Bluesky and Mastodon. A text-as-data approach was employed to analyze 61,285 posts collected from Bluesky and Mastodon between January 1, 2023, and January 1, 2025. The methodology integrated topic modeling, sentiment analysis, and text analysis to identify prevalent themes, sentiment polarity, and discussion patterns within AI-related discourse. Findings demonstrate predominantly positive sentiment towards AI across both platforms, with trust, anticipation, and joy as primary emotional responses, accompanied by underlying fear and anxiety. Platform-specific variations emerged: Mastodon discourse centers on creativity, digital art, and societal-ethical implications including regulation, bias, and disinformation concerns. Conversely, Bluesky posts emphasize economic and geopolitical dimensions, featuring startups, funding, stock markets, and international policy. The analysis reveals significant fragmentation in public AI perception, characterized by discourse division into distinct economic and ethical spheres across platforms. While this fragmentation accommodates diverse social group perspectives, it presents challenges for establishing comprehensive societal consensus on AI governance. The analytical framework provides insights for understanding decentralized social network dynamics and implications for policy makers examining AI perception in federated digital environments.

records.title: Artificial Intelligence for Net-Zero and Climate-Resilient Sustainable Cities: Technologies, Challenges, and Future Perspectives
records.authors: Rakesh A. Afre; Bhavana B. Thakre; Radha Panchal; Sandhyatai Kadam
records.abstract: Urbanization, climate change, increasing energy demand, and rapid infrastructure development have created significant challenges for achieving sustainable and resilient cities. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative technology that enables data-driven decision-making, intelligent automation, and efficient resource management, making it an important enabler of net-zero and climate-resilient urban systems. This narrative review examines AI applications relevant to urban climate mitigation and adaptation, drawing on literature identified through Google Scholar and ScienceDirect. The review examines the role of machine learning, deep learning, Internet of Things (IoT), big data analytics, cloud computing, digital twins, and generative AI in improving urban energy systems, sustainable transportation, environmental monitoring, infrastructure management, and smart governance. The study also discusses how these technologies contribute to carbon emission reduction, renewable energy integration, climate adaptation, disaster preparedness, and efficient urban planning. In addition, major challenges associated with AI implementation are critically analyzed, including data privacy, cybersecurity, algorithmic bias, lack of interoperability, high energy consumption of AI systems, digital inequality, and governance issues. Emerging research trends such as explainable AI, green AI, AI-enabled digital twins, federated learning, and human-centered smart governance are highlighted as important directions for future research. Based on the reviewed literature, the study proposes future research priorities that emphasize interdisciplinary collaboration, responsible AI governance, standardized urban data frameworks, and sustainable policy development. Overall, AI has the potential to accelerate the transition toward intelligent, low-carbon, and climate-resilient cities. The synthesis is qualitative and non-exhaustive, with limitations arising from unavailable original search and screening records and differences between study settings and outcome measures. However, the successful implementation of AI will depend on integrating technological innovation with ethical governance, public participation, and long-term sustainability planning to achieve the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals.

records.title: Public Affairs Communication in the Era of Climate Change and Artificial Intelligence: Strategies for Policy Advocacy and Governance in Nigeria
records.authors: Austin Mathias OTUOGHA, (PhD)
records.abstract: This study examined public affairs communication in the era of climate change and artificial intelligence: strategies for policy and advocacy and governance in Nigeria. The technological determinism theory was anchored in this study. This study adopted a qualitative research method, utilising in-depth interviews to explore the role of artificial intelligence in public affairs communication for climate policy advocacy and governance in Nigeria. The population of the study consisted of 120 key stakeholders involved in climate policy advocacy and governance, including government officials, policymakers, environmental NGOs, media professionals and AI experts. The sample size comprised 20 purposively selected respondents with expertise in climate policy, artificial intelligence applications in governance and public affairs communication. The sampling technique used was purposive sampling, allowing the selection of individuals who possess specialized knowledge and experience relevant to the study. The method of data collection involves semi-structured, in-depth interviews and method of data analysis followed thematic analysis, where transcribed interview data were systematically coded to identify emerging patterns, themes and relationships. The findings revealed that, AI-driven tools significantly enhance public affairs communication by improving message dissemination, audience targeting and engagement strategies in climate advocacy. AI-powered chatbots, predictive analytics and automated content generation have been instrumental in personalizing climate messages and countering misinformation. The study concluded that AI has emerged as a transformative tool in public affairs communication, enabling more effective climate advocacy through targeted messaging, audience engagement and misinformation management. However, its full potential can only be realised if challenges such as algorithmic bias, inadequate digital infrastructure and the need for human-centred communication strategies are addressed. The study recommended that Policymakers and communication professionals should invest in AIdriven tools while ensuring ethical guidelines and human-centred approaches to enhance climate advocacy in Nigeria

records.title: The Relationship Between Artificial Intelligence Systems, Voice-Based Technologies and the Sociolinguistic Formation of Hausa People Within the Developing Digital Domain
records.authors: SHUAIBU Abdulwaheed
records.abstract: The fast proliferation of voice technologies based on artificial intelligence prompted the concern of how indigenous languages will survive and have access and visibility in cyberspace. This paper analyses how the Hausa language fits in the changing digital linguistic space, but more specifically, AI-based voice recognition and sociolinguistic consequences. The research is based on the Language Ecology Theory of Haugen (1972), in which Hausa is conceptualised as an interactive ecosystem that is influenced by sociocultural, technological, and environmental factors. The qualitative research design is chosen based on a critical analysis of current AI voice systems, an analysis of voice-enabled apps, and ideas on the subject from appropriate academic sources and opinion leaders. It has been found out that Hausa is still far under-represented in large AI voice technology systems because of inadequate training datasets, orthographic variation, and dialect. The consequences of this exclusion include technological access, linguistic presence and retention of sociolinguistic identity among Hausa speakers. This paper states that language representation of AI systems is a technical and ethical problem, which is inextricably connected with digital rights and cultural sustainability. It is thus supportive of culturally responsive AI design by creating Hausa voice corpora, working with linguists and developers, and community contributions. In general, the paper makes significant contributions to the existing discussions about linguistic equity and inclusive AI development in multilingual communities.

records.title: Integrating Generative Artificial Intelligence into Institutional Arbitration: A Comparative Analysis of Procedural Readiness and Due Process Between India and Singapore
records.authors: Surya Saxena; Mr. Deepak Bansal; M Taneja; Mr. Vishal Bansal; Ms. Akriti Gupta
records.abstract: The integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into international commercial arbitration introduces transformative procedural efficiencies alongside complex legal and constitutional challenges. This comprehensive research paper explores the regulatory, procedural, and doctrinal implications of utilizing Large Language Models (LLMs) and automated legal reasoning tools within arbitral decision-making workflows. By establishing a robust comparative framework between India and Singapore, the study critically evaluates how institutional rules, statutory mandates, and judicial oversight manage the intersection of cutting-edge technology and fundamental guarantees of natural justice. The paper begins by contrasting Singapore’s mature, digitally integrated arbitral ecosystem—anchored by the SIAC 2025 Rules and advanced institutional governance protocols—with India’s rapidly evolving domestic framework comprising institutions such as the India International Arbitration Centre (IIAC) and the Mumbai Centre for International Arbitration (MCIA). It investigates the non-delegation doctrine, examining whether over-reliance on AI-generated legal reasoning and draft awards violates an arbitrator's core duty of independent evaluation under Section 34 of the Indian Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, and Singapore’s International Arbitration Act. Furthermore, the study analyzes severe cybersecurity and data governance vulnerabilities, contrasting India's Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act compliance requirements with Singapore's commercial data protocols during cross-border digital discovery. Finally, the research evaluates award enforceability hurdles under the New York Convention framework. It scrutinizes how national courts handle procedural challenges related to algorithmic opacity, data hallucinations, and public policy exceptions. Ultimately, the paper provides actionable regulatory reform recommendations and institutional guidelines for emerging arbitral seats to safeguard due process integrity and procedural fairness while safely embracing technological innovation.

records.title: Managerial Transformation in Natural Resource Enterprises and Industry 4.0: Theoretical Perspectives
records.authors: Ali Emin İslamoğlu; Kadir Çıray
records.abstract: Enterprises operating in natural resource sectors (mining, oil and gas, agriculture, and forestry) form the fundamental backbone of global supply chains, energy security, and industrial production. However, these organizations face critical challenges such as complex geological and climatic uncertainties, significant environmental risks, volatile commodity markets, and increasingly stringent Environmental, Social, and Governance compliance standards. The inadequacy of traditional, hierarchical, and command-and-control management models in handling this operational complexity makes the adoption of the Industry 4.0 approach (integrated with Information and Communication Technologies) a strategic imperative. Advanced technologies such as the Internet of Things, Cyber-Physical Systems, Artificial Intelligence, Big Data Analytics, Blockchain, and Digital Twins are radically transforming traditional production processes by enabling real-time field traceability, predictive maintenance, improved occupational health and safety, transparent supply chains, and efficient resource utilization. Accordingly, the study aims to demonstrate the strategic imperative of adopting the Industry 4.0 paradigm (integrated with Information and Communication Technologies) and to highlight the solutions offered by these technologies. Within the scope of this study, technological transformation and organizational adaptation processes are addressed through an interdisciplinary theoretical framework. The role of regulatory and societal pressures in technology adoption is analyzed using Institutional Theory, while the transformation of data assets into sustainable competitive advantage is examined through the lenses of the Resource-Based View and Dynamic Capabilities. Furthermore, the necessity of balancing human-machine integration and equipping the workforce with new competencies (reskilling) is evaluated within the context of Socio-Technical Systems Theory. Ultimately, the study emphasizes the pivotal role that advanced technologies such as the Internet of Things, Cyber-Physical Systems, Artificial Intelligence, Big Data Analytics, Blockchain, and Digital Twins play in ensuring real-time traceability, predictive maintenance, occupational health and safety, and transparent supply chains in the field. However, the success of this transformation depends not only on technical infrastructure but also on a holistic organizational shift encompassing leadership approaches, corporate culture, and management structures. The long-term resilience of the sector requires the simultaneous implementation of cybersecurity, data sovereignty, and environmental sustainability principles aligned with the vision of Industry 5.0 and Green Digital Twins, alongside operational efficiency.

records.title: Cybersecurity for sustainable product performance through management quality, innovation intensity, and board risk oversight
records.authors: Richard Arhinful; Leviticus Mensah; Bright Akwasi Gyamfi
records.abstract: Cybersecurity plays a critical role in protecting digital systems and enabling organizations to deliver reliable, innovative, and sustainable products. Effective cybersecurity regulations strengthen product functionality and support long-term organizational resilience. This study explores the impact of cybersecurity on sustainable product performance and analyzes the moderating effects of management quality, innovation intensity, and board risk oversight. Using purposive sampling with predefined selection criteria, the study analyzes 25 years of data (2000–2025) from 482 non-financial firms listed on the London Stock Exchange, obtained from the Bloomberg database. Diagnostic test results require the application of advanced estimation techniques, including the Common Correlated Effects Mean Group (CCEMG), Augmented Mean Group (AMG), and two-step difference Generalized Method of Moments (GMM) estimators. The findings indicate a positive and statistically significant relationship between cybersecurity and sustainable product performance. Management quality, innovation intensity, and board risk oversight significantly and positively moderate this relationship, strengthening the relationship between cybersecurity and sustainable product performance. The results suggest that firms should strengthen cybersecurity frameworks to protect digital assets, improve product outcomes, support innovation, ensure regulatory compliance, and enhance long-term competitiveness and sustainability.

records.title: Mapping Baseline Perceptions of Industry 5.0 Technology: A Survey Design for Pilot Organisations
records.authors: Siobhan B O’Neill; Kenneth N. Brown
records.abstract: Background As the focus shifts towards Industry 5.0, successful implementation requires an understanding of how workers and teams perceive key ELSA dimensions, such as cybersecurity, privacy, trust, and fairness. Despite the centrality of these factors, there is limited systematic baseline data on how these dimensions interact and support AI adoption. The Horizon Europe SEISMEC project aims to co-design and pilot Industry 5.0 technologies in the workplace. Establishing a baseline for this project is essential for examining the efficacy of the co-design process, and for supporting innovation within SEISMEC. Research Approach This study aims to determine a baseline for worker perceptions on factors which may impact AI adoption. We have developed a survey, utilising standardised instruments, which is being administered to the organisations participating in SEISMEC. Respondents are asked to answer either with reference to (a) the technologies they currently use in their work, or (b) the SEISMEC technology that will be implemented in the future. The survey includes measures covering cybersecurity and privacy perceptions and practices, trust and understanding, perceived fairness, organisational learning opportunities, and existing co-design practices. It also incorporates items on the SEISMEC CAPS factors which include productivity, collaboration, automation and autonomy, and physical and psychological safety. Findings Data collection is currently underway. This contribution focuses on the survey design, conceptual rationale, and preliminary findings. The presentation will focus on the baseline measures for the concepts and the CAPS empowerment factors, distinguishing between current and anticipated technologies implemented by the pilot organisations. Conclusion This work provides a methodological foundation for evaluating Industry 5.0 implementation across diverse pilot contexts. The baseline survey will inform subsequent co-design activities within the SEISMEC project as well as enabling longitudinal comparisons once the technologies are deployed. Future stages will analyse changes over time and explore how organisational conditions shape adoption.
