records.title: TECHNOLOGY-ENABLED CSR AND WOMEN’S EMPOWERMENT: DIGITAL TECHNOLOGIES AND EMERGING AI FOR ADVANCING SDG 5
records.authors: Mrs. Josephin. G; Dr. Well Haorei
records.abstract: Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) has moved beyond philanthropy and is now considered a strategic business action, and is connected to social outcomes like gender equality and women's empowerment. Digital technologies have already transformed the approach to designing, delivering, measuring and communicating CSR programmes. This paper provides a literature review on technology-based CSR and how it can empower women. It explores three tracks: Digital Literacy, Financial Inclusion via Digital Platforms, Women entrepreneurs and employment. It also consolidates evidence from its effect on such programmes in countries such as India, Indonesia, Nigeria, Kenya and Pakistan. A qualitative and thematic review of peer-reviewed research was conducted to uncover themes, outcomes and constraints. The results indicate that technology-facilitated CSR can have an impact on the income, confidence, financial independence, market access and involvement in household and community decision-making of women. These gains rely on a number of factors, such as local cultural norms, the cost of technology, digital infrastructure, targeting, and the design of the programmes that address women's particular constraints. Main challenges that remain are the digital gender divide, low digital literacy, lack of CSR funding for women, and threats to data ethics and cybersecurity. The paper ends with recommendations for the integration of digital tools in CSR monitoring and reporting, the adoption of corporate digital responsibility and the build-in of programmes with Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) 5.

The transition from traditional vertical integration to a digital platform model has fundamentally altered the nature of risks in the energy sector. The study evaluates the role of Big Data, intelligent analytics, and agile management methodologies in minimizing risks. To form a modern management system, a synthesis of strategic planning and forecasting of digital risks is proposed. Consequently, a flexible and decentralized risk management model that ensures the sustainable development of industrial enterprises is substantiated. The digital transformation environment creates new technological threats in the oil and gas industry, such as cybersecurity issues and data dependency. For this reason, traditional reactive management methods lose their effectiveness, making proactive approaches a necessity. In the course of the research, the application of scenario analysis and predictive analytics tools comes to the forefront. The proposed innovative mechanism increases the speed of decision-making by companies, ensures the flexibility of internal structures, and strengthens corporate resilience. This approach enhances the energy sector's stability against global macroeconomic shocks and market volatility, fundamentally securing the competitiveness of the national industry in the digital era. records.title: The Dynamics of Crime and the Contemporary World: Moral and Existentialist Dilemmas in Adaobi Nwaubani’s I Do Not Come to you by Chance
records.authors: Micah Okon Asukwo; Dele Maxwell Ugwanyi
records.abstract: Literature reflects the milieu and the moment, and echoes society’s zeitgeist and the enabling contexts. It recreates society vividly with a view to projecting its positives sides and values and attacking its imperfections. Literature offers qualitative evaluation of contemporary trends in the society in a bid to retain the cherished and discard the obnoxious. These assertions constitute the thrust of this study which examines the depiction of crime and related trends in the contemporary Nigerian society as inscribed in Adaobi Nwaubani’s I Do Not Come to You by Chance. Specifically, the work interrogates the moral, economic, social, and existential circumstances that make criminal behaviours appear attractive or even necessary to an individual. The study, which adopts Existentialism as its theoretical framework, argues that contemporary crime has moved beyond judging the criminal to interrogating the conditions that produce, normalise, justify, or complicate criminal behaviour. The research finds unmitigated criminalities typified by advanced fee fraud, cybercrime, unbridled corruption, and decay/erosion of society’s fundamental values as some of the amoral, cynical, and gloomy issues raised in Nwaubani’s realistic artistry. The study submits that beyond being a mere willful act, behaviour or habit, crime, as depicted in Ubani’s craft, is a consequence of social and economic pressure which is given impetus by the amazingly weak, vacillating, complacent, and inept political leadership as well as insidiously weakening societal values. Nwaubani’s work aptly recreates existentialist and modernist dystopia in contemporary times characterised by pessimism, hedonism, anxiety, agony, nihilism, criminalities, despair, and death.

records.title: Review of Program of Instruction Among Security Training Schools: Basis for Adaptive Competency-Based Instructional Framework
records.authors: Hernando Sta. Ana Jr.
records.abstract: This study aimed to review the existing Program of Instruction (POI) implemented among selected accredited security training schools in Davao City as the basis for developing an enhanced and more responsive instructional framework. The study is anchored on Tyler's Curriculum Theory, Becker's Human Capital Theory, and von Bertalanffy's Systems Theory, which collectively emphasize curriculum relevance, investment in training, and the integration of instructional components to improve learning outcomes. Employing a qualitative descriptive research design, the study involved fifteen (15) licensed security training instructors with at least five years of industry experience, selected through purposive sampling. Data were gathered through a researcher-developed in-depth interview guide and analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis to identify recurring patterns and themes regarding the current implementation of the POI, its strengths, limitations, and opportunities for enhancement. The study examines the POI in terms of content, instructional delivery, relevance to contemporary security challenges, and compliance with existing standards, while exploring the integration of crime and threat detection competencies. The findings are expected to serve as the foundation for proposing an enhanced Program of Instruction that incorporates modern security concepts, including crime and threat detection, cybersecurity awareness, situational assessment, crisis response, and emerging industry practices.

records.title: Toward the governance of a legal framework for artificial intelligence: A comparative analytical legal study
records.authors: Faisal Abdulhafez Alshawabkeh; Abdallah Al-Shawabkeh; Rashed Alkaabi; Abdulla Alteneiji; Hamad Alshehhi
records.abstract: This study examines how the United Arab Emirates (UAE) legal and regulatory framework for artificial intelligence (AI) in the public sector can enhance governance effectiveness, including governance opportunities, through concrete recommendations regarding legislating AI accountability within UAE laws. Adopting a comparative legal-analytical approach, the article reviews UAE laws (personal data protection and cybercrimes) such as Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 on Personal Data Protection and No. 34 of 2021 on Combating Rumors and Cybercrimes, as well as national strategies and administrative practices. We compare the UAE framework against Singapore’s AI governance model across four dimensions of risk, rights, institutional structures, and ethics. The study indicates that the UAE is building an adaptive and multilevel AI governance framework guided by foundational moral principles and institutions, including the UAE Data Office and the Artificial Intelligence Office. Major gaps still exist in relation to holding people accountable for decisions made by AI autonomously. The UAE is on a fast track through innovation hubs and public-private partnerships, where Singapore equips itself with complete regulation, uniform AI testing, and clear accountability mechanisms. The paper offers policy implications for Arab governments and contributes to legal scholarship on AI governance in civil-law jurisdictions.

records.title: Engineering Intelligent Decision-Support Systems for Sustainable Crop Productivity in Emerging Economies
records.authors: Olumayowa Iyanda; Oluwadare Oyebode; Iretiayo Adelaiye; Ayomide Afolabi; Damilola Loko; Damilola Itadare
records.abstract: Developing economies face major challenges in achieving sustainable agricultural productivity, including poor infrastructure, climate change and poor resource use. Intelligent decision-support systems (IDSS) provide a data-driven approach to enhancing agricultural management practices, resulting in enhanced crop production, resource efficiency, and resilience to environmental issues. This paper discusses the engineering principles of IDSS in agriculture with a focus on the application of Internet of Things (IoT) sensor networks, cloud computing, machine learning methods, and geospatial analysis. The research looks in detail at models for forecasting crop production, controlling diseases and pests, scheduling irrigation and optimising nutrients. We study architectural issues in depth, including modularity, scalability, interoperability and energy-efficient design. The paper discusses challenges faced by the developing economies like limited connectivity, diversity of data sources and cyber security threats and suggests strategies to overcome them. In this paper we propose a reference framework for the combination of edge intelligence, predictive analytics and user-centric decision dashboards that facilitate smallholder farmers and agribusiness actors to make informed, timely and sustainable decisions. Results suggest that well-designed IDSS can increase efficiency of water and fertiliser use by up to 40%, decrease crop losses due to biotic and abiotic stresses, and increase total productivity. This review further contributes to the literature by providing a systematic engineering perspective on the design, implementation, and improvement of IDSS for agricultural systems in resource-limited settings.

records.title: Strategic Formulation of Digital Literacy Learning in Indonesian Elementary Education: A SWOT-AHP Approach
records.authors: Mohammad Bhanu Setyawan; Angga Prasetyo; Arif Rahman Yusuf; Abdul Azis; Sutrisno; Aang Kisnu Darmawan; Puput Dani Prasetyo Adi Adi; Akio Kitagawae
records.abstract: The implementation of digital literacy in Indonesian elementary schools is essential for 21st-century education, yet it faces persistent challenges in teacher competence, infrastructure availability, and curriculum integration. This study aims to develop prioritized digital literacy strategies for elementary schools in Indonesia based on a comprehensive analysis of internal and external factors. A sequential mixed methods approach was used. The qualitative phase involved focus group discussions and interviews with 71 educators and experts, selected through purposive sampling, to identify Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats (SWOT). The quantitative phase applied the Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP) with eight key experts to weigh the SWOT factors and the resulting alternative strategies. The SWOT analysis identified high student motivation and potential for developing 21st-century skills as key strengths; limited teacher pedagogical and technological competence and limited access to infrastructure as major weaknesses; government support and digital learning resources as main opportunities; and cybersecurity and disinformation as serious threats. The AHP results showed that Opportunities had the highest priority (weight 0.385), followed by Weaknesses (0.310). The priority strategies were: (1) improving teacher competence through continuous training (WO1, 0.350); (2) developing students' critical thinking skills (ST2, 0.330); (3) leveraging students' enthusiasm for learning innovation (SO1, 0.320); and (4) simultaneously improving teacher competence and students' digital ethics awareness (WT2, 0.300). These findings offer actionable priorities to guide national efforts in advancing digital literacy at the elementary level.

records.authors: Gameel Mohamed Ahmed Mohamed; Yasmin Mohamed Hussein Elnahreer; Mohamed Sabry Mohamed Mohamed Osman; Mohamed Hany Mohamed Ahmed; Farid Moharram
records.abstract: This paper provides a strategic analysis of financial technology (FinTech) in global markets and in Egypt. It defines FinTech as a structural transformation of the financial industry and traces its development through three eras, from the infrastructure era of the telegraph to the current era of digital disruption. It concludes that FinTech success depends on strategic alignment between technology, business models and regulation, and recommends investing in data and AI capabilities, adopting platform-based business models, promoting financial inclusion, strengthening cybersecurity and digital trust, using RegTech for compliance, building partnerships between banks and FinTech firms, keeping cost structures scalable, and diversifying revenue streams.

records.title: Mapping Global Research Trends in Digital Transformation and Cyberpreneurship Through Bibliometric Analysis
records.authors: Syahyono Syahyono; Lilik Sulistyowati; Aurelie Zelene
records.abstract: Digital transformation has become a major driver of change across various business sectors, including the rapid growth of cyberpreneurship in the digital economy era. The utilization of technologies such as artificial intelligence, big data, and digital platforms enables entrepreneurs to create innovations and enhance their global competitiveness. However, research on digital transformation and cyberpreneurship remains fragmented and has not been systematically mapped, making it difficult to understand research trends, key focus areas, and existing gaps. Therefore, this study aims to map the development of research trends, intellectual structures, and major themes in the fields of digital transformation and cyberpreneurship. This study employs a bibliometric analysis method with a quantitative approach to scientific publications indexed in databases such as Scopus and Web of Science within a specified period. The data are analyzed using software tools such as VOSviewer to identify collaboration patterns, dominant keywords, and relationships among research topics. The findings indicate a significant increase in the number of publications related to these topics in recent years, reflecting the growing academic interest in digital transformation and cyberpreneurship. The main findings identify several major research clusters, including technological innovation, digital business strategies, consumer behavior, and startup ecosystems. Furthermore, the research focus has shifted from technical aspects toward strategic and policy-related dimensions. The study concludes that digital transformation plays a crucial role in fostering the growth of cyberpreneurship. However, significant research gaps remain, particularly in the context of developing countries and practical implementation aspects. Therefore, future studies are recommended to explore more contextual and sustainable approaches to support the inclusive development of digital entrepreneurship ecosystems.

records.title: AI and Media: Challenges, Prospects and Opportunities
records.authors: Sushmita Kumari -; Atish Prashar -; Anand Kumar -
records.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming the media ecosystem by changing how information is gathered, verified, produced, personalized, distributed and monetized. News organisations can use AI for transcription, translation, data analysis, recommendation, automated production, audience analytics, fact-checking support, visualisation and the creation of new formats. At the same time, AI introduces significant risks concerning misinformation, deepfakes, algorithmic bias, privacy, intellectual property, opacity, labour displacement, editorial accountability and the erosion of public trust. These tensions are particularly important in India, where the media environment is linguistically diverse, mobile-first, platform-dependent and characterised by a rapid expansion of digital and creator-led news. This conceptual paper examines the challenges, prospects and opportunities created by AI for Indian media and develops an integrated framework for responsible AI-enabled journalism. Drawing on stakeholder theory, the resource-based view, institutional theory, diffusion of innovations and the emerging literature on algorithmic and automated journalism, the paper conceptualises AI capability as an enabling resource whose value depends on editorial governance, human oversight, professional competence, data quality and regulatory conditions. The framework proposes that AI adoption influences media performance through a mediating mechanism of newsroom capability and workflow transformation, while ethical governance, organisational readiness and regulatory clarity moderate the relationship. The paper argues that AI should be treated neither as a substitute for journalism nor simply as a productivity tool, but as a socio-technical capability that must remain accountable to journalistic values. For Indian media, the most promising opportunities lie in multilingual journalism, accessibility, local and hyperlocal coverage, data-driven reporting, personalised public-interest information, newsroom efficiency and new digital business models. However, these opportunities can be realised only when media organisations establish transparent AI-use policies, verification protocols, disclosure standards, staff training, data safeguards and mechanisms for human editorial responsibility. The paper concludes with implications for media managers, journalists, educators, regulators and technology providers, and proposes directions for future empirical research.

records.title: Co-creating a Trauma-Informed Accessibility Research Practice
records.authors: Maryam Bandukda; Xandra Miguel Lorenzo; Tigmanshu Bhatnagar; Victoria Austin; Catherine Holloway; Monica Lakhanpaul
records.abstract: Trauma-informed care practices are gaining momentum across sectors that work with potentially vulnerable groups, including education, healthcare, social work, and the criminal justice system. In parallel, trauma-informed research and design have emerged as a growing area of interest, with a substantial increase in publications since 2020 that focus on technology-mediated psychological trauma, technologies that support people who have experienced trauma, and technology design with and for trauma survivors. This trend is evident in SIGACCESS (n=30) and SIGCHI (n=200) conference proceedings, as well as the wider ACM computing research landscape (n=810). Given this growing attention, there is an urgent need for a shared understanding of trauma-informed practices and for guidelines for applying them in computing research. This need is especially acute in accessibility research, due to the strong association between disability and psychological trauma [15]. As the inaugural workshop dedicated to trauma-informed accessibility research, our goal is to convene ASSETS community members interested in research practices that safeguard both researcher and participant well-being and to formulate guidelines for conducting trauma-informed research.

records.title: he Perceived Role of Artificial Intelligence Technology in Enhancing Internal Audit Quality in the Iraqi Banking Sector: An Empirical Study
records.authors: Aseel A Matrood; Hassan H Kanso
records.abstract: Background: Artificial Intelligence Technology (AIT) is increasingly transforming internal auditing through automated data analysis, continuous monitoring, anomaly detection, and enhanced professional decision-making. In the Iraqi banking sector, growing financial complexity, cybersecurity risks, and regulatory requirements highlight the importance of examining how AI-related organizational capabilities are associated with internal audit quality. Objectives: This study investigates banking professionals' perceptions of the relationship between AIT and internal audit quality in Iraqi banks. Specifically, it examines three dimensions of AIT: technological infrastructure availability, cognitive and digital skills, and digital governance and ethical controls. Methods: A quantitative, cross-sectional, descriptive-analytical research design was employed. Data were collected through a structured questionnaire administered to 257 banking professionals involved in auditing, accounting, compliance, and related financial control activities. The questionnaire comprised 30 items measuring AIT and internal audit quality. Data were analyzed using SPSS, incorporating descriptive statistics, reliability assessment, and multiple regression analysis. Results: The findings revealed significant positive associations between all three AIT dimensions and perceived internal audit quality. The regression model explained 70.7% of the variance in perceived internal audit quality (R² = 0.707). Technological infrastructure availability demonstrated the strongest positive regression coefficient (B = 0.342), followed by digital governance and ethical controls (B = 0.315) and cognitive and digital skills (B = 0.184). All three predictors were statistically significant (p < 0.001). Conclusion: The findings suggest that effective AI-supported internal auditing requires an integrated approach combining technological infrastructure, professional digital competencies, and appropriate governance mechanisms. Iraqi banks should strengthen their technological readiness, invest in continuous professional training, and implement robust ethical and cybersecurity controls. Since the findings are based on cross-sectional perceptions, they indicate statistical associations rather than causal improvements in actual audit performance.

records.title: Digital Finance for Sustainable Financial Inclusion
records.authors: Zouhair Chiban
records.abstract: Digital banking can reduce the costs and geographical obstacles to payments, savings and credit, but access to technology does not necessarily lead to meaningful financial inclusion. This paper explores the conditions under which FinTech can contribute to sustainable financial inclusion in Morocco, and the legal and policy safeguards that are needed to ensure that digital finance is safe, egalitarian and sustainable. It has been conceived as a narrative appraisal of selected academic studies, mainly released between 2020 and 2026, with a focus on Morocco and the MENA region, and as a documentary investigation of the Moroccan regulatory environment. The summary shows that mobile payments, digital lending and regulated alternative-finance channels may reach rural populations, women in the informal economy and small firms. But their reach is hampered by financial capacity, connectivity, cost, unequal digital skills, mistrust and risk of fraud or inappropriate lending. Morocco already has important legislative underpinnings in the areas of payment institutions, personal data, cybersecurity, mobile payments and crowdfunding. The real challenge, therefore, is not the absence of regulation but the absence of coordinated implementation, clarity for digital consumer protection, accountable data use and impact monitoring. The article proposes an integrated framework of access-capability-trust-sustainability to provide guidance for policy and future research.

records.title: Digital Decoupling as Managed Dependence in Geopolitical Technology Fragmentation
records.authors: Thinh Gia Hoang; Nam Hai Vu
records.abstract: This chapter examines how digital decoupling enables firms to adapt to geopolitical tensions by reconfiguring digital infrastructure, technology dependence, and data governance in fragmented technology markets. Drawing primarily on Dynamic Capabilities Theory, supported by Resource Dependence Theory and institutional perspectives, the chapter develops a Digital Decoupling Adaptation Model and illustrates it through the anonymized case o a multinational digital services firm operating across the United States, Europe, China, India, and Southeast Asia. The chapter finds that globally integrated digital architectures can create strategic exposure when cloud services, data flows, cybersecurity systems, software vendors, and AI-enabled analytics become subject to geopolitical risk, data sovereignty pressures, and regulatory fragmentation. The chapter contributes to geopolitical risk, dynamic capabilities, and digital transformation research, while offering managerial implications for digital dependency mapping,and resilience-oriented digital infrastructure design.

records.title: Bi‐Model Deep Learning Architectures: A Systematic Review of Fusion Strategies and Design Taxonomies
records.authors: Jasmin Z. K. Chu; Joel C. M. Than; Colin C. L. Tan; Ngoc Dinh Tan
records.abstract: ABSTRACT Bi‐model deep learning, the coordinated use of two complementary models or modalities, has emerged as a powerful paradigm for improving predictive accuracy and robustness in complex real‐world applications. However, existing research remains scattered across domain‐specific studies, with no unified account of the architectural patterns, fusion strategies, and evaluation practices that distinguish bi‐model designs from broader multimodal learning. This systematic review addresses this gap by consolidating 136 publications into a unified taxonomy of parallel, stacked, and interactive bi‐model architectures, together with feature‐level, model‐level, decision‐level, and hybrid fusion strategies. Representative applications across insurance analytics, cybersecurity, medical imaging, emotion recognition, and brain‐computer interfaces are examined to demonstrate how bi‐model systems consistently outperform unimodal baselines when modalities carry complementary information. The review further identifies recurring challenges, including data heterogeneity, representation mismatch, sensitivity to missing modalities, interpretability limitations, and high computation overhead, and proposes future research directions such as adaptive quality‐aware fusion, resilient handling of incomplete modalities, lightweight dual‐encoder designs, and inherently interpretable multimodal reasoning. Beyond synthesizing existing evidence, this review contributes a unified conceptual taxonomy, a consolidated cross‐domain view of practical and real‐time applications, and a structured foundation of open challenges and future directions to guide the design of more accurate, efficient, transparent, and deployable bi‐model systems.

records.title: IMPACT OF E-BANKING AND CASHLESS POLICY ON CUSTOMER SATISFACTION AMONG BUSINESS EDUCATION GRADUATES IN IBADAN, OYO STATE
records.authors: Kazeem Adewale MUIBI; Seyi David
records.abstract: This study investigated the impact of e-banking and cashless policy on customer satisfaction among Business Education graduates using commercial banks in Ibadan, Oyo State. Specifically, the study examined the joint and relative influence of e-banking and cashless policy on customer satisfaction. A descriptive research design was adopted. The population comprised Business Education graduates aged 18 years and above who were customers of the 26 commercial banks in Ibadan and had used e-banking services within the preceding six months. A sample of 1,700 respondents was selected using stratified random and multistage sampling techniques. Data were collected electronically using a structured questionnaire titled E-banking, Cashless Policy and Commercial Banks Business Education Graduates Questionnaire (ECCBBEDQ). The instrument was validated by experts in Business Education and Research methodology, with a validity index of 0.78, while its reliability coefficient was 0.87 using Cronbach’s alpha. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics and multiple regression analysis. The findings revealed a significant joint influence of e-banking and cashless policy on customer satisfaction (R = 0.949, R² = 0.901, F(6, 1694) = 2563.608, p < .05). The results further showed that all six dimensions significantly influenced customer satisfaction, with cashless policy accessibility exerting the strongest positive influence, while e-banking personal alignment and usability had significant negative influences. The study concluded that accessible, secure, reliable, and user-friendly digital banking services are essential for improving customer satisfaction. It was recommended that commercial banks should strengthen digital infrastructure, cybersecurity, customer education, and technical support.

records.title: TITLE AUTONOMOUS SELF-REPAIRING ROBOTIC SWARMS AT THE LIMIT SUBTITLE Distributed Intelligence, Causal Fault Diagnosis, Reversible Repair, and Independent Requalification AUTHOR Feng Cheng-en (33) x STARLI Research Institute XXVII ENGLISH PUBLICATION DESCRIPTION What would count as genuine repair in a robot swarm? Mission continuation is not enough. A swarm may route around a damaged agent, reduce an unannounced requirement, sacrifice unmeasured capability, or transfer risk to its neighbors while appearing successful. Autonomous Self-Repairing Robotic Swarms at the Limit develops a falsifiable research architecture for distributed fault detection, causal diagnosis, risk isolation, reversible intervention, task redistribution, physical and morphological repair, and independent post-repair requalification. The central claim is deliberately bounded: when fault genealogy, capability envelopes, uncertainty-aware local evidence, reversible action, and independent qualification operate together, local repair should improve functional recovery without increasing latent failure. The monograph contains thirty linked research equations, eighty-two chapters with five substantial research sections each, and two hundred detailed Research Gates. Every gate specifies a question, registered hypothesis, minimum experiment, observables, strong baseline, falsifier, stopping rule, successor evidence package, and DOI anchors. The single-section / single-page architecture makes each research unit independently addressable and suitable for future human and AI reconstruction. The book separates repair from redundancy, rerouting, graceful degradation, replacement, and self-certification. It examines gradual and abrupt faults, common-cause failure, partial observability, calibration drift, network partition, Byzantine behavior, docking and connector fatigue, repair-induced damage, predictive maintenance, residual-life estimation, blind fault injection, withheld missions, human override, cybersecurity, vendor independence, retirement, and cross-generational handoff. Evidence is anchored in modular reconfigurable robotics, swarm fault diagnosis, self-healing collectives, resilient coordination, distributed metrology, and safe swarm design. The equations are transparent design heuristics rather than universal physical laws, and the integrated system remains a research hypothesis. Unknown states must trigger abstention; the repairer cannot be the sole verifier; moving thresholds invalidate success; irreversible harm and failed override are hard stops. This volume is written for robotics researchers, systems engineers, safety and verification specialists, autonomous-systems designers, AI researchers, and future successors who need not merely a vision of self-healing machines, but a testable path for deciding when a swarm has truly restored function - and when it must stop. records.title: EU Security Challenges in the Context of the Russia - Ukraine War
records.authors: Miranda Mikadze; Gela Giorgadze
records.abstract: The Russia–Ukraine war has significantly transformed the European security environment and exposed the systemic challenges facing the European security architecture. The conflict has demonstrated that the post-Cold War European security model, largely based on the principles of international law, economic interdependence, and cooperative security, has proven insufficient to address emerging security threats. The aim of this study is to analyze the impact of the Russia–Ukraine war on the transformation of the European Union's foreign and security policy and to identify the key factors shaping the EU's capabilities and limitations as a security actor. The study is based on a qualitative research design and employs a combination of document analysis, comparative analysis, and historical-analytical methods. The research examines official European Union documents, strategic policy papers, reports of international organizations, and contemporary academic literature. The theoretical framework draws upon Neorealism, Liberal Institutionalism, and Constructivism, enabling an assessment of the influence of the balance of power, institutional capacities, and normative factors on the development of the European Union's security policy. The findings demonstrate that the Russia–Ukraine war has significantly accelerated the transformation of the EU's security policy and reinforced the importance of defence capabilities, strategic autonomy, and energy security. The European Union has gradually shifted from a policy primarily based on economic and diplomatic instruments toward a more comprehensive security approach encompassing military, cyber, hybrid, energy, and information security challenges. The research concludes that the European Union is at a historic turning point, facing the choice between maintaining its traditional role as primarily an economic and political union or evolving into a fully-fledged security actor. The Russia–Ukraine war has reaffirmed the importance of collective defence and highlighted the necessity of further strengthening the European Union's security policy to ensure long-term European stability and resilience.

records.title: AN ASSESSMENT OF THE 1961 VIENNA CONVENTION ON DIPLOMATIC RELATIONS AS A LEGAL FRAMEWORK FOR DIGITAL DIPLOMACY AND ITS CONSEQUENCES FOR GLOBAL DIPLOMATIC STABILITY
records.authors: Desmond O.N. Agwor; Raphael Bappaluk Tokma
records.abstract: For over six decades, the 1961 Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations (VCDR) has endured as the indispensable juridical bedrock of interstate intercourse, codifying with remarkable durability the immunities, privileges, and functional prerogatives upon which the entire edifice of modern statecraft repose. Yet this venerable instrument, conceived within a pre-digital epistemology of physical presence and paper-based correspondence, now confronts an unprecedented normative crisis occasioned by the ascendancy of information and communication technologies it was never conceived to accommodate. This article undertakes a rigorous doctrinal assessment of the VCDR's continued efficacy as the legal cornerstone of statecraft, illuminating the significant "legal vacuum" that digital technologies have precipitated within the architecture of diplomatic law. Employing a critical analytical methodology, the study interrogates how digital diplomacy and e-diplomacy have reconfigured the modalities of interstate communication through virtual platforms, engendering negotiation processes that are simultaneously more inclusive and yet impoverished by the absence of non-verbal cues indispensable to high-stakes discourse. The inquiry further scrutinises the contested legal status of virtual embassies, which unsettle the territorial premises upon which the Convention's definitional architecture rests and complicate, in equal measure, the identification of a cognisable "receiving state". In this connection, the article advances a case for a "transformative interpretation" of Article 22, urging that the principle of inviolability be extended to a mission's official digital infrastructure, inclusive of websites and social media assets, as a digital extension of physical premises. The research also probes, with particular attention to doctrinal nuance, the complexities attending diplomatic immunity in relation to cybercrimes, alongside the formidable evidentiary and technical hurdles that beset the legal attribution of state-sponsored cyberattacks. It evaluates, moreover, the transformative implications of Artificial Intelligence and regional regulatory frameworks, notably the European Union's AI Act, for the evolution of global standards of ethical state conduct, while drawing upon the national blueprints of Estonia and Romania as instructive paradigms for the integration of technological expertise into diplomatic institutional structures. Arising from this comprehensive analysis of the hurdles attending the attribution of state-sponsored cyber espionage and the farreaching implications of Artificial Intelligence for global diplomatic standards, the paper proffers six critical recommendations calculated to secure long-term global diplomatic stability within an increasingly borderless digital order.

records.title: Digital Communication Disruption and Changing Social Relations in Global Media
records.authors: Hermansyah Hermansyah; Mochammad Kresna Noer
records.abstract: This study aimed to synthesize existing literature on how digital communication disruption has transformed media practices, social relationships, identity formation, and public participation in an increasingly globalized environment. A qualitative narrative literature review was conducted using scholarly books, journal articles, and other relevant secondary sources cited in the manuscript. The review examined and compared theoretical and empirical perspectives from digital sociology, networked communication, digital platform labor, online communities, and the broader social implications of digital technologies. The reviewed literature highlighted the expansion of communication across geographic boundaries, increased opportunities for collective participation and identity formation, and transformations in information production and dissemination. However, persistent challenges were also identified, including inequalities in digital access, privacy concerns, misinformation, algorithmically mediated labor, and uncompensated user contributions to commercial digital platforms. The findings further indicated that the social consequences of digital disruption were not uniform but varied according to technological accessibility, platform design, institutional structures, and individual circumstances. Digital communication disruption was understood as a dynamic, reciprocal relationship between technological infrastructures and evolving social practices rather than merely a consequence of technological advancement. The synthesis emphasized the importance of digital literacy, ethical platform governance, equitable technological access, and more rigorous empirical research to address emerging social challenges. As a narrative literature review, the study did not generate original survey data or establish causal relationships, and its conclusions should therefore be interpreted as a synthesis of existing scholarship rather than definitive empirical evidence.

records.title: Resilience of standalone microgrids: indicators, enhancement strategies, and challenges—an integrative review
records.authors: Nafisul Musfiq; Bharath Kumar Sugumar; Jonathan Ntiaka Muzakwene; Bruno Estibals; Norma Anglani
records.abstract: Microgrids have emerged as a promising solution for improving energy access, enhancing local energy independence, and strengthening resilience against environmental, technical, and operational disturbances. Resilience refers to the ability of a system to withstand, adapt to, and recover from disruptive events while maintaining reliable operation. Unlike grid-connected systems, standalone or islanded microgrids must operate autonomously during disturbances, making resilience a critical design and operational consideration. This paper presents an integrative review of the state-of-the-art (SOTA) strategies, indicators, and challenges associated with enhancing the resilience of standalone microgrids. Following a PRISMA-guided review methodology, the study synthesizes 60 primary studies published between 2014 and 2025, supported by 28 contextual references. Coding of the primary studies shows that 95% rely on simulation or analytical modeling, with only three reporting experimental or hardware-in-the-loop validation, which remains the principal limitation of the current evidence base. The discussion is categorized into four major areas: design and planning, control strategies, energy management, and protection systems. In addition, the review examines resilience assessment metrics and emerging cyber-physical resilience approaches for modern standalone microgrids. The paper further identifies major technical, economic, environmental, and regulatory challenges affecting the operation of resilient microgrids, including protection coordination, renewable intermittency, communication dependence, cybersecurity risks, economic limitations, and vulnerability to extreme weather events. Various resilience enhancement approaches—distributed energy resource diversification, adaptive reconfiguration, hierarchical control, predictive energy management, and the interconnection of neighboring standalone microgrids—are critically analyzed to provide a broader understanding of resilient standalone microgrid development. Finally, the review highlights important research gaps and future directions, including the need for standardized resilience metrics, integrated cyber-physical security frameworks, climate-adaptive planning models, and practical implementation strategies. Although significant progress has been achieved in microgrid modeling, control, and optimization, considerable challenges remain in bridging theoretical research with large-scale real-world deployment of resilient standalone microgrids.

records.title: Ambient Journalism after Twitter
records.authors: Alfred Hermida
records.abstract: The concept of ambient journalism emerged to describe how digital platforms, particularly Twitter, enabled wide and incidental news consumption. I defined it as a broad, asynchronous, lightweight, and always-on communication system that enabled citizens to maintain a “mental model” of news, with Twitter highlighted as a leading example (Hermida, Twittering the News 297). However, the last decade has seen significant changes in the digital media environment. Twitter, now rebranded as X, has significantly declined in importance as a platform for journalists, politicians, celebrities, and the public. In this article, I revisit the theoretical foundations of ambient journalism. It examines how the concept and its connection to Twitter have evolved since 2010, reflecting the rise and fall of platforms, the increase in algorithmic curation, and the fragmentation of public attention. The decline of Twitter as a central hub for journalistic activity, competition from alternative platforms, the spread of mis- and disinformation, and the role of artificial intelligence in news curation have all contributed to a more complex ambient news environment. This development has shifted ambient journalism from a focus on collective intelligence toward an algorithmically driven stream that privileges affective resonance over narrative continuity, often leading to atomised rather than shared mental models. Looking ahead, the rise and rapid diffusion of generative AI raise questions about whether there is now an epistemological turn toward synthetic ambience. Synthetic ambience describes a phenomenon where human-like AI bots and generative AI summaries reshape how information flows. I analyse these changes, arguing that the move to algorithmic and synthetic ambience requires a critical rethinking of how news is experienced, understood, and verified in a post-Twitter world. The Roots of Ambient Journalism With the emergence and growth of social media platforms in the early 2000s, it became common for the public to share, document, and discuss news, experiences, and opinions. Twitter’s architecture was ideal for news, with its reverse-chronological format, immediacy, follower structure, and the ability to connect diverse messages through hashtags (Burgess and Baym 33). The platform thrived on expectations of sharing and public engagement, as shown in retweets, replies, and direct messages. Reports of major events like plane crashes and earthquakes often first appeared on Twitter, frequently from people involved, with the platform acting as “a nervous system for the planet” (Hermida, Tell Everyone 134). Drawing on the concept of awareness systems from ubiquitous computing, I defined ambient journalism as “an awareness system that offers diverse means to collect, communicate, share and display news and information, serving diverse purposes” (Hermida 301). The concept was developed in the context of Twitter as a media environment characterised by immediacy, serendipity, and the blending of professional and citizen journalism (Goode 1288). The original ambient journalism framework marked a departure from traditional, intentional consumption, like reading a newspaper or watching a TV news bulletin. The main features of ambient journalism were immediacy, unexpected discoveries, and the blending of professional and citizen journalism enabled by Twitter. Its architecture, with a reverse-chronological feed, a 140-character limit, and a social graph-based network structure, supported what Axel Bruns called produsage, where publics act as both users and producers of information. In this ambient environment, retweeting was not just an engagement metric but a curatorial act of journalism. This reflects a broader shift in digital journalism research toward the news ecosystem and landscape, including ambient and networked forms of journalism emerging from social media practices (Steensen and Ahva 1). The ambient news landscape has changed as platforms have developed. Algorithm-driven feeds, misinformation, and alternative sites have made the environment more fragmented and unpredictable. Where Twitter once served as a key, real-time hub during breaking news, from natural disasters to elections, now no single platform fully serves that connecting role. Newsrooms that previously relied on Twitter as an informal wire service now need to monitor multiple platforms, each with its own algorithms and norms. For audiences, losing a shared ambient space means that breaking news no longer appears through a common stream but arrives unevenly, reaching different groups at different times. This results in a more scattered, algorithmically curated mosaic that challenges the idea of ambient journalism and calls for a rethinking and redefining of the term. Networked Publics, Uneven Power The concept of a pervasive, participatory news ecosystem enabled by digital platforms, particularly Twitter, was based on users acting as both producers and consumers of news and information. Driven by the socio-technical structures of social networking sites, users formed networked publics where news was co-created and shared (boyd). Scholars have examined Twitter as a public space for networked publics during events like natural disasters, protests, or political instability, from the Arab Spring to the Occupy movement. The activist movements of the early 2010s exemplified the participatory and collective nature of ambient journalism, with Twitter serving as the link that allowed like-minded individuals to connect, communicate, and organise (Hermida, Tell Everyone 187; Papacharissi 52). Over the past decade, research has questioned the participatory concept of ambient journalism. Scholars have challenged the idea of Twitter as a mirror of public opinion (Mellon and Prosser 6; Mitchell and Hitlin par. 13), even though journalists frequently used tweets as a measure of the vox populi (Beckers and Harder 910). They viewed it as a helpful tool for newsgathering (McGregor and Molyneux 607) or to showcase ordinary people’s opinions (Tworek par. 1). While Twitter promoted an ambient awareness system, ambient journalism overlooked the power disparities between those who are seen and heard on specific issues at certain times (Hermida, Tell Everyone 101). Twitter was never a town square representing all voices. Only a minority of citizens used it, and only a minority of those users were highly active (Leetaru et al. par. 7). Accounts managed by journalists, politicians, celebrities, and bloggers were overrepresented among heavy users and dominated attention, giving them outsized influence on the network. A study on COVID-19 news sharing shows that 14 percent drove most circulation, and these creators accounted for 82 percent of false content in the dataset (Castioni et al. 1). The presence of a small group of active and influential users explains how Twitter became a key arena for highlighting important topics and political signals, even if it did not reflect the views of the broader public (Robertson). This concentration created a steady stream of signals such as retweets, replies, and metrics that spread widely beyond the core participants. Ambient journalism explains why Twitter changed how publics matter. Although the wider effects on the public sphere remain debated, this ambient environment provided a platform for networked publics to influence which stories are told and how, especially for place-based news events (Barnard 14; Bruns and Highfield 332). Taken together, these dynamics demonstrate how ambient journalism affected newsroom judgment in real time by making audience signals more immediate and difficult to ignore, without displacing editorial authority. Shifts in Platform Infrastructure Since 2010, the technological infrastructure underpinning ambient journalism has undergone a radical shift. My original conceptualisation was tethered to the affordances of early Twitter. The contemporary social media landscape, including Twitter, is defined by an algorithmic turn. In March 2016, the platform moved to algorithmic curation based on the presumed interests, preferences, and tastes of users, unless people chose to opt out. This shift transformed the ambient experience from a social utility that helps people keep up with friends and news into a relevance engine optimising passive watch time. For ambient journalism, it represented a significant shift. The ambient news in a feed became less about reflecting the priorities of a user’s connections and more about mirroring their individual habits and cues. While algorithms can help surface engaging content, they can also prioritise sensational or polarising stories over those that serve the public interest (Dujeancourt and Garz 264). The lack of transparency around algorithms exacerbates these issues, as people are often unaware of the biases and incentives shaping their news feeds. They amplify some tweets while reducing the visibility of others, playing a crucial yet hidden role in gatekeeping on Twitter (Huszár et al. 1). The mental model of news and events shifts from being based on the collective intelligence of the network (Malone et al. 2) to the social power of algorithms (Beer 1). Elon Musk’s acquisition of Twitter in 2022 and its rebranding as X in 2023 marked a turning point for ambient journalism, as the billionaire reshaped the socio-technical infrastructures underpinning the platform. He sought to reinvent it as a versatile utility, shifting from its original event-based microblogging to accommodate long-form posts and extended videos. Verification, once a symbol of trust for public figures and journalists, shifted to a subscription model based on payment rather than prominence. Musk has used the rhetoric of free speech to justify dismantling trust-and-safety teams and reinstating previously banned extremist and deceptive accounts. His portrayal as a free speech absolutist is mostly self-promotional branding rather than a consistent principle. In practice, his leadership of X has been characterised by selective enforcement, indicating that his priority is to control narratives rather than to foster open dialogue (See). These structural changes triggered cascading effects on the ambient journalism environment. The dismantling of trust-and-safety infrastructure, along with X’s withdrawal from third-party content-monitoring partnerships, undermined confidence in the platform. A more permissive moderation policy has encouraged a cultural acceptance of extreme and violent rhetoric, further degrading the quality of ambient news streams (de Keulenaar et al.). Many left-leaning academics, journalists, and news organisations reduced their presence on X or moved to alternatives like Bluesky and Mastodon (Ng and Ray 1), hollowing out the very network of professional and civic voices that supported ambient journalism on the platform. The overall result was a more unpredictable, volatile, and untrustworthy news and information environment. Collectively, Musk’s actions tore down Twitter as a place where weak ties formed the connective tissue of public conversation and, more broadly, led to “the waning of ideals in relation to the communicative potentials of the open web more generally” (Tkacz and Gehl 1). Fragmentation, Fatigue, and Fabrication The original framework for ambient journalism proposed that ubiquitous information flows would help citizens develop a mental model of public affairs through peripheral awareness of news content. Twitter was one of many ambient systems that created conditions for incidental exposure to news, with people encountering news passively rather than intentionally seeking it out (Schäfer 242). Ambient journalism predicted that news consumption would become ubiquitous, fragmented, and incidental, but it overestimated how much this peripheral exposure would help build knowledge. Instead, a decade of research shows that for many people, constant connectivity leads to less coherent understanding, increased cognitive fragmentation, and psychological stress (Bawden and Robinson par. 3). Since 2010, the relentless flow of updates has intensified, with a proliferation of platforms, smartphones, and push services, let alone major news events from Brexit to COVID-19 to Trump’s elections. Ambient infrastructures have become too successful, leading to a reaction against the very awareness systems I described. When the flow becomes too much, people have sought to limit exposure, actively avoiding updates and further coverage. While news avoidance is a complex and multilayered phenomenon (Andersen et al. 1367), it is partly driven by feelings of news overload, fatigue, and paralysis (Newman et al. 35). Ambient journalism does not create mental models of news but instead increases the cognitive load on audiences. For many, the sheer volume of news feels overwhelming and harmful to their well-being, with the constant focus of newsrooms on conflict and crisis leading to emotional exhaustion (Toff et al. 3). At the same time, the fragmentation of the social media landscape and the splintering of audiences across different platforms with unique algorithmic logics, content norms, and user demographics mean that ambient journalism can no longer be understood through just one platform. Platforms like TikTok, Instagram, Bluesky, and LinkedIn influence much of the casual news consumption, each offering different features that impact how news is presented, encountered, and interpreted. TikTok’s short videos and Instagram’s visual, story-driven format create experiences that are different from the text-based and conversational style of Twitter. The design logics of TikTok and Instagram have altered how people encounter and make sense of news. TikTok centres an algorithmically driven For You stream that learns from viewing behavior and surfaces clips that fit personal interests. This creates an incidental and episodic flow driven by affect and momentary relevance more than by ongoing narratives or social ties. Similarly, Instagram Stories pull content into a visual, short-lived format, creating a highly visual, ephemeral environment. In a high-choice and fragmented media landscape, the lightweight, always-on nature of ambient journalism can hinder rather than help understanding. These pressures intensify during crises. While mis- and disinformation are far from novel, the networked, digital media environment has amplified the scale, speed, and reach of false information (Waisbord 1866). Ambient news streams have become polluted with a chaotic mix of mis- and disinformation, rumors, hate, and emotional outbursts, making it hard to distinguish between credibility and noise. These trends have accelerated since Musk took control of Twitter, increasing the reach of toxic content. While it was once “widely lambasted as a cesspool of vanity and triviality” (Puschmann et al. 425), it is now condemned as a “sewer” polluted by disinformation, harassment, and hate (Hammond-Errey). The shift from cesspool to sewer marks a notable escalation. Early criticisms focussed on the platform’s obsession with triviality, self-promotion, and banality. Now the criticism emphasises a space where disinformation, coordinated harassment, and hate speech not only coexist with news but actively pollute it. The shift to algorithmic curation favours sensational and polarising content over credible reporting (Dujeancourt and Garz 264), while X has lost the institutional checks that once helped moderate the platform’s most extreme issues. The pay-for-verification model has removed the heuristics that helped users distinguish reliable sources from unreliable ones. The result is a fundamentally changed incentive system where news pollution is financially rewarded, algorithmically amplified, and institutionally unchecked (Hermida et al. par. 1). This weakens trust, spurs inaction and news fatigue, and contributes to polarised views (Hasell and Halversen 1448; Tandoc and Kim 1187). Discussion The core of ambient journalism, that news and information would shift from a discrete product to a pervasive environment, has largely occurred as people encounter these through networked, asynchronous, and always-on communication infrastructures. The background flow of updates from various sources, not solely journalists, has become the primary information environment for many, particularly those under 34 years old (Newman et al. 12). For these audiences, news is less an appointment and more an atmosphere. No single item constitutes the whole story. Instead, people encounter continuously updated slivers of information. The evolution of the media environment and news habits highlights the limitations of the initial, more optimistic framing of ambient journalism. Fragmented attention, mis- or disinformation, and news fatigue have undermined the value of peripheral awareness for audiences. What was once considered a tool for collective intelligence now poses risks of anxiety, fragmentation, and news avoidance. The widespread use of algorithmic curation has reshaped ambient flows, prioritising attention over informing the public. The importance of Twitter has diminished with the rise and growing use of competing platforms like Instagram, TikTok, and AI-powered aggregators. Musk’s purchase and the era of X have increased uncertainty about how news is surfaced and consumed, creating a more unpredictable environment where visibility can surpass verification. As many journalists and news organisations reduce their use of X (Ng and Ray 1), its role as a place for ambient awareness, especially during breaking news, becomes more contested and less central than it was in the 2010s. It is even questionable whether X remains a platform for ambient journalism. Algorithmic curation on X now actively de-prioritises quality journalism in favour of content that maximises engagement, while the platform’s financial incentive structure rewards the most attention-grabbing posts regardless of their veracity or public value (Dujeancourt and Garz 264). The dismantling of trust-and-safety infrastructure, the shift to pay-for-verification, and the reinstatement of previously banned accounts have collectively undermined the good-faith assumptions on which ambient journalism relied. In these conditions, what persists on X may be better understood as ambient information noise rather than ambient journalism. In a sense, the epistemological foundations that justified the term journalism have been so thoroughly compromised that the label risks lending unwarranted legitimacy to a deeply polluted environment. X still generates ambient awareness, but whether that awareness constitutes a form of journalism, even in the loose, peripheral sense originally intended, is highly questionable. Ambient journalism has, then, outgrown Twitter, prompting a re-evaluation of the concept to address the complex, algorithmically mediated, and uneven ways in which news is encountered and understood, incorporating affective resonance (Mühlhoff 1001). To account for the socio-technical and cultural changes since 2010, ambient journalism can now be defined as incidentally consumed, algorithmically guided streams of episodic news and information fragments that privilege affective resonance over narrative continuity, fostering atomised rather than collective mental models of public events. This definition recognises an epistemological shift in the infrastructures of news and information. It captures the shift from receiving news and information in fixed editions from authoritative sources to a persistent, pervasive flow of snippets from numerous voices. Outlook Recent and ongoing socio-technical advances in artificial intelligence could ultimately challenge the very concept of ambient news. Here, I introduce the term synthetic ambience, which describes a phenomenon where the ambient news environment is increasingly shaped by AI-generated content that mimics the look and rhythms of human journalism, rather than by human journalists or networked publics. AI-generated signals imitate, compress, and ultimately replace the organic flows that ambient journalism once relied on. Synthetic ambience suggests an epistemological turn, signaling a move from social ambience, rooted in networked publics, to algorithmic ambience, driven by platform curation. What distinguishes synthetic ambience from its earlier concept is the dual processes of fabrication and compression. AI-created bots and automated accounts flood information streams with fake social proof and emotional signals that shape perception. AI-produced summaries and chatbot responses shorten the diverse, multi-source signals that formed ambient journalism into a single, pre-processed synthesis, bypassing traditional human sense-making. Fabrication pollutes the system’s inputs, the signals, while compression interferes with the outputs, the cognitive processes citizens use to piece together meaning from fragments. Together, they reshape an information landscape that maintains the constant, all-pervasive nature of ambient journalism while removing its epistemic core. As a concept, synthetic ambience lies at the crossroads of journalism studies, platform studies, AI ethics, and the epistemology of information. It addresses growing concerns about how generative AI not only transforms content creation but also the very infrastructure of public knowledge, effectively creating ambient layers through which publics develop impressions of the world. The fabrication mechanism is already here. While bots have always been present on Twitter (Carlon et al.), advances in generative AI suggest that platforms like X can expect to be flooded by AI bots that are nearly indistinguishable from real accounts (Yang and Menczer 20). Where earlier forms of astroturfing and coordinated inauthentic behaviour were labour-intensive and easier to detect, generative AI now enables the mass creation of synthetic voices that imitate the tone, cadence, and emotional range of genuine users in ways that are procedurally indistinguishable from organic activity. AI bots on X and other platforms turn ambient journalism into synthetic ambience by polluting streams with a large volume of posts. Emotional triggers and synthetic social proof can create the illusion of consensus or outrage on a much larger scale than previous attempts to influence public opinion. Synthetic ambience risks overshadowing verified reporting through intentional news pollution, diverting attention and mimicking emotion at scale. The result is a reduction in viewpoint diversity and erosion of trust, benefiting those with the resources to use AI extensively for these purposes. The compression mechanism operates through a different but complementary logic. Since Google introduced AI-generated summaries in 2025, such rundowns have become one of the most common ways to interact with generative AI (Simon 57). The immediacy, convenience, and perceived veracity of the summaries are most appealing to audiences (36). Algorithmic compression, through AI-generated summaries or responses from AI chatbots like ChatGPT and Perplexity, collapses the diverse, multi-source signals that make up ambient journalism into a single, synthesised answer, shaped by the AI model’s weighting. Audiences receive a ready-made interpretation influenced by a model, rather than encountering multiple voices and gradually forming their own understanding. Algorithmic compression both models and usurps human editorial authority. AI summaries and chatbot answers offer a pre-assembled model, effectively ending the ambient journalism cycle by taking over the cognitive labour of synthesis and producing a processed sense of events. The risk is not just homogenisation but also epistemic displacement, where publics never experience the diversity of reporting, sourcing, and perspectives that once defined the ambient news environment. This makes it harder to spot gaps, contradictions, or contested claims within the information landscape. Future research could explore whether there is now an epistemological shift toward synthetic ambience. Conceptually, future work should examine whether synthetic ambience operates differently across platforms and cultural contexts, and whether its dual mechanisms of fabrication and compression produce distinct or compounding effects on public knowledge formation. As ambient journalism continues to outgrow the platform that nurtured it, there remains a need to understand how people learn and interpret news within systems shaped by networks, algorithms, and generative AI. The rise of AI-powered synthetic ambience points to an information environment that is persistent, pervasive, and increasingly processed by machine models rather than human minds. If the ambient journalism of the 2010s described how citizens understood the world through the peripheral hum of networked voices, synthetic ambience suggests an emerging situation where that hum is increasingly generated, curated, and condensed by machines, raising questions about what it means to be informed in an age of artificial intelligence. This editorial outlines the journal’s vision to serve as a global platform for theoretical, empirical, experimental, and applied research across diverse domains, including artificial intelligence, machine learning, big data analytics, cybersecurity, blockchain technologies, Internet of Things, robotics, smart manufacturing, and sustainable technologies. TRR emphasizes methodological rigor, originality, and real-world applicability while promoting cross-disciplinary integration among engineering, computer science, data science, and innovation studies. The journal also highlights emerging frontiers such as quantum computing, digital twins, advanced materials, and AI governance, while critically engaging with ethical, regulatory, and societal implications of technological advancement. By fostering research that bridges scientific discovery and practical implementation, TRR aims to contribute to sustainable, inclusive, and responsible technological progress globally. records.title: AI, Geopolitics, and National Security (Chapter 8)
records.authors: Sarah Kreps; Michael Horowitz; Ben Buchanan; Erica Lonergan
records.abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping geopolitics by transforming how states generate, interpret, and project power. Rather than producing a single new weapon, AI operates as a general-purpose technology that scales perception, prediction, and decision-making across military, civilian, and informational domains. This chapter argues that AI rivalry increasingly depends on control over material and organizational foundations, including semiconductors, compute infrastructure, data centers, industrial coordination, and institutional adoption. It examines battlefield integration, U.S.–China competition, semiconductor statecraft, cyber operations, information power, and governance. The chapter shows that AI capabilities diffuse rapidly through commercial platforms, open-source ecosystems, and wartime experimentation, while frontier development remains constrained by infrastructure and supply-chain chokepoints. Because AI capability is difficult to measure or verify, governance is shifting away from traditional arms-control models toward export controls, standards, voluntary commitments, and multistakeholder coordination.

records.title: OSINT Report on Current Vulnerabilities in Indonesia
records.authors: WEI MENG
records.abstract: This report provides an open-source intelligence assessment of Indonesia’s principal national vulnerabilities as of May 17, 2026. The overall judgment is that Indonesia is not on the edge of systemic collapse. Macroeconomic growth, inflation, and reserve buffers continue to provide a measure of resilience. Its most dangerous vulnerabilities, however, do not sit in a single economic indicator. They lie in the coupled amplification among policy credibility, fiscal space, energy-import pressure, capital-market transparency, social protest, disaster exposure, cyber governance, and resource policy. If a Middle East energy shock, rating or index pressure, implementation failures in large social programs such as free meals, local protests, or major disasters emerge at the same time, Indonesia could move from a zone of manageable pressure into a zone of compound stress. The report divides the vulnerabilities into 10 categories and reviews them through evidence layering, an impact-probability matrix, trigger monitoring, alternative explanations, and scenario analysis. The core conclusion is that over the next 0-18 months, the main issue to monitor is not any isolated event but a chain of events linking declining fiscal credibility, rising foreign-investor risk premiums, expanding energy subsidies, defects in social-policy implementation, and disaster-related emergency fiscal burdens.

Advances in multimodal AI systems—capable of integrating text, images, audio, and video—have become essential for achieving more comprehensive and context-aware intelligence, especially in domains such as medical imaging and interactive systems. records.title: MRP-LLM: Multitask Reflective Large Language Models for Privacy-Preserving Next POI Recommendation
records.authors: Ziqing Wu; Zhu Sun; Dongxia Wang; Lu Zhang; Jie Zhang; Yew Soon Ong
records.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promising potential for next Point-of-Interest (POI) recommendation. However, existing methods only perform direct zero-shot prompting, leading to ineffective extraction of user preferences, insufficient injection of collaborative signals, and a lack of user privacy protection. As such, we propose a novel Multitask Reflective Large Language Model for Privacy-preserving Next POI Recommendation (MRP-LLM), aiming to exploit LLMs for better next POI recommendation while preserving user privacy. Specifically, the Multitask Reflective Preference Extraction Module first utilizes LLMs to distill each user's fine-grained (i.e., categorical, temporal, and spatial) preferences into a knowledge base (KB). The Neighbor Preference Retrieval Module retrieves and summarizes the preferences of similar users from the KB to obtain collaborative signals. Subsequently, aggregating the user's preferences with those of similar users, the Multitask Next POI Recommendation Module generates the next POI recommendations via multitask prompting. Meanwhile, during data collection, a Privacy Transmission Module is specifically devised to preserve sensitive POI data. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed MRP-LLM in providing more accurate next POI recommendations with user privacy preserved.

records.title: Ingress phase
records.authors: Michael McDonagh; Charles Swanson
records.abstract: The ingress phase of any global event encompasses the journey from attendee arrival to venue entry, and I believe it is far more than a security process; it is a critical determinant of an event‘s safety, operational efficiency and enduring reputation. In support of the other chapters, I want to explore the multifaceted strategic considerations essential for mastering ingress, defining it as an introductory element that helps shape the attendee experience from the ‘ formal’ outset. We now need consider the core components of effective ingress management, including meticulous strategic planning and dynamic capacity calculation, advanced crowd and queue management techniques and comprehensive security and access control measures. The indispensable human element, encompassing staffing awareness, training and proactive communication, is highlighted as crucial for influencing crowd behaviour and ensuring compliance. records.title: Principles for navigating responsible use of AI for conservation
records.authors: Sam Reynolds; Nabilla N. Kaunain; Lauren Coad; Catie Johnston; Isaac Rutenberg; Zuliehat O. Abdullahi; Hani R. El Bizri; Michelle Kenyon; Neema C. Mtenga; Emanuely Silva; Romaric P. Tegang; Carolina S. Ugarte; Amy Hinsley; Chris Sandbrook
records.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is being widely adopted across conservation tasks, such as species identification, habitat mapping and threat detection. However, its adoption has rapidly outpaced governance and ethical guidance for its responsible integration into conservation research and practice. AI raises ethical, social and environmental challenges distinct from those associated more broadly with the integration of conservation technology (e.g., camera traps, drones, audio monitoring systems). These challenges include the environmental footprint of AI infrastructure, the difficulty of tracing or removing data from trained models, opaque decision-making and the uneven distribution of risks and benefits. AI systems are frequently presented as neutral and objective technologies; however, unlike other technological tools, they embed ethical and political assumptions, with little oversight of whose values or interests are reflected in their design. Building on Sandbrook et al.’s (2021) framework for socially responsible integration of surveillance technologies in conservation, we propose seven principles for the responsible use of AI in conservation research and practice: recognising social impacts; deploying AI according to necessity and proportionality; evaluating impacts on people; seeking meaningful consent; ensuring transparency and accountability; respecting rights and vulnerabilities; and protecting privacy, data sovereignty and intellectual property. We interpret the term AI broadly, to encompass both task-specific machine learning models and general-purpose generative AI such as large language models, which raise overlapping but distinct ethical concerns. We translate these seven principles into a set of guiding questions for practitioners, funders and NGOs.

records.title: Digital Communities
records.authors: Fabienne Cadet; François Sainfort; Julie A. Jacko
records.abstract: Digital communities, or online/virtual communities, are deeply embedded in modern society, emerging with Web 2.0 and social media in the mid-2000s. They are virtual platforms where individuals interact, share experiences, and engage in common interests, maintaining relationships through computer-mediated communication (CMC) technologies. These communities significantly influence communication and relationship-building and, with the advances in artificial intelligence (AI), are continuously transforming not only the way we interact with digital content, but also the world around us. This chapter discusses the evolution of CMC and Web Technologies from Web 1.0 to the conceptual Web 4.0 – intelligent web with advanced AI and human–machine collaboration – and critically reviews the Deep Web, mobile apps, social networking, wikis, and the social cloud. Technological advances continue to foster digital communities by providing accessibility and real-time interaction. However, while digital communities offer benefits like enhanced social connections and support, they also present challenges. These include accessibility issues to special and vulnerable populations, the “dark side” of online communication, such as cyberbullying and the proliferation of negative views, and unresolved concerns about privacy and data security. The future will involve continued advancements in AI and extended realities, requiring careful consideration of ethical governance and inclusive design.
